selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2. What this tests: config_001 is the simplest RNA-only single-profile model, using PCA (2000 components) with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference point. Later runs can change one factor at a time against it: the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), the profile setting and aggregation (avgpool, transformer), and adding images with fusion (concat, weighted). 3. Why now: With a limited budget, a cheap and interpretable baseline is the best first step. It shows whether added complexity actually helps, rather than assuming multimodal or multiprofile models win, and it makes each later single-factor comparison informative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder (2000 components), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.536 and a supporting validation F1 of 0.516. The two metrics are close, which loosely suggests performance is not heavily skewed across classes, but this is only an initial observation. No other experiments have been run, so it is unknown whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, or image fusion would improve on this, and the result should serve as the reference point for later single-factor comparisons rather than as evidence about which design choices matter.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, an RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.536, F1 0.516). Nothing yet tells us which design factor matters most. 2) Test: config_002 changes one factor. It keeps RNA-only and PCA fixed and switches from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles per sample improves accuracy and F1 over the baseline. 3) Why now: profile setting is a structural choice that applies across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal models. Answering it early tells us whether most of the remaining configurations, which are multiprofile, are worth prioritizing. Using avgpool rather than the transformer avoids mixing the profile effect with aggregation complexity. A single-factor RNA-encoder swap (config_004) would also be informative, but resolving the profile question first prunes the search space more.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the llm_summary_001 baseline fixed (RNA-only, PCA encoder with 2000 components, no image encoder or fusion) and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with simple average pooling. Validation accuracy rose from 0.536 to 0.688 (+0.152), and supporting validation F1 rose from 0.516 to 0.659 (+0.143). Because only the profile setting and its required aggregation changed, this is reasonably direct evidence that multiprofile input with avgpool helps the RNA-only PCA model, which makes multiprofile configurations a promising direction. However, the effect comes from a single run with no variance estimate, profile setting and avgpool cannot be separated, and it is unknown whether the gain carries over to other RNA encoders, image-only or multimodal models, or more complex aggregators such as a transformer.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Moving the RNA-only PCA model from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised validation accuracy from 0.536 to 0.688, and F1 rose by a similar amount (0.516 to 0.659). This is the strongest signal so far. However, it comes from one run, and the multiprofile effect cannot yet be separated from the choice of avgpool as the aggregator. 2) Test: config_003 keeps the best configuration fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n2000) and changes only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. This shows whether learned aggregation adds anything beyond simple pooling, or whether avgpool is enough. 3) Why now: It extends the most promising direction while changing just one factor. Its result also tells us which aggregator to use when we later test other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only models and multimodal models. That avoids spreading the limited budget across both aggregator options in every later branch.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the best configuration so far fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA encoder with 2000 components, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the aggregator from avgpool (llm_summary_002) to a transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.688 to 0.512 (-0.176), and supporting validation F1 fell from 0.659 to 0.477 (-0.181). That puts it below even the single-profile baseline (0.536 / 0.516). Because aggregation was the only change, this is direct single-run evidence that in this setup the transformer aggregator underperforms simple average pooling, so avgpool is the stronger default for later branches (other RNA encoders, image-only, multimodal). However, there is no variance estimate. It is also unknown whether the drop reflects the transformer itself or untuned training or hyperparameters (e.g., overfitting or optimization issues on low-dimensional PCA inputs), and whether the result carries over to other encoders or modalities.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA with avgpool (config_002, 0.688 accuracy / 0.659 F1). That run clearly beat the single-profile baseline (0.536) and the transformer aggregator (0.512), so multiprofile with avgpool is the current default. The largest untested question is whether the image modality adds any value. No image-only or multimodal run has been done, which leaves half of the design space unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_018 keeps config_002's multiprofile, PCA and avgpool settings fixed. It adds a ResNet50 image branch with the simplest fusion, concat. Comparing it directly with config_002 isolates the effect of adding images to the best known setup, without mixing in a new RNA encoder or a different aggregator. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: Whether to go multimodal determines whether the many remaining multimodal configurations are worth exploring. A gain would justify follow-ups on fusion type and image encoder. No gain or a loss would point the budget toward RNA encoder comparisons (e.g., config_005) and away from multimodal branches. Either result reduces uncertainty about a major design choice while staying close to the best configuration.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best configuration so far fixed (multiprofile, PCA encoder with 2000 components, avgpool aggregation; llm_summary_002) and added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. Validation accuracy fell from 0.688 to 0.532 (-0.156), and supporting validation F1 fell from 0.659 to 0.516 (-0.143), roughly matching the single-profile RNA-only baseline (0.536 / 0.516). Because adding the image branch with concat was the only change, this is direct single-run evidence that this particular multimodal setup underperforms RNA-only in this setting, which argues for shifting budget toward RNA encoder comparisons rather than broad multimodal exploration. However, there is no variance estimate. The image branch and the concat fusion cannot be separated, and no image-only run exists to gauge how informative the image features are on their own. It is also unknown whether the drop reflects image features adding noise, scale or dimensional imbalance between the concatenated features, or untuned training. Alternative fusion methods or image encoders might therefore still behave differently.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Our best result is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA with avgpool (0.688 acc / 0.659 F1). Two changes from that configuration both hurt it by roughly 0.15 to 0.18. Swapping avgpool for a transformer aggregator was worse, and adding a ResNet50 branch with concat fusion was also worse. The RNA encoder is the main design choice we have not tested at all, since every run so far used PCA. 2) Test: Keep the best configuration fixed and change only the RNA encoder from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. This isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional representation improves on PCA in the multiprofile avgpool setting. If it does, scVI becomes the basis for later branches, including a fairer multimodal retest. 3) Why now: It is a clean single-factor comparison anchored to the strongest configuration. It has a real chance of beating the current best, and it tests whether the multiprofile gain holds beyond PCA. That makes better use of the limited budget than further multimodal or transformer variants, which have already underperformed in single runs.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best configuration fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, no image encoder or fusion; llm_summary_002) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA with 2000 components to scVI with 200 latent dimensions. Validation accuracy fell from 0.688 to 0.635 (-0.053), and supporting validation F1 fell from 0.659 to 0.618 (-0.040). Because the encoder was the only change, this is single-run evidence that this scVI setting does not beat PCA here, so PCA remains the default. The drop is much smaller than the transformer (llm_summary_003) or ResNet50 concat (llm_summary_004) changes, and scVI still clearly exceeds the single-profile PCA baseline (0.536 / 0.516). That loosely suggests the multiprofile avgpool gain is not specific to PCA, though this has not been directly tested without a single-profile scVI run. There is no variance estimate, so the gap may partly reflect run-to-run noise. The encoder type cannot be separated from the large difference in dimensionality (200 vs 2000), and the scVI hyperparameters and training were not tuned, so other scVI latent sizes or other encoders (e.g., scGPT) remain open questions.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 with avgpool (0.688 acc / 0.659 F1). Three single-factor changes from it all did worse. A transformer aggregator gave 0.512. Adding ResNet50 with concat gave 0.532. Swapping PCA for scVI-200 gave 0.635, a moderate drop. The RNA encoder is the dimension still only partly explored: scGPT, a pretrained foundation-model representation, is untested, so we cannot yet say whether PCA's lead reflects encoder type in general or just this scVI setting. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the best setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder to scGPT. Comparing it with config_002 (PCA) and config_005 (scVI) completes a clean three-way encoder comparison under the strongest profile and aggregation settings. It also checks whether the multiprofile avgpool benefit holds across encoders. 3. Why now: This is a single-factor experiment on the most promising branch. It could either produce a new best result or confirm PCA as the RNA default before more budget goes to multimodal branches. Fixing the RNA encoder first matters because every multimodal configuration depends on it. Testing weighted fusion (config_019) or image-only baselines makes more sense once the RNA side is settled.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, no image encoder or fusion; llm_summary_002) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT, completing a three-way encoder comparison under these settings. Validation accuracy was 0.530 (-0.157 vs PCA's 0.688; -0.105 vs scVI-200's 0.635), and supporting F1 was 0.515 (vs 0.659 and 0.618). This puts scGPT roughly at the single-profile PCA baseline (0.536 / 0.516), so the encoder ranking here is PCA > scVI > scGPT, PCA remains the RNA default, and the multiprofile avgpool gain is not evident for scGPT, although no single-profile scGPT run exists to test this directly. These are single runs with no variance estimates, and it is unknown whether the drop reflects scGPT representations themselves or untested factors such as embedding dimensionality, the domain match of pretraining, whether scGPT was frozen or fine-tuned, or untuned training.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only multiprofile PCA-2000 with avgpool is the best result so far (0.688 accuracy / 0.659 F1). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion (config_018) dropped performance to 0.532 / 0.516. That run cannot tell us whether the image features are uninformative or whether naive concatenation hurt, for example through scale or dimensional imbalance swamping the RNA signal. The RNA encoder and aggregator comparisons have already settled on PCA and avgpool as defaults, so fusion is now the largest unresolved design question. 2. What this tests: config_019 keeps config_018 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of fusion. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds RNA-only performance, the concat result was a fusion failure and multimodal remains viable. If it still falls well short, the image branch itself is the likely problem, and an image-only run (config_011) becomes the logical next diagnostic. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: it is a clean single-factor comparison against an existing run. It resolves an important ambiguity before committing budget to the many remaining multimodal configurations. It also has real upside, because weighted fusion could learn to down-weight a noisy image branch and possibly beat the current best.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept llm_summary_004 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, ResNet50, avgpool) and changed only the fusion from concat to weighted, which isolates the fusion choice. Validation accuracy rose from 0.532 to 0.650 (+0.118), and supporting F1 rose from 0.516 to 0.628 (+0.111). This is single-run evidence that concat fusion was a major part of the earlier multimodal drop, so multimodal remains viable. However, the result is still below the RNA-only PCA-2000 avgpool best (0.688 / 0.659; -0.038 accuracy), so adding images has not yet shown a net benefit. There are no variance estimates, and the gap to RNA-only may partly be run-to-run noise. The learned fusion weights were not reported, so it is unknown whether weighted fusion gains by making use of image information or by largely down-weighting the image branch. An image-only run and alternative fusion methods or image encoders remain the open diagnostics.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool is the best result so far (0.688 accuracy / 0.659 F1). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion hurt badly (0.532). Switching to weighted fusion recovered most of that loss (0.650) but still did not beat RNA-only. We do not know whether the ResNet50 image features carry useful signal, or whether weighted fusion recovered simply by down-weighting the image branch. 2. What this tests: an image-only, multiprofile, avgpool ResNet50 run uses the same profile setting and aggregation as the best configuration, with the modality as the only change. It measures how informative the images are on their own. Strong image-only accuracy would justify putting more budget into fusion and image-encoder variants (e.g., ViT-L with weighted fusion). Weak image-only accuracy would suggest focusing on RNA-only refinements. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: every multimodal branch depends on this answer, and the remaining untested configurations are mostly multimodal. One diagnostic run therefore lowers the risk of the remaining budget more than another single-factor multimodal tweak would.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 was a diagnostic run that used the same multiprofile avgpool setup as the best configuration (llm_summary_002) but with ResNet50 images only, to measure how informative the image features are on their own. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.535 and a supporting F1 of 0.519, well below RNA-only PCA-2000 (0.688 / 0.659; -0.152 accuracy) and multimodal weighted fusion (0.650 / 0.628). It roughly matches the single-profile RNA baseline (0.536) and the concat multimodal run (0.532). This is single-run evidence that ResNet50 image features are much weaker than PCA RNA features in this setup, which favors putting budget into RNA-only refinements over broad fusion exploration. However, the run does not show whether images add complementary signal in fusion, or whether weighted fusion recovered by down-weighting the image branch, since the fusion weights were not reported and there is no chance-level reference. There are also no variance estimates, and it is unknown whether other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) or different ResNet50 training choices, such as frozen vs fine-tuned, would be more informative.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool is the best so far (0.688 acc / 0.659 F1). Adding ResNet50 images with weighted fusion (config_019) recovered most of the large concat drop but still trails RNA-only (0.650 / 0.628). ResNet50 image-only is weak (0.535 acc). So the main open question on the multimodal side is whether the image encoder is the bottleneck, and ViT-L has not been tested at all. 2) This run keeps config_019 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. That isolates the image representation in the best-performing fusion setup. A clear gain would show the image encoder is limiting multimodal performance and could let fusion surpass RNA-only. No gain would further support RNA-only as the main direction. 3) It is the best use of the next run because it is a single-factor change from the strongest multimodal configuration and tests the largest untested design axis (image encoder). It also has a plausible chance of beating the current best, unlike transformer aggregation or the weaker RNA encoders, which existing evidence already disfavors. An image-only ViT-L run would be informative but would not directly tell us whether fusion can beat RNA-only.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the strongest multimodal configuration fixed (llm_summary_007: multimodal, multiprofile, PCA-2000, avgpool, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, isolating the image representation. Validation accuracy fell from 0.650 to 0.520 (-0.130), and supporting F1 fell from 0.628 to 0.479 (-0.148). That is well below the RNA-only PCA-2000 avgpool best (0.688 / 0.659), below the ResNet50 image-only run (0.535), and close to the weak transformer-aggregation run (0.512 / 0.477). This is single-run evidence that swapping in ViT-L does not relieve the multimodal shortfall in this setup and may hurt, which further supports RNA-only as the main direction. Uncertainties remain: there are no variance estimates, and no ViT-L image-only run exists to tell whether the ViT-L features are themselves weak or interact poorly with fusion. It is also unknown whether the drop reflects ViT-L representations or untested factors such as feature dimensionality or scale relative to PCA, frozen vs fine-tuned use, the domain mismatch of ImageNet pretraining, or training hyperparameters tuned for ResNet50. The learned fusion weights were again not reported.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool is the best run so far (0.688 accuracy / 0.659 F1). Weighted fusion with ResNet50 recovered most of the concat drop (0.650 / 0.628) but still trails RNA-only, and ResNet50 image-only is weak (0.535). So it is still unclear whether images add complementary signal or whether weighted fusion simply down-weights the image branch. One untested explanation is a scale or dimensional imbalance between 2000-dim PCA and the image features. 2. What this tests: config_031 keeps the multimodal ResNet50 avgpool weighted setup from config_019 and changes only the RNA encoder to the lower-dimensional scVI-200. It can be read against two existing runs. Against RNA-only scVI (config_005, 0.635), it shows whether images help when the RNA representation is weaker and more compact. Against config_019, it shows whether the RNA encoder ranking (PCA > scVI) holds under fusion. If accuracy exceeds 0.635, that is evidence of complementary image signal. If it does not, that strengthens the case for focusing the budget on RNA-only refinements. 3. Why this is the best next run: it changes a single factor, has a clean baseline on both comparison axes, and addresses the most important open question, whether multimodal fusion can ever add value here. The alternatives are less useful at this point: transformer variants have already failed, and a ViT-L image-only run would mostly confirm features that already look weak.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the multimodal ResNet50 avgpool weighted-fusion setup from llm_summary_007 and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. It reached 0.713 validation accuracy and 0.695 supporting F1, the best run so far: +0.078 / +0.076 over RNA-only scVI-200 (llm_summary_005, 0.635), +0.063 over the same fusion setup with PCA-2000 (llm_summary_007, 0.650), and +0.025 over the previous best RNA-only PCA-2000 run (0.688 / 0.659). The comparison with llm_summary_005 isolates adding the ResNet50 branch with weighted fusion and gives the first single-run evidence that images can add complementary signal, at least alongside compact scVI features. The comparison with llm_summary_007 shows that the RNA ranking seen in RNA-only runs (PCA > scVI) reversed under fusion, which is consistent with, but does not prove, the hypothesized scale or dimensional imbalance between 2000-dim PCA and image features, because scVI-200 differs from PCA-2000 in both encoder type and dimensionality. Uncertainties remain: there are no variance estimates, so the small margin over RNA-only PCA may partly be noise; the learned fusion weights were not reported; and it is untested whether PCA reduced to around 200 dimensions, other scVI latent sizes, or concat fusion with scVI would behave similarly.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about how well individual modalities, encoders, profile settings, aggregation methods or fusion strategies perform. 2) config_001 is the simplest pipeline: RNA-only, single profile, PCA (2000) encoding, with no aggregation or fusion. It gives a reference accuracy and F1 that later changes can be compared against one factor at a time. Natural next steps from here are swapping the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), switching to multiprofile with avgpool (config_002), and adding the image modality. 3) With a limited budget, a cheap baseline is the most useful first experiment. It anchors every later comparison and shows whether added complexity (multimodal, multiprofile, foundation-model encoders) actually helps, rather than assuming it does.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest pipeline as a first baseline: RNA-only input, a single profile, a PCA encoder with 2000 components (pca_n2000), and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.494 (the primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.453. The F1 below accuracy hints that performance may be uneven across classes, though this is not confirmed. Because no other experiments exist yet, this is only an initial reference point. It is still unknown how other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, or adding the image modality would compare. The result comes from a single run, so its sensitivity to run-to-run variability is also unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: we have one result, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001): accuracy 0.494, F1 0.453. Every other design axis is untested: RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, image modality and fusion. 2) Test: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from single to multiprofile, using simple avgpool aggregation. All else stays fixed (RNA-only, pca_n2000). Any difference can therefore be attributed to multiprofile aggregation itself, which is a core design choice that applies across all modalities. 3) Why now: this is a clean one-variable comparison against the only reference point. Avgpool is the simplest aggregator, so it tells us whether multiprofile helps at all before we pay for a transformer. The answer determines whether multiprofile configurations deserve priority in the rest of the budget. Swapping the RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT) is an equally clean next step, but the profile effect likely affects more of the remaining configurations. One run is not conclusive, so a small difference should be read cautiously and confirmed on another encoder or modality.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the llm_summary_001 baseline fixed (RNA-only, pca_n2000 encoder, no image encoder or fusion) and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with simple average-pooling aggregation, reaching a validation accuracy of 0.519 (vs. 0.494) and an F1 of 0.480 (vs. 0.453). This modest gain of about 2.5 points on both metrics is an initial signal that multiprofile input with avgpool may help, though the effect cannot be separated from the use of avgpool as the aggregator, and F1 remains below accuracy, consistent with possibly uneven per-class performance. Both results come from single runs with no estimate of run-to-run variance, so the difference may fall within noise. It is still unknown whether the gain holds with other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), with the image modality, or with stronger aggregators such as a transformer.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Only RNA-only runs with pca_n2000 exist. Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a small gain (0.494 to 0.519 accuracy, with F1 up by a similar amount). That is a single-run difference, so it may be noise. The largest open question is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all, and 42 of the 48 untested configurations depend on it. 2) Test: config_011 runs image-only with resnet50, keeping multiprofile and avgpool fixed. Only the input modality changes relative to config_002, so the comparison isolates how informative images are compared with RNA under the same profile and aggregation setup. 3) Why now: Under a limited budget, this result decides how to treat the large multimodal part of the search space. If images are weak, multimodal gains are doubtful and effort should go to RNA encoders and aggregation. If images are strong, fusion experiments become a priority. Testing RNA encoders or transformer aggregation first would refine only the RNA-only branch and say nothing about the modality question.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested the first image-only pipeline: a resnet50 image encoder with multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation, matching llm_summary_002 except that resnet50 image features replaced pca_n2000 RNA features. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.421 (vs. 0.519 for llm_summary_002) and an F1 of 0.412 (vs. 0.480). This is an initial signal that, in this setup, resnet50 image features are less predictive alone than PCA RNA features, though the modality effect cannot be separated from the specific encoders, and the smaller accuracy–F1 gap may hint at more even per-class performance. All results are single runs with no variance estimate and no reported chance level, so it remains unknown whether images carry meaningful signal above chance, whether other image encoders or aggregators would do better, and whether image features add complementary information to RNA in fusion, which the image-only comparison cannot answer.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: the best result is RNA-only multiprofile pca_n2000 with avgpool (config_002, acc 0.519, F1 0.480). The matching image-only resnet50 setup (config_011) is weaker (acc 0.421, F1 0.412). However, image-only performance cannot tell us whether image features add complementary information to RNA. Whether fusion helps is the central untested design question in this multimodal study. 2) Test: config_018 keeps the config_002 setup fixed (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds resnet50 image features with simple concat fusion. Both unimodal arms are already measured, so any change can be attributed to adding the image modality. 3) Why now: this is a clean one-factor comparison on the study's most important open question. Either outcome is informative. A gain would justify exploring encoders and fusion types within multimodal setups. No gain or a loss would suggest putting more budget into RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation. With single runs, small differences should be read cautiously, and F1 will serve as supporting evidence.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested whether image features add information beyond RNA. It kept the best setup so far fixed (llm_summary_002: multiprofile, pca_n2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation) and added resnet50 image features through simple concat fusion, making this a one-factor test of adding the image modality. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.535 (vs. 0.519 for RNA-only and 0.421 for image-only) and an F1 of 0.519 (vs. 0.480 and 0.412). This is an initial signal that the image features may carry some information complementary to RNA, with a modest accuracy gain of about 1.6 points, a larger F1 gain of about 3.9 points, and a narrower accuracy–F1 gap that may hint at more even per-class performance. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, so the accuracy gain in particular may fall within run-to-run noise. It is also unknown whether the benefit comes from complementary signal or simply from the larger concatenated feature space, and whether it holds with other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), other image encoders, other aggregators, or fusion methods beyond concat.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000 + resnet50, avgpool, concat), at 0.535 accuracy and 0.519 F1. RNA is clearly the stronger single modality (0.519 vs 0.421 for image-only), so the RNA representation is probably a major driver of performance. Yet only PCA has been tested, and the choice of RNA encoder is the largest open uncertainty. 2. What this tests: config_042 keeps the current best setup fixed and changes only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scGPT. This is a clean one-factor test of whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding beats PCA when images are also present. 3. Why it is the best next step: It targets the design choice most likely to matter, given that RNA carries most of the signal, while staying near the best-known region of the search space. Whether scGPT helps or hurts, the result will tell us whether to keep exploring alternative RNA encoders (scVI is the natural follow-up) or to shift effort to secondary choices such as aggregation, fusion and image encoder.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 was a one-factor test of the RNA encoder: it kept the best setup so far fixed (llm_summary_004: multimodal, multiprofile, resnet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) and swapped the pca_n2000 RNA encoder for pretrained scGPT embeddings. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.591 (vs. 0.535) and an F1 of 0.573 (vs. 0.519), the best result so far and the largest single-step gain in the search (about 5.5 points on both metrics), with a similar accuracy–F1 gap of about 1.8 points. Because only the encoder changed, this is a fairly direct initial signal that scGPT beats PCA as the RNA representation in this multimodal concat setting, though it may also reflect differences such as embedding dimensionality. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, and it remains unknown whether the gain holds RNA-only or with other aggregators and fusion methods, how scVI or other RNA encoders would compare, and whether image features still add complementary value on top of scGPT embeddings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: In single runs, multiprofile input with avgpool beat single-profile (+2.5 pts), concat fusion of resnet50 with PCA beat RNA-only (+1.6 acc, +3.9 F1), and swapping PCA for scGPT gave the largest gain (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1, config_042). Aggregation is the main axis never varied: every multiprofile run used avgpool. The transformer aggregator, weighted fusion and the ViT-L image encoder are all still unexplored. 2. Test: config_044 keeps the best setup fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT, resnet50, concat) and changes only avgpool to transformer. This is a one-factor test of whether learned, attention-based pooling across profiles beats simple averaging on the strongest representation. 3. Why now: It explores a completely untested design choice while staying anchored to the best configuration, so it can both reveal a large improvement and isolate the aggregation effect. Ablations such as scGPT RNA-only (config_008) or weighted fusion (config_043) are valuable but can follow once the aggregation question is settled. Any small difference should be read cautiously given single runs.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 was a one-factor test of the aggregation method. It kept the best setup so far fixed (llm_summary_005: multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT RNA encoder, resnet50 image encoder, concat fusion) and replaced avgpool with a learned transformer aggregator across profiles. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.715 (vs. 0.591) and an F1 of 0.687 (vs. 0.573), the best result so far and by far the largest single-step gain in the search (about 12.4 accuracy and 11.5 F1 points), with a slightly wider accuracy–F1 gap of about 2.8 points. Because only the aggregator changed, this is a fairly direct but still initial signal that transformer pooling outperforms simple averaging in this configuration, though it may also partly reflect added model capacity rather than attention-based pooling specifically. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, and it remains unknown whether the gain holds with PCA or other RNA encoders, in RNA-only or image-only settings, with weighted fusion or ViT-L image features, and whether image features still add value on top of scGPT with transformer aggregation.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_044 (scGPT + resnet50, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat), with 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. That result came from large one-factor gains for scGPT over PCA and for transformer over avgpool aggregation. The only evidence that images help is a modest gain (about 1.6 accuracy points) in the weaker PCA/avgpool setting, which may be within run-to-run noise. Image-only resnet50 was also clearly weaker than RNA. So it is unclear whether the image branch still adds anything once RNA uses scGPT with transformer aggregation. 2. What this tests: config_009 removes only the image modality from config_044 and keeps scGPT, multiprofile input and transformer aggregation. This isolates the modality's contribution in the strongest setup. It also shows whether the transformer gain holds without images. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Future work could explore either image-side choices (ViT-L, weighted fusion) or RNA-side and aggregation choices. This ablation decides which direction deserves the remaining experiments. If RNA-only matches or beats config_044, image variants are a poor use of budget. If it drops clearly, that justifies next testing ViT-L (config_050) or weighted fusion (config_045).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 was a one-factor ablation of the image modality: it kept the best configuration (llm_summary_006: multiprofile, scGPT RNA encoder, transformer aggregation) fixed and removed the resnet50 image branch and concat fusion, reaching a validation accuracy of 0.471 (vs. 0.715) and an F1 of 0.442 (vs. 0.687), a drop of about 24 points on both metrics. Because only the modality changed, this is an initial signal that the image branch contributes substantially in the scGPT+transformer setup, which would favor image-side follow-ups such as ViT-L or weighted fusion over RNA-only variants. However, the result is surprisingly low, falling below the simpler RNA-only PCA baselines (0.494 single-profile, 0.519 multiprofile avgpool). This raises the possibility that the scGPT+transformer pipeline underperforms or trains unstably without images, rather than images simply adding complementary signal; an interaction among modality, encoder and aggregator also cannot be ruled out. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, so it remains unknown whether this gap is robust, and an RNA-only scGPT+avgpool run or a repeat run would help distinguish a genuine image contribution from an RNA-only training problem.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far (0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1) comes from scGPT + resnet50 with transformer aggregation and concat fusion. Replacing avgpool with the transformer gave the largest single gain (+12.4 points). Removing the image branch dropped accuracy to 0.471, below even the PCA RNA-only baselines. So it is unclear whether the transformer's benefit comes mainly from aggregating image profiles, or whether this RNA-only run simply trained poorly. Image-only has only been tested with avgpool (0.421). 2) Test: config_012 changes only the aggregator relative to config_011 (image-only resnet50, avgpool to transformer). If image-only accuracy rises sharply, the transformer gain is largely image-driven, which would favour image-side follow-ups such as ViT-L or weighted fusion. If it stays near 0.42, the gain likely needs both modalities together, or the RNA-only result reflects a training problem. In that case config_008 (RNA-only scGPT with avgpool) would be the natural next check. 3) Why now: This single one-factor run helps explain the main performance driver found so far. It also helps interpret the surprising RNA-only ablation, and it guides how to spend the remaining budget on image-encoder and fusion choices rather than guessing.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 was a one-factor test of the aggregator in the image-only setting. It kept llm_summary_003 fixed (multiprofile, resnet50, no RNA or fusion) and replaced avgpool with a transformer, reaching a validation accuracy of 0.629 (vs. 0.421) and an F1 of 0.599 (vs. 0.412), gains of about 20.7 and 18.7 points with an accuracy–F1 gap of about 2.9 points. This is an initial signal that much of the transformer benefit seen in llm_summary_006 is available from image profiles alone: this image-only run beats every RNA-only run (best 0.519) and all avgpool multimodal runs (best 0.591), though it remains about 8.6 points below the scGPT+resnet50 transformer concat model (0.715), suggesting RNA may still add complementary value. Whether the gain reflects attention-based pooling or simply added capacity is unresolved, and it remains unexplained why RNA-only scGPT with a transformer scored so low (0.471); an RNA-only scGPT+avgpool run would help tell an RNA-side training problem from an aggregator–modality interaction. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, so image-side follow-ups such as ViT-L or weighted fusion look promising but are not yet established.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best model so far is config_044 (scGPT + resnet50, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. The transformer aggregator gave the largest gains. The image branch looks like the dominant signal: image-only with a transformer reached 0.629, while RNA-only scGPT with a transformer reached only 0.471. Despite that, the image encoder has never been varied; every image run used resnet50. 2) Test: This run keeps config_044 fixed and swaps only resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l. It is a clean one-factor test of whether a stronger image representation improves the best pipeline. 3) Why now: Image features carry most of the signal, so the image encoder is likely the highest-impact untested choice. This test both exploits the leading configuration and resolves a major open design question. Weighted fusion (config_045) and the RNA-only scGPT+avgpool check (config_008) remain good follow-ups. All results are single runs, so a small difference should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 was a one-factor test of the image encoder. It kept the best configuration (llm_summary_006: multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT RNA encoder, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) fixed and swapped resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l, reaching a validation accuracy of 0.599 (vs. 0.715) and an F1 of 0.578 (vs. 0.687), drops of about 11.6 and 11.0 points with an accuracy–F1 gap of about 2.1 points. The ViT-L result falls below the image-only resnet50 transformer run (0.629) and only roughly matches the scGPT+resnet50 avgpool model (0.591), so this is an initial signal that ViT-L features did not help, and may have hurt, in this pipeline, contrary to the expectation that a stronger image representation would improve results. Because this is a single run with no variance estimate, it remains unknown whether the drop is robust or reflects training instability, settings tuned for resnet50, or differences in feature dimensionality, and whether ViT-L would also underperform in image-only or avgpool settings or with weighted fusion; resnet50 remains the image encoder in the best configuration, and an image-only ViT-L transformer run or a repeat run would help localize the effect.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is config_044 (multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT + resnet50, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. One-factor tests have probed representation, profile setting, aggregation and image encoder. Fusion is the only major design choice never varied: every multimodal run used concat. The image-only transformer run (0.629) and the weak RNA-only scGPT transformer run (0.471) suggest the two modalities contribute unevenly, which is the situation where learned weighting could matter. 2) What this tests: config_045 keeps the best configuration fixed and swaps concat for weighted fusion. Any change in accuracy and F1 can therefore be attributed to the fusion method. 3) Why this is the best next use of the budget: it closes the largest remaining gap in our understanding of the design space. It also exploits the strongest configuration, so it has a realistic chance of improving the best result. The diagnostic runs (e.g., RNA-only scGPT avgpool, image-only ViT-L) are useful, but they are less likely to change which final configuration we choose. All results are single runs, so a small difference should be read cautiously, with F1 as supporting evidence.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 was a one-factor test of the fusion method, the only major design choice not previously varied. It kept the best configuration (llm_summary_006: multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT RNA encoder, resnet50 image encoder, transformer aggregation) fixed and replaced concat with weighted fusion, reaching a validation accuracy of 0.619 (vs. 0.715) and an F1 of 0.610 (vs. 0.687), drops of about 9.6 and 7.7 points, with a narrower accuracy–F1 gap of about 0.8 points. Because only fusion changed, this is a fairly direct initial signal that weighted fusion underperformed concat in this setup: it falls slightly below the image-only resnet50 transformer run (0.629), which raises the possibility that the learned weighting did not exploit the RNA branch well, though the learned weights were not reported and this is not confirmed. All results are single runs with no variance estimate, and it remains unknown whether the drop is robust or instead reflects training instability, hyperparameters tuned for concat, or the specific weighting implementation; concat with scGPT+resnet50+transformer remains the best configuration, and repeat runs of the best configuration would help gauge how much of these differences is noise.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so nothing is known yet about how much each design choice matters, including modality, RNA or image encoder, profile setting, aggregation and fusion. 2. What this tests: config_001 is the simplest setup: RNA only, single profile, a standard PCA (2000) encoder, and no aggregation or fusion. It gives a reference baseline. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time against it, such as swapping in scVI or scGPT, switching to multiprofile with avgpool or transformer, or adding an image encoder. Each of those differences can then be attributed to a single change. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Starting with a simple, low-variance baseline avoids changing many factors at once. It also avoids assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models will win. This makes every later experiment easier to interpret under a limited budget.
experiment_summary: This first experiment set a reference baseline using the simplest configuration: RNA-only input, a single profile, a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder, and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.650 (primary metric), with a validation F1 of 0.628 as supporting evidence. Because no other configurations have been run, this is only an initial observation. It says nothing yet about whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, or adding imaging would help or hurt. Its run-to-run variance is also unknown, so future one-factor-at-a-time comparisons against it should allow for the possibility that small differences are noise.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: Only one experiment has been run, the RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000 baseline (accuracy 0.650, F1 0.628). We have no information yet about the imaging modality, and imaging appears in most of the remaining search space (all image-only and multimodal configurations). 2) What this tests: config_010 is the simplest image-only configuration (single profile, ResNet50, no aggregation or fusion). It matches the baseline on profile setting and complexity, so the comparison isolates the effect of modality. It shows whether images alone carry predictive signal comparable to RNA. 3) Why it is the best next step: The value of imaging determines whether the large multimodal portion of the search space is worth pursuing. If images are weak, the budget can shift to RNA encoders and aggregation. If images are strong or comparable, multimodal fusion becomes a well-motivated next direction. This one-factor comparison resolves more uncertainty than tuning RNA encoders or aggregation alone, though one run per configuration means small accuracy gaps should still be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: This experiment tested the simplest image-only configuration: a single profile, a ResNet50 image encoder, no RNA input, and no aggregation or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.721 (F1 0.681), compared with 0.650 accuracy (F1 0.628) for the matched RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile baseline. This is an initial observation that imaging carries predictive signal at least comparable to, and possibly stronger than, RNA in this setting. That makes the image-only and multimodal parts of the search space worth exploring further. However, the comparison changes the modality and the specific encoder together (ResNet50 vs PCA-2000), so the gap cannot be attributed to modality alone, since other RNA encoders such as scVI or scGPT might narrow it. With one run per configuration and unknown run-to-run variance, the size of the roughly 7-point gap remains uncertain. It is also untested whether combining both modalities, or adding multiprofile aggregation, would improve on either single-modality result.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: two single-profile baselines. Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.721 accuracy (F1 0.681) and RNA-only PCA-2000 reached 0.650 (F1 0.628). This shows both modalities carry signal, with imaging possibly stronger. Whether they are complementary is completely unknown, and that question is central to the whole search space, since most remaining configurations are multimodal. 2) config_016 fuses exactly the two encoders already tested (PCA-2000 RNA plus ResNet50 image) with simple concat fusion. It keeps the single-profile setting and uses no aggregation. Every other design choice matches the two baselines, so any change can be attributed to adding the other modality. If it clearly beats 0.721, multimodal fusion is worth exploring further, including weighted fusion, better encoders and multiprofile aggregation. If it matches or underperforms, the budget should shift toward image-only refinements such as ViT-L or multiprofile aggregation. 3) Under a limited budget, this one experiment answers the highest-leverage open question, whether fusion helps, while changing only one factor. It also has a reasonable chance of becoming the new best configuration, so it serves both exploration and exploitation.
experiment_summary: This experiment fused the two previously tested single-profile encoders, PCA-2000 RNA and ResNet50 image, using simple concatenation, with no aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.527 (F1 0.510), well below both the image-only baseline (0.721, F1 0.681) and the RNA-only baseline (0.650, F1 0.628), so naive concat fusion of these encoders clearly did not help in this setup and may have degraded performance. The drop is large (about 19 points below image-only), so it is unlikely to be explained by run-to-run noise alone, although that variance is unmeasured with one run per configuration. The result does not show that the modalities lack complementary signal, because the cause is unresolved: possibilities include the concat fusion mechanism itself (e.g., feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between 2000 PCA features and ResNet50 embeddings) or training or optimization issues, and alternatives such as weighted fusion, feature normalization, other encoders, or multiprofile aggregation remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 (0.721 acc, F1 0.681) beat RNA-only PCA-2000 (0.650 acc, F1 0.628). Concat fusion of these same two encoders fell to 0.527 acc, far below either modality alone. The cause is unresolved. It could be the concat mechanism, such as scale or dimensionality imbalance, or it could be that this encoder pairing does not combine well. 2) This experiment changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, and keeps the encoders and single-profile setting fixed. If weighted fusion recovers to the single-modality level or above, the concat mechanism was the main problem. If it stays low, the issue is likely with fusing these encoders or with multimodal training here in general. 3) Most of the remaining search space (about 36 of 48 configurations) is multimodal, and roughly half uses concat. Learning whether the fusion mechanism caused the drop is therefore the most decision-relevant uncertainty. It tells us whether to keep investing in multimodal configurations, and with which fusion, or to focus on image-only refinements such as multiprofile aggregation and ViT-L. One clean comparison answers this, which makes it the best use of the next experiment.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the multimodal single-profile setup of llm_summary_003 (PCA-2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted, to test whether the concat mechanism caused the earlier multimodal collapse. Weighted fusion reached a validation accuracy of 0.579 (F1 0.563). That is about 5 points above concat (0.527, F1 0.510) but still well below both RNA-only (0.650, F1 0.628) and image-only (0.721, F1 0.681). So fusion choice may account for part of the drop, but switching to weighted fusion did not recover single-modality performance, and multimodal fusion of these encoders has not yet beaten image-only. With one run per configuration and unmeasured variance, the concat-vs-weighted gap may be partly noise. The remaining underperformance is unexplained: candidate causes include feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance not addressed by either fusion method, optimization or training issues in the multimodal setting, or this particular encoder pairing. Feature normalization, other RNA or image encoders, and multiprofile aggregation in multimodal settings remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 single-profile is the best result so far (0.721 accuracy, F1 0.681). It beats RNA-only PCA-2000 (0.650). Both multimodal fusions of these encoders did worse (concat 0.527, weighted 0.579). Multiprofile aggregation has not been tested in any modality, so a whole design axis is still unknown. 2. Test: config_011 changes one factor from the best configuration, moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation while keeping image-only ResNet50. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles adds signal. Avgpool is the simplest aggregator, so it is a cleaner first test than a transformer. 3. Why now: It extends the strongest direction found so far, so it may give the best immediate result. It also answers a key open question about the profile setting, whatever the outcome. That answer will guide whether later multiprofile runs, including multimodal ones, are worth the budget. It avoids spending more runs on the multimodal pairing before simpler factors are understood.
experiment_summary: This experiment changed one factor from the best configuration so far (image-only ResNet50, single-profile, 0.721 accuracy, F1 0.681), switching from single-profile to multiprofile input with simple avgpool aggregation, to test whether pooling multiple profiles adds signal. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.421 (F1 0.412), about 30 points below the single-profile counterpart and the lowest result so far, below RNA-only (0.650) and both multimodal fusions (0.527 concat, 0.579 weighted). So multiprofile avgpool clearly did not help in this image-only setting, and the drop is too large to be plausibly explained by run-to-run noise alone, although variance remains unmeasured with one run per configuration. It is still unclear whether the problem lies with multiprofile input in general or with avgpool specifically (e.g., averaging may wash out discriminative per-profile features), or with training or optimization issues. Other aggregators (e.g., attention or transformer pooling), multiprofile with RNA-only, and multiprofile in multimodal settings remain untested, so this result alone does not rule out the multiprofile design axis.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 single-profile is the best result so far (0.721 accuracy, F1 0.681). Switching to multiprofile with avgpool (config_011) dropped accuracy to 0.421, about 30 points lower. That result cannot tell us whether multiprofile input is harmful in general or whether avgpool is the problem, for example by washing out discriminative per-profile features. 2) Test: config_012 changes only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer and keeps everything else from config_011 the same. It therefore isolates the aggregation effect directly. If transformer aggregation recovers or exceeds single-profile performance, the multiprofile axis is worth pursuing. If it also collapses, multiprofile input itself is likely the issue. 3) Why now: Roughly half of the remaining configurations, including many multimodal ones, depend on multiprofile aggregation. Settling whether that axis is viable will guide many later choices, making this the most uncertainty-reducing experiment for the budget. Testing the ViT-L image encoder (config_013) is a strong follow-up for exploiting the best direction.
experiment_summary: This experiment kept the multiprofile image-only ResNet50 setup of llm_summary_005 and changed only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer, to test whether avgpool caused the earlier multiprofile collapse. Transformer aggregation reached a validation accuracy of 0.632 (F1 0.607). That is about 21 points above avgpool (0.421, F1 0.412), so in this one-factor comparison aggregation choice appears to account for much of the drop, and multiprofile input is not inherently unworkable. However, it still falls about 9 points short of the single-profile image-only baseline (0.721, F1 0.681) and slightly below RNA-only (0.650). Multiprofile aggregation has therefore not yet shown a benefit over single-profile input. The cause of the remaining gap is unresolved; possibilities include transformer capacity or optimization or training issues, or limited extra signal in additional profiles. With one run per configuration and unmeasured variance, the gap sizes are uncertain. Other aggregators, stronger image encoders such as ViT-L, and multiprofile RNA-only or multimodal settings remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is image-only, single-profile ResNet50 (0.721 acc, F1 0.681). Every added complexity has underperformed it so far. Multimodal fusion reached 0.527 with concat and 0.579 with weighted. Multiprofile aggregation reached 0.421 with avgpool and 0.632 with transformer. The image encoder axis is entirely untested, since ResNet50 is the only one run. 2) Test: Swapping only the image encoder to ImageNet ViT-L, with everything else matching the best configuration, isolates the effect of image representation on the strongest-performing branch. This builds directly on the strongest evidence. It also shows whether the image representation, rather than profile setting or fusion, is where the gains lie. The answer will decide whether later multiprofile and multimodal runs should use ViT-L or ResNet50. 3) Why now: This one-factor change probes an important unexplored design choice and could also raise the best score. Revisiting multiprofile or multimodal variants first would mean testing those weaker directions before settling which image encoder to carry forward. The other RNA-encoder test (scVI, config_004) is a strong candidate for the following experiment.
experiment_summary: This experiment changed one factor from the best configuration so far (image-only, single-profile ResNet50, 0.721 accuracy, F1 0.681), swapping the image encoder for ImageNet ViT-L, to test whether image representation is where gains lie. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.411 (F1 0.378), about 31 points below the ResNet50 counterpart and the lowest result so far, below multiprofile avgpool (0.421), both multimodal fusions (0.527 concat, 0.579 weighted) and RNA-only (0.650). In this one-factor comparison, swapping to ViT-L clearly did not help, and the drop is too large to be plausibly explained by run-to-run noise, although variance is unmeasured with one run per configuration. This result supports carrying ResNet50 rather than ViT-L forward for now. It remains unclear whether the collapse reflects ViT-L itself (e.g., an ImageNet domain mismatch with cellular images), or issues such as input resolution or preprocessing, embedding dimensionality, or training and optimization settings not adapted to a larger encoder. Other image encoders and ViT-L under different training setups remain untested, as does the scVI RNA encoder.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only ResNet50 single-profile is the best result so far (0.721 acc, F1 0.681). Swapping in ViT-L, moving to multiprofile (avgpool or transformer), and both PCA-2000-based fusions all fell short of it. The RNA representation axis is the largest untested design choice: every RNA-containing run used PCA-2000, so the 0.650 RNA-only baseline and the weak multimodal results may reflect that encoder rather than the RNA modality itself. 2) What this tests: config_004 changes one factor from config_001, swapping PCA-2000 for scVI-200, while keeping RNA-only and single-profile. This isolates the effect of RNA representation. It also checks whether a compact 200-dimensional latent might later ease the dimensionality and scale imbalance suspected in the concat and weighted fusions. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: this cheap single-factor comparison addresses a core uncertainty that bears on many remaining configurations, since scVI appears in most multimodal options. If scVI clearly beats PCA, it points to scVI+ResNet50 multimodal runs as the logical next step. If it does not, it strengthens the case that image-only ResNet50 is the main direction to exploit. With one run per configuration, only a clear gap should be treated as meaningful.
experiment_summary: This experiment changed one factor from the RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (llm_summary_001, 0.650 accuracy, F1 0.628), swapping the RNA encoder for a 200-dimensional scVI latent, to test whether PCA-2000 was limiting RNA and multimodal results. scVI-200 reached a validation accuracy of 0.635 (F1 0.618), about 1.5 points below PCA-2000. With one run per configuration and unmeasured variance, this gap is small enough to be noise, so the two encoders look roughly comparable in this setting and scVI shows no clear advantage. RNA-only remains well below the image-only ResNet50 single-profile best (0.721, F1 0.681), which strengthens the case for prioritizing image-based directions. It is still untested whether scVI's compact latent would behave differently in multimodal fusion, for example by easing the suspected dimensionality or scale imbalance seen with PCA-2000 concat and weighted fusion, and other RNA encoders such as scGPT also remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only ResNet50 single-profile is the best result so far (0.721 accuracy, F1 0.681). Both multimodal fusions with PCA-2000 + ResNet50 fell well below either single modality (concat 0.527, weighted 0.579). One suspected cause is a dimensionality or scale imbalance from the 2000-dimensional PCA input. scVI-200 performed about the same as PCA-2000 in RNA-only (0.635 vs 0.650, a gap that may be noise), so the two encoders carry similar RNA signal but differ greatly in dimensionality. 2) What this tests: config_029 is a one-factor change from config_017. It keeps single-profile input, ResNet50 and weighted fusion, and swaps only PCA-2000 for scVI-200. RNA-only performance is matched, so a clear change in multimodal accuracy would point to the RNA representation's size or scale as a driver of the fusion failure. No change would point instead to fusion or optimization issues. Weighted fusion is used because it was the better of the two fusion methods. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: whether multimodal fusion can ever beat image-only is the most consequential unresolved question in the search space. This controlled test addresses it directly and has a plausible chance of producing a competitive result. Lower-priority options, such as scGPT RNA-only or RNA multiprofile runs, are less likely to change the overall direction of the search.
experiment_summary: This experiment changed one factor from llm_summary_004 (multimodal single-profile, ResNet50, weighted fusion), swapping the PCA-2000 RNA encoder for the 200-dimensional scVI latent, which performed about the same as PCA-2000 in RNA-only runs (0.635 vs 0.650). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.653 (F1 0.628), about 7 points above the PCA-2000 weighted fusion (0.579, F1 0.563) and the best multimodal result so far. Because the RNA-only performance of the two encoders is roughly matched, this suggests the RNA representation used in fusion contributes to the earlier multimodal underperformance. However, the swap changes dimensionality, scale and representation type together, so dimensionality or scale imbalance specifically is not isolated, and with one run per configuration and unmeasured variance the gap size is uncertain. Multimodal fusion still falls about 7 points short of image-only ResNet50 (0.721, F1 0.681) and only roughly matches RNA-only, so it has not yet shown complementary benefit; concat fusion with scVI, explicit feature normalization or projection of PCA-2000, other RNA encoders such as scGPT, and multiprofile multimodal settings remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only ResNet50 single-profile (0.721 accuracy, F1 0.681) is still the best result. Multimodal fusion has improved only when the RNA representation changed: scVI-200 weighted fusion reached 0.653, versus 0.579 for PCA-2000. That points to the RNA encoder as a key lever. The two RNA encoders tested so far look roughly equivalent alone (PCA 0.650, scVI 0.635). scGPT, the third RNA encoder and a major design axis, is completely untested. 2) What this tests: Swapping only the encoder to scGPT in the simplest RNA-only single-profile setting gives a clean one-factor comparison against both PCA-2000 and scVI-200. It shows whether a foundation-model RNA representation carries more signal. 3) Why now: If scGPT clearly beats about 0.65, the scGPT multimodal configurations (e.g., config_041) become the most promising route to beating image-only. If it does not, we can deprioritize the 12 scGPT configurations and focus the remaining budget on scVI/ResNet50 fusion and aggregation variants. The run is cheap, interpretable and narrows the search space more than another fusion or aggregation tweak.
experiment_summary: This experiment changed one factor from the RNA-only single-profile baselines, swapping the RNA encoder to scGPT, to test whether a foundation-model RNA representation carries more signal than PCA-2000 (0.650, F1 0.628) or scVI-200 (0.635, F1 0.618). scGPT reached a validation accuracy of 0.422 (F1 0.405), roughly 21-23 points below both other RNA encoders and well below the image-only ResNet50 best (0.721, F1 0.681). In this one-factor comparison scGPT clearly did not help, and the drop is too large to be plausibly explained by run-to-run noise, although variance is unmeasured with one run per configuration. That supports deprioritizing the scGPT configurations, including the scGPT multimodal ones, in favor of scVI/ResNet50 fusion and aggregation variants. It remains unclear whether the collapse reflects scGPT's representation itself (e.g., pretraining domain mismatch) or issues such as gene-vocabulary or tokenization mismatch, embedding extraction or pooling, preprocessing, or training settings not adapted to this encoder, and scGPT under alternative setups or in fusion remains untested.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 is the simplest baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (2000 dims), with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 for later controlled comparisons. Each later step can change one factor against it: scVI or scGPT as the encoder (config_004, config_007), multiprofile pooling (config_002, config_003), or adding an image encoder (config_016, config_017). 3) With a limited budget, a cheap and interpretable anchor is the most efficient first experiment. Without it, we could not tell whether gains from more complex multimodal or multiprofile models are real or simply reflect the task's baseline difficulty.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder with 2000 dimensions, no image encoder, no aggregation, and no fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.422 with a supporting validation F1 of 0.405, and the similar values suggest predictions are not heavily skewed toward a few classes. Because no other configurations have been run, this is only a reference point. It says nothing yet about whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, or adding image features would help. The number of classes and chance-level performance are not given, so how difficult the task is and how much the RNA signal alone contributes remain unclear. Later experiments should change one factor at a time against this anchor to attribute any differences to a specific design choice.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (config_001), at 0.422 accuracy and 0.405 F1. We do not yet know how any other design factor affects performance. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). The RNA encoder, modality and fusion stay fixed. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to using multiple profiles rather than one. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: the profile setting applies across every modality and encoder, and most of the remaining configurations are multiprofile. Learning early whether it helps will narrow the search space considerably. Avgpool is the least confounded test of the multiprofile effect before trying the more complex transformer aggregation or other encoders and modalities.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an RNA-only multiprofile model with avgpool aggregation, keeping the PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, no image encoder, and no fusion, so the only change from the single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001) was the profile setting and its required aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.422 to 0.485 (+0.063), and the supporting F1 rose from 0.405 to 0.464 (+0.059), so moving to multiprofile input with avgpool is associated with a meaningful gain for this RNA-only PCA setup. Because multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation change together, the gain cannot be split between using multiple profiles and the choice of pooling. Each result also comes from a single run with no variance estimate, and it is unknown whether the benefit holds for other aggregations (e.g., transformer), other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or image and multimodal settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only RNA-only PCA models have been tested. Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised accuracy from 0.422 to 0.485 and F1 from 0.405 to 0.464. Whether the image modality carries useful signal is still completely unknown, yet about 42 of the remaining 49 configurations use images, alone or fused with RNA. 2. What this tests: An image-only ResNet50 model under the same multiprofile avgpool setting as the current best (config_002). Only the modality changes, so the result directly compares image and RNA signal strength. 3. Why it is the best use of budget: If image features are weak, the large multimodal region can be deprioritized in favor of RNA encoder and aggregation tuning. If they are competitive, it motivates fusion experiments. Testing aggregation (config_003) or RNA encoder (config_005) is narrower and can follow once this larger question is resolved.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested an image-only ResNet50 model under the same multiprofile avgpool setting as the current best RNA-only PCA (n=2000) model (llm_summary_002), so the comparison is between modality-plus-encoder pairs (ResNet50 images vs PCA RNA), not image vs RNA signal in general. It reached validation accuracy 0.471 (F1 0.442), slightly below the RNA-only multiprofile model (0.485 / 0.464; -0.014 accuracy, -0.022 F1) but above the single-profile RNA baseline (0.422 / 0.405). This is an initial observation that image features carry substantial signal, roughly competitive with RNA, so it does not support deprioritizing image-based or multimodal configurations. Because each result is a single run with no variance estimate, the small gap may be within noise, and it remains unknown whether the image and RNA signals are complementary (which fusion experiments would test), whether other image encoders or aggregations would change the ranking, and how the multiprofile/avgpool choice interacts with the image modality.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: going from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool improved RNA-only PCA from 0.422 to 0.485 accuracy. Image-only ResNet50 under the same multiprofile avgpool setting reached 0.471, close to RNA. Both modalities carry substantial signal, but whether they are complementary is untested, and this is a major design question. 2) Test: config_018 combines exactly these two tested components (PCA n2000 and ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool) using the simplest fusion, concat. Both unimodal anchors therefore share every other setting, so any gain or loss above 0.485 can be credited to adding a second modality via fusion. F1 will help judge small differences. 3) Why now: the multimodal configurations are the largest part of the search space. One controlled experiment tells us whether to prioritize fusion variants (weighted, transformer aggregation, other encoders) or focus the remaining budget on unimodal encoder and aggregation choices. It also has a reasonable chance of producing a new best model.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 tested the first multimodal model: multiprofile, avgpool aggregation, with the two encoders already tested alone (PCA n2000 for RNA and ResNet50 for images) combined by simple concat fusion, so its only difference from each unimodal anchor is the addition of the other modality through concat. It reached validation accuracy 0.421 (F1 0.412), well below both RNA-only multiprofile (0.485 / 0.464; -0.063 accuracy) and image-only multiprofile (0.471 / 0.442), and roughly level with the single-profile RNA baseline (0.422 / 0.405). In this setup, naive concat fusion therefore did not exploit any complementary signal and was associated with a clear drop, but this does not show that the modalities are redundant or that fusion in general is unhelpful. Possible explanations, such as feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between the PCA and ResNet50 features, untuned training, or a limitation specific to concat, are untested, and with single runs and no variance estimates it remains open whether other fusion strategies (e.g., weighted), other aggregations (e.g., transformer), or feature normalization would recover or exceed unimodal performance.

selection_reason: Evidence: multiprofile avgpool helped RNA-only PCA, going from 0.422 to 0.485 accuracy. Image-only ResNet50 under the same setting was nearly as good at 0.471. Yet concat fusion of the two (config_018) dropped to 0.421 accuracy (F1 0.412), below both unimodal models. Since both modalities carry substantial signal, the key open question is whether this failure is specific to naive concat (e.g., scale or dimensionality imbalance) or means fusion does not help here. config_019 changes only the fusion method (concat to weighted) and keeps everything else identical to config_018, so it cleanly isolates the effect of fusion strategy. If weighted fusion recovers or beats about 0.485, the whole multimodal branch of the search space stays worth exploring. If it also falls short, we can deprioritize multimodal configurations and focus the budget on unimodal encoder and aggregation choices. This makes it the most decision-relevant single-factor experiment right now.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 changed only the fusion method from llm_summary_004 (concat to weighted), keeping the multiprofile, avgpool, PCA n2000 RNA and ResNet50 image setup, so it isolates fusion strategy within this configuration. It reached validation accuracy 0.332 (F1 0.315). That is below concat fusion (0.421 / 0.412; -0.090 accuracy), well below RNA-only multiprofile (0.485 / 0.464) and image-only multiprofile (0.471 / 0.442), and the lowest result so far. Swapping concat for weighted did not recover unimodal performance and was associated with a further drop, so neither fusion strategy tried so far supports prioritizing multimodal configurations over unimodal ones in this setup. These are single runs with no variance estimates, and it remains untested whether the shared multimodal failure comes from something both fusions inherit, such as feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance, lack of normalization, untuned training or fusion weights, or the avgpool aggregation, rather than fusion being unhelpful in general. Other fusion methods, transformer aggregation and other encoders also remain unexplored.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n2000 with avgpool (0.485 accuracy / 0.464 F1). Moving from single-profile to multiprofile gave +0.063, but that gain is confounded with the avgpool choice. Both multimodal fusions dropped well below the unimodal models (concat 0.421, weighted 0.332). Avgpool is a shared factor that might contribute to that failure. Aggregation has never been varied. 2. Test: config_003 changes only avgpool to transformer, applied to the current best model. It shows whether learned attention over profiles beats mean pooling. It also helps separate the benefit of using multiple profiles from the specific pooling choice. 3. Why now: Aggregation affects every multiprofile configuration, whether RNA, image or multimodal, so this result will guide many later choices, including whether transformer aggregation is worth trying to rescue fusion. It is also a clean one-factor extension of the strongest configuration, so it is both informative and has a reasonable chance of improving the best score. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) are natural follow-ups once the better aggregation is known.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 changed only the aggregation of the previous best configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n2000) from avgpool to transformer, which isolates aggregation within this RNA-only setup. It reached validation accuracy 0.520 (F1 0.479), the best result so far, compared with avgpool (0.485 / 0.464; +0.035 accuracy, +0.015 F1) and the single-profile baseline (0.422 / 0.405). Within this configuration, transformer aggregation is associated with a further gain on top of the multiprofile improvement. Because the multiprofile-vs-avgpool confound in llm_summary_002 remains (multiprofile beats single-profile under both aggregations), the profile benefit is not fully separable from the pooling choice. The F1 gain is smaller than the accuracy gain, which may mean the improvement is uneven across classes. These are single runs with no variance estimates, so the modest margin may partly reflect noise. It also remains untested whether transformer aggregation helps image-only or multimodal models (including rescuing the failed concat and weighted fusions) or holds with other encoders such as scVI, scGPT or ViT-L.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Within RNA-only models, two single-factor steps have each been associated with gains. Multiprofile input raised accuracy from 0.422 to 0.485, and transformer aggregation raised it further to 0.520, the current best (F1 0.479). Image-only ResNet50 is roughly competitive at 0.471. Both multimodal fusions tried so far did worse than either single modality (concat 0.421, weighted 0.332). The RNA encoder is a major design choice that has not been tested at all, since every RNA result so far uses PCA n2000. 2) What this tests: config_009 keeps the best configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and changes only the encoder from PCA to the pretrained scGPT.
