This isolates whether a foundation-model RNA representation beats PCA under the strongest setting found so far. 3) Why it is the best use of the budget: it explores an untested dimension while building directly on the best result, so it has both learning value and a realistic chance of a new best. The answer also decides which RNA encoder later multimodal and fusion experiments should use. Testing whether transformer aggregation rescues fusion (config_020) is a reasonable alternative. However, multimodal has already failed twice, and its outcome would still be tied to the possibly suboptimal PCA encoder.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 changed only the RNA encoder of the previous best configuration (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) from PCA n2000 to pretrained scGPT, which isolates the encoder choice within this setup. It reached validation accuracy 0.542 (F1 0.483), a new best, compared with PCA (0.520 / 0.479; +0.022 accuracy, +0.004 F1), so in this configuration scGPT is associated with a modest gain over PCA. The F1 gain is much smaller than the accuracy gain, which suggests the improvement may be uneven across classes. With single runs and no variance estimates, the margin may partly reflect noise, and it remains untested whether the scGPT advantage holds under avgpool aggregation, in single-profile or multimodal settings (including whether it changes the failed concat and weighted fusions), or against scVI.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: transformer aggregation beat avgpool for RNA-only PCA (0.520 vs 0.485), and scGPT added a smaller further gain (0.542). Both multimodal runs so far used avgpool, and both fell below the unimodal anchors (concat 0.421, weighted 0.332). It is still unclear whether the problem is fusion itself or something those runs share, such as avgpool aggregation. 2) This experiment changes only the aggregation of config_018 (PCA n2000 + ResNet50, multiprofile, concat) from avgpool to transformer. That directly tests whether a learned aggregator recovers or exceeds unimodal performance (RNA-only PCA transformer: 0.520). 3) Whether multimodal fusion can work at all is the largest unresolved question, since it governs most of the remaining search space. A clean one-factor test against an existing anchor resolves it more efficiently than exploring encoders (scVI, ViT-L), which would only refine the already strong RNA-only branch. A remaining limitation is that the image-only transformer result (config_012) is still unknown, so a gain could not be fully credited to fusion rather than to the image branch alone.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 changed only the aggregation of the failed multimodal concat model (llm_summary_004: multiprofile, PCA n2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, concat fusion) from avgpool to transformer, which isolates aggregation within this multimodal setup. It reached validation accuracy 0.586 (F1 0.574), a new best: well above avgpool concat (0.421 / 0.412; +0.164 accuracy), and above RNA-only PCA transformer (0.520 / 0.479; +0.066) and RNA-only scGPT transformer (0.542 / 0.483; +0.044). The F1 gain is larger here than in the RNA-only runs, which may mean more balanced performance across classes. Within this configuration, transformer aggregation is associated with a large recovery, which suggests the earlier multimodal failures were at least partly tied to avgpool rather than to fusion being unhelpful in general. However, the image-only transformer result is still unknown, so the gain over RNA-only cannot yet be credited to complementary fusion rather than to a stronger image branch. These are single runs with no variance estimates, and it remains untested whether weighted fusion, scGPT, or other encoders (scVI, ViT-L) help under transformer aggregation in the multimodal setting.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is multimodal multiprofile PCA+ResNet50 with transformer aggregation and concat fusion (0.586 acc / 0.574 F1). It beats RNA-only transformer with PCA (0.520) and with scGPT (0.542). Transformer aggregation helped RNA-only modestly but rescued the multimodal model dramatically. However, image-only has only been tested with avgpool (0.471, close to RNA-only avgpool at 0.485), so we do not know how strong the image branch is under transformer aggregation. 2) Test: Image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile transformer aggregation changes only the aggregation relative to config_011. It is also the missing unimodal control for config_020. If it scores near 0.586, the multimodal gain is mostly a strong image branch plus transformer, not complementary fusion. If it scores well below, fusion is adding real complementary signal. 3) Why now: This single experiment determines whether to keep investing in fusion variants such as weighted fusion or scGPT+ResNet50 under transformer, or in image encoders such as ViT-L. Running those extensions first would compound an unresolved confound, so this control is the most informative use of the next run.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 ran the missing unimodal control for llm_summary_008: image-only ResNet50, multiprofile, with transformer aggregation. Its only difference from llm_summary_003 is the aggregation (avgpool to transformer). It reached validation accuracy 0.632 (F1 0.607), a new best, well above image-only avgpool (0.471 / 0.442; +0.161 accuracy) and above both multimodal PCA+ResNet50 concat transformer (0.586 / 0.574; +0.046) and RNA-only scGPT transformer (0.542 / 0.483). Within this setup, transformer aggregation is associated with a large gain for the image branch. Adding PCA RNA through concat fusion did not add complementary signal and was associated with lower performance than image alone, so the earlier multimodal gain over RNA-only appears attributable mainly to a strong image branch under transformer aggregation rather than to fusion. These are single runs with no variance estimates, and it remains untested whether other fusion strategies (e.g., weighted), a stronger RNA encoder (scGPT+ResNet50), or alternative image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) under transformer aggregation would surpass image-only performance.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation (0.632 accuracy, 0.607 F1). Transformer aggregation gave large gains in every setting tested. Adding PCA RNA through concat fusion lowered performance (0.586), so the image branch, not fusion, appears to drive current performance. The image encoder is the main untested factor: ViT-L has never been run. 2. Test: This experiment changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, in the current best image-only multiprofile transformer setup. It shows whether the strongest modality can be improved by a different backbone and whether the ResNet50 result is encoder-specific. 3. Why now: It exploits the strongest direction while answering an open design question with a clean one-factor change. The result will also decide which image encoder later multimodal runs should use (for example, scGPT plus the better image encoder with transformer aggregation). That makes it more informative per experiment than another fusion variant built on a possibly suboptimal image branch.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 changed only the image encoder of the previous best configuration (image-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation; llm_summary_009) from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, which isolates the encoder choice within this setup. It reached validation accuracy 0.653 (F1 0.628), a new best, compared with ResNet50 (0.632 / 0.607; +0.021 accuracy, +0.021 F1), so in this configuration ViT-L is associated with a modest gain that also shows up evenly in F1, and the strong image-only result does not appear specific to ResNet50. With single runs and no variance estimates, the margin may partly reflect noise. It remains untested whether the ViT-L advantage holds under avgpool aggregation or in multimodal settings, for example whether pairing ViT-L with scGPT or with other fusion strategies under transformer aggregation can finally exceed image-only performance, given that PCA+ResNet50 concat fell below image alone.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2. Test: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000 encoder) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference accuracy and F1. Later experiments can then each change one factor against it, such as encoder (scVI or scGPT), profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool), or modality (adding imaging). That lets us attribute each gain to a specific design choice. 3. Why now: With a limited budget and no prior evidence, a clean, low-complexity reference point is the most useful first experiment. It avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better, and every later comparison depends on it.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration in the search space: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.535 (F1 0.519). Because this is the first completed experiment, the result is a baseline reference point, not evidence that any design choice is better or worse. It is still unknown whether alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings with aggregation, or adding imaging via fusion would improve on it. Future experiments that change one factor at a time against this baseline are needed to attribute any differences.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001: acc 0.535, F1 0.519). We know nothing yet about whether the image modality is informative on its own. That is the most basic open question for a multimodal study, and every image-only and fusion configuration depends on the answer. 2) Test: config_010 is the simplest image-only model (single-profile, ResNet50, no aggregation or fusion). It matches the baseline's profile setting and has no extra components, so comparing it with config_001 isolates the effect of modality: RNA versus imaging. 3) Why now: knowing whether imaging is weaker than, similar to, or stronger than RNA tells us how much of the remaining budget to put into image-encoder choice and fusion versus RNA-encoder and multiprofile variations. One caveat: this single comparison uses only one encoder per modality, so it shows whether the image modality is worth pursuing, not which modality is better overall. It is still the best value for the second experiment, ahead of changes to RNA encoder, profile setting, or fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested the simplest image-only configuration: a single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.523 (F1 0.508), which is slightly below the RNA-only PCA baseline from llm_summary_001 (accuracy 0.535, F1 0.519). This initial observation suggests that imaging alone carries a broadly similar level of predictive signal to RNA alone under these settings, so the image modality looks worth pursuing. However, the roughly 1-point gap is small, comes from single runs with no variance estimate, and confounds modality with encoder choice (ResNet50 vs PCA), so it does not establish that either modality is better. It remains unknown whether other image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or RNA–image fusion would improve on either single-modality result, and whether the two modalities provide complementary information.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: we have two single-profile baselines. RNA-only with PCA reached 0.535 accuracy (F1 0.519). Image-only with ResNet50 reached 0.523 (F1 0.508). These are similar, so each modality carries comparable signal. It is still unknown whether the two modalities are complementary. 2) What this tests: config_016 fuses exactly these two tested encoders (PCA and ResNet50) in the single-profile setting with simple concat fusion. Any change from both baselines can therefore be attributed to adding the second modality, not to a new encoder, profile setting, or aggregation. 3) Why it is the best next experiment: whether multimodality helps is the most consequential design question in this search, because most of the remaining configurations are multimodal. A clean answer now tells us whether to spend the budget on fusion variants or on single-modality improvements such as multiprofile aggregation or alternative encoders. Concat is the simplest fusion choice, so it gives an interpretable reference before trying weighted fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a multimodal, single-profile model that concatenates the two previously tested encoders, PCA (2000 components) for RNA and ResNet50 for images, with no aggregation. Because the encoders and profile setting match the baselines, this run directly tests what adding the second modality via concat contributes. It reached validation accuracy 0.532 (F1 0.517), essentially matching the RNA-only baseline (0.535, F1 0.519) and slightly above image-only (0.523, F1 0.508), so simple concat fusion showed no evidence of complementary gain over the better single modality in this setting. These are single runs with no variance estimate and differences under about 1 point, so it remains uncertain whether this reflects true redundancy between modalities or a limitation of naive concat (e.g., dimensionality imbalance between 2000 PCA features and ResNet50 features), and whether weighted fusion, multiprofile aggregation, or alternative encoders would make multimodality beneficial.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: All three completed runs are single-profile and land within about 1 point of each other (0.523 to 0.535 accuracy). Concat fusion gave no gain over RNA alone. Profile setting and aggregation, which cover more than half of the remaining configurations, have never been tested. 2) What this tests: config_002 matches the RNA-only PCA baseline (config_001) except that it uses multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles improves accuracy and F1 over 0.535 and 0.519. Avgpool is the simplest aggregation, so it gives a clean first estimate before trying the transformer variant. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: whether multiprofile helps decides whether to prioritise the large multiprofile part of the space. That makes it more informative than refining fusion type or swapping encoders, since those factors could be revisited after this structural question is answered.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested a multiprofile version of the RNA-only PCA (2000-component) baseline with simple avgpool aggregation. All other settings match llm_summary_001, so this run isolates switching from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool. It reached validation accuracy 0.530 (F1 0.515), essentially matching or marginally below the single-profile baseline (0.535, F1 0.519). This initial observation gives no evidence that naive mean-pooling over multiple profiles improves RNA-only performance. These are single runs with no variance estimate, and the difference is under 1 point, so it remains uncertain whether multiprofile information is genuinely uninformative or whether avgpool fails to exploit it; learned aggregation (e.g., the transformer variant), multiprofile with imaging or fusion, and alternative encoders remain untested. All four completed configurations now fall within about 1.2 points of each other (0.523 to 0.535).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: All four completed runs fall within about 1.2 points of each other (0.523–0.535 accuracy, F1 0.508–0.519). Changing modality, adding concat fusion, and switching to multiprofile avgpool each produced no clear gain. Every run so far used the same encoders (PCA-2000 for RNA, ResNet50 for images), so representation quality is the largest untested factor and may be what limits the other design choices. 2. What this tests: Swapping only the RNA encoder from PCA to the pretrained scGPT foundation model, while keeping RNA-only and single-profile settings, isolates the effect of RNA representation against the strongest current baseline (config_001). 3. Why it is the best next experiment: RNA is currently the marginally stronger modality, and any later fusion or aggregation gains depend on having informative per-profile embeddings. A meaningful change in either direction will tell us whether encoder choice is a lever worth exploiting before spending budget on more complex multiprofile or multimodal combinations. scGPT also contrasts most strongly with PCA, giving the most uncertainty reduction per run; scVI (config_004) is a natural follow-up.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 changed only the RNA encoder of the RNA-only, single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001), swapping PCA-2000 for the pretrained scGPT foundation model, so it isolates the RNA representation. It reached validation accuracy 0.536 (F1 0.516), essentially identical to the PCA baseline (0.535, F1 0.519): accuracy is marginally higher and F1 marginally lower, and both differences are under 0.3 points. This initial observation gives no evidence that scGPT embeddings improve on PCA in this setting. All five completed configurations now fall within about 1.3 points of each other (0.523–0.536), which suggests a shared performance ceiling that none of the tested changes (modality, concat fusion, avgpool multiprofile, RNA encoder) has clearly moved. These are single runs with no variance estimate, so it remains uncertain whether encoder choice is truly unimportant or whether scGPT's potential is limited by how its embeddings are used here, for example frozen versus fine-tuned, or by the downstream head. Other untested options include scVI, alternative image encoders, learned (transformer) aggregation, and non-concat fusion. The search may also be limited by the task or labels rather than by architecture.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: All five completed runs fall within about 1.3 points (0.523–0.536 accuracy). Swapping the RNA encoder (PCA to scGPT), adding multiprofile avgpool, and adding concat fusion each produced no clear gain. The image encoder is the one major design axis that has not been varied, and image-only ResNet50 was the weakest result (0.523, F1 0.508). That leaves open whether imaging is limited by its representation. 2. Test: config_013 differs from config_010 only in the image encoder, replacing ResNet50 with ImageNet ViT-L. It therefore cleanly isolates the effect of image representation. 3. Why now: If ViT-L clearly improves image-only performance, that identifies the image encoder as a lever and points to the ViT-L multimodal and fusion configurations as the next targets. If it does not, that strengthens the evidence for a shared ceiling not driven by encoder choice, and future budget can shift to aggregation (transformer) or fusion (weighted). It is a cheap single-factor test of an untouched design choice, which is more informative under a limited budget than further RNA-side variations that have so far shown no effect.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the image encoder of the image-only, single-profile ResNet50 run (llm_summary_002), replacing ResNet50 with ImageNet ViT-L, so it isolates the image representation. It reached validation accuracy 0.421 (F1 0.412), about 10 points below ResNet50 (0.523, F1 0.508) and well outside the roughly 1.3-point band (0.523–0.536) of all earlier runs. This suggests that in this pipeline image encoder choice can strongly affect performance, but here only by lowering it; it gives no evidence that image representation is a lever for breaking the apparent shared ceiling, and it makes ViT-L multimodal and fusion configurations look less promising. This is a single run with no variance estimate, so it is uncertain whether ViT-L features are inherently worse for this task or whether the drop comes from implementation factors such as preprocessing or resolution mismatch, frozen versus fine-tuned use, or a downstream head poorly suited to ViT-L embeddings; learned (transformer) aggregation, weighted fusion, scVI, and other image encoders remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: all five comparable runs sit within about 1.3 points of each other (0.523–0.536). The only multiprofile run (config_002, RNA PCA with avgpool) matched the single-profile baseline (0.530 vs 0.535). That leaves open whether multiprofile data carries no extra signal or whether naive mean-pooling simply fails to use it. 2) Test: config_003 differs from config_002 only in aggregation (transformer instead of avgpool), keeping the RNA-only PCA-2000 multiprofile setup. This cleanly isolates whether learned aggregation can extract information from multiple profiles that averaging misses. 3) Value: aggregation affects about half of the remaining search space, because every multiprofile configuration, including all multiprofile fusion options, depends on it. A clear gain would point to a way past the apparent ceiling. A null result would let us down-weight the multiprofile branch and focus the remaining budget on fusion (weighted vs concat) and the scVI encoder. Using the cheap, well-understood RNA-only PCA setting avoids confounding the result with the image-encoder variability seen with ViT-L.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 changed only the aggregation of the RNA-only, multiprofile PCA-2000 run (llm_summary_004), replacing avgpool with a learned transformer aggregator, to test whether learned aggregation can extract multiprofile signal that mean-pooling misses. It reached validation accuracy 0.328 (F1 0.288), about 20 points below avgpool (0.530, F1 0.515) and far below the roughly 0.523–0.536 band of earlier runs. This is the largest drop seen so far, larger than ViT-L's 0.421. Because aggregation is the only changed factor, the drop is attributable to the transformer aggregator as implemented, so this run gives no evidence that learned aggregation breaks the apparent ceiling and weakens the case for transformer-based multiprofile and fusion configurations. However, this is a single run with no variance estimate, and the collapse may reflect implementation or training factors (e.g., undertraining, optimization instability, overfitting, or poorly tuned hyperparameters for the transformer) rather than an inherent limitation, so it remains unresolved whether multiprofile data carries extra signal at all.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: All reasonable runs fall in a narrow 0.523–0.536 band. Simple concat fusion of PCA-2000 and ResNet50 (config_016, 0.532 accuracy) showed no gain over RNA-only (0.535). It is still unclear whether the two modalities are redundant or whether naive concat cannot exploit them, for example because 2000 PCA features may swamp the ResNet50 features. Fusion type is the one major design axis not yet tested in isolation. ViT-L and transformer aggregation both dropped sharply, so they are poor carriers for further comparisons. 2) Test: config_017 changes only the fusion from concat to weighted. Encoders (PCA-2000, ResNet50) and profile setting (single-profile) are kept, so the run directly asks whether learned modality weighting gets complementary signal past the single-modality ceiling. 3) Why now: It is a clean one-factor comparison against an existing run and uses the best-performing encoders. Its result is relevant to roughly half of the remaining multimodal configurations, all of which use weighted fusion. A gain would point to a clear direction to exploit, such as multiprofile avgpool with weighted fusion. No gain would strengthen the case that the modalities are redundant and steer the remaining budget toward the untested scVI encoder or image multiprofile avgpool.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 changed only the fusion of the multimodal, single-profile PCA-2000 + ResNet50 run (llm_summary_003) from concat to weighted, isolating the fusion mechanism. It reached validation accuracy 0.688 (F1 0.659), about 15.6 points above concat (0.532, F1 0.517) and well above the 0.523–0.536 ceiling shared by all earlier runs, including the best single-modality result (RNA-only, 0.536). This is the first clear evidence that the two modalities can carry complementary signal. Because fusion is the only changed factor, the gain is attributable to weighted fusion as implemented, which makes the remaining weighted-fusion configurations (e.g., multiprofile avgpool, or scGPT/scVI with ResNet50) promising. However, this is a single run with no variance estimate, and the jump is unusually large, so it should be replicated and checked for implementation differences. It also remains uncertain which component of the weighted fusion module drives the gain (learned modality weights versus any per-modality projection or normalization that corrects the 2000-feature PCA dominance), and whether it transfers to other encoders or multiprofile settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Weighted fusion of PCA-2000 and ResNet50 (config_017) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. That is far above the 0.523-0.536 band of every other run, including concat fusion (0.532). This is the only strong positive signal so far, but it comes from a single run. Multiprofile has only been tested in RNA-only models. There, avgpool was neutral (0.530 vs 0.535) and the transformer aggregator collapsed (0.328). So it is unknown whether multiprofile helps once the modalities are fused effectively. 2) What this tests: config_019 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. It shows whether multiprofile adds signal on top of weighted fusion. It also gives a partial check on whether the weighted-fusion gain holds up in a neighboring setting. 3) Why this is the best next step: It exploits the strongest finding with a one-factor extension, so any difference can be attributed to the profile setting. It uses avgpool rather than the transformer aggregator, which already failed badly, so a poor result would not just repeat a known failure. Swapping the RNA encoder (config_041) is a reasonable alternative, but scGPT showed no gain over PCA in RNA-only runs. Profile setting is therefore the more open question.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 took the best configuration so far, multimodal PCA-2000 + ResNet50 with weighted fusion (llm_summary_008, 0.688 accuracy, F1 0.659), and changed only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. It reached validation accuracy 0.540 (F1 0.524), about 15 points below the singleprofile weighted-fusion run and back near the 0.523–0.536 band shared by every other run (only about 0.4 points above the earlier best of 0.536). Because multiprofile and avgpool necessarily change together here, the drop can be attributed to the multiprofile+avgpool combination as implemented rather than to either part alone. This gives no evidence that multiprofile adds signal on top of weighted fusion, consistent with avgpool being neutral in RNA-only runs (llm_summary_004). However, all results are single runs with no variance estimate, so two readings remain possible: multiprofile avgpool may genuinely erase the weighted-fusion gain (e.g., by mean-pooling diluting the complementary per-profile signal), or the 0.688 result may be fragile or an outlier. Replicating llm_summary_008 and testing weighted fusion with other encoders (e.g., scGPT + ResNet50, singleprofile) are needed to tell these apart.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Weighted fusion of PCA-2000 and ResNet50 in the single-profile setting (config_017) is the only run to break the 0.52–0.54 band shared by almost every other run. It reached 0.688 accuracy (F1 0.659). But it is a single run with an unusually large jump, and it remains unclear whether the gain is robust or specific to the PCA encoder. One possibility is that weighted fusion mainly corrects the dimensional dominance of the 2000 PCA features. Multiprofile avgpool erased the gain (config_019), and transformer aggregation and ViT-L both hurt, so single-profile weighted fusion with ResNet50 is the promising region. 2. What this tests: config_041 changes only the RNA encoder of config_017, from PCA-2000 to scGPT. scGPT matched PCA in the RNA-only setting (0.536 vs 0.535), so any difference here would reflect how the RNA representation interacts with weighted fusion. Replicating the gain would support weighted fusion as a robust driver and reduce concern that 0.688 is a fluke. A collapse back to about 0.53 would suggest the gain is PCA-specific or fragile. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It exploits the strongest direction found so far, with a reasonable chance of matching or beating the best result. It also isolates a single factor and directly addresses the main open question about the robustness and mechanism of the weighted-fusion gain. That makes it more informative than exploring the ViT-L or transformer-aggregation regions, which have already performed poorly.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 changed only the RNA encoder of the best configuration so far (llm_summary_008: multimodal, single-profile, ResNet50, weighted fusion, PCA-2000; 0.688 accuracy, F1 0.659), swapping PCA-2000 for scGPT. This isolates how the RNA representation interacts with weighted fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.653 (F1 0.628), about 3.5 points below the PCA version but about 12 points above the 0.523–0.540 band shared by every non-weighted-fusion single-profile run and the multiprofile avgpool run. This includes scGPT RNA-only (0.536), and scGPT had matched PCA in the RNA-only setting. This second large gain with a different RNA encoder reduces concern that 0.688 was a one-off. It also weakens the idea that the gain depends only on correcting the dimensional dominance of the 2000 PCA features, and it supports single-profile weighted fusion with ResNet50 as a robust promising region. Uncertainties remain: all results are single runs with no variance estimate, so the 3.5-point PCA-over-scGPT gap may not be meaningful. The specific component of the weighted fusion module driving the gain is still unidentified. Untested directions include scVI + ResNet50 with weighted fusion, replicates of either run, and whether any multiprofile aggregation can retain the gain.

selection_reason: 1. No experiments have been run yet, so we know nothing about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2. config_001 is the simplest model: RNA-only, a single profile, PCA features, and no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference point. Every later change can then be compared against it one factor at a time: a learned RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), the image modality, and fusion. 3. Starting with a cheap, interpretable baseline is the best use of a limited budget. It anchors later comparisons and guards against assuming that more complex models will do better.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) set a baseline using the simplest configuration: an RNA-only model with a single profile, PCA features (pca_n2000), and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.4849 and validation F1 0.4639. The F1 is close to the accuracy, which loosely suggests performance is not dominated by a few classes, though class balance and chance-level performance are not known here. No other experiments have been completed, so this is an initial reference point only. It is still unknown whether learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, the image modality, or fusion would improve on it, and run-to-run variance has not been estimated.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.485, F1 0.464). There is no information yet on the image modality, which is the largest open question for the multimodal half of the search space. 2) Test: config_010 is image-only, single-profile, ResNet50, with no aggregation or fusion. It is the simplest image counterpart to the baseline, so it measures how much signal the image modality carries on its own. Only the modality changes. 3) Value: whether images are informative decides if the ~36 multimodal configurations deserve budget. Image-only performance near or above RNA would make fusion worth pursuing; weak image performance would shift effort toward RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and multiprofile aggregation. This single run likely prunes more of the space than an RNA encoder or aggregation swap would at this stage.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested the simplest image counterpart to the RNA baseline: image-only, single-profile, ResNet50 image encoder, with no aggregation or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.6352 (F1 0.6183), above the RNA-only PCA baseline from llm_summary_001 (0.4849 / 0.4639). This is an initial indication that the image modality carries substantial standalone signal and that multimodal/fusion configurations may be worth budget. However, the comparison swaps both modality and encoder (ResNet50 vs pca_n2000), so it cannot separate the value of images from the choice of RNA representation; learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) might narrow the gap. Each result is a single run with no variance estimate, and it remains untested whether fusion or multiprofile aggregation improves on image-only.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Two single-profile, single-run baselines exist. Image-only ResNet50 (0.635 acc / 0.618 F1) clearly beats RNA-only PCA (0.485 / 0.464). So images carry strong standalone signal, but we do not know whether RNA adds information the image lacks. 2) Test: config_016 keeps the image setup of config_010 and the RNA setup of config_001, and combines them with simple concat fusion. Comparing it with both baselines gives a clean answer to whether multimodality helps, adds nothing, or hurts. 3) Why now: Most of the remaining search space (about 36 of 49 configs) is multimodal. Knowing early whether fusion adds value tells us whether to spend budget there or focus on image-only refinements such as ViT-L or multiprofile aggregation. Using the simplest fusion and the existing encoders avoids mixing in other design changes.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested the simplest multimodal combination of the two existing baselines: single-profile, PCA RNA features (pca_n2000) plus a ResNet50 image encoder, concat fusion, no aggregation. It reached validation accuracy 0.6530 (F1 0.6283), slightly above image-only ResNet50 (0.6352 / 0.6183, llm_summary_002) and well above RNA-only PCA (0.4849 / 0.4639, llm_summary_001). Because the encoders and profile setting match the baselines, this comparison isolates adding RNA via concat fusion. However, the gain over image-only is small (about +0.018 accuracy, +0.010 F1), and each result is a single run with no variance estimate, so it is only weak initial evidence that RNA adds complementary information. It is still unknown whether the gain is robust across seeds, whether stronger RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), other fusion methods, or multiprofile aggregation would widen it, and how multimodal gains compare with image-only refinements such as ViT-L.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: images carry most of the signal so far (image-only 0.635 vs RNA-only 0.485). Adding PCA RNA through concat fusion gave only a small, single-run gain (0.653 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Profile setting and aggregation have not been tested at all; every run so far is single-profile. 2. Test: config_018 keeps the best configuration (config_016: pca_n2000 + resnet50, concat) unchanged except for switching to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation, avgpool. This isolates the effect of multiprofile aggregation in the current best setting. 3. Why now: profile setting is a major untested design axis that may have a large effect. A one-variable change from the best configuration both explores that axis and exploits the strongest result. Its outcome will tell us whether later budget should go to aggregation variants (transformer) or to encoder and fusion refinements such as ViT-L, scVI or weighted fusion.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 tested multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation, keeping the otherwise-best configuration (llm_summary_003: multimodal, pca_n2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, concat fusion) unchanged. Validation accuracy fell to 0.5191 (F1 0.4797), well below the single-profile version (0.6530 / 0.6283) and image-only ResNet50 (0.6352 / 0.6183), and only slightly above RNA-only PCA (0.4849 / 0.4639). Because profile setting and aggregation were changed together, this is initial single-run evidence that multiprofile with simple avgpool hurts performance in this setup, but it cannot show whether the cause is multiprofile input itself or mean pooling. Several things remain open: run-to-run variance (the drop of about 0.13 accuracy looks larger than plausible noise but is unmeasured), whether learned aggregation such as a transformer would recover or exceed single-profile performance, and whether the effect is the same for image-only or RNA-only models. Until those are checked, encoder and fusion refinements in the single-profile setting look like the safer use of budget.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is single-profile multimodal PCA + ResNet50 with concat fusion (0.653 accuracy / 0.628 F1). Moving to multiprofile with avgpool (config_018) dropped accuracy sharply to 0.519. That run changed profile setting and aggregation together, so we cannot tell whether multiprofile input itself hurts or whether mean pooling throws away useful per-profile information. 2. What this tests: config_020 keeps config_018 exactly and swaps only avgpool for transformer aggregation. If accuracy recovers to or above about 0.65, mean pooling was the problem and multiprofile with learned aggregation stays a viable direction. If it stays near 0.52, multiprofile input is likely harmful here, which would justify deprioritizing about half of the remaining search space. 3. Why now: the profile-setting effect is the largest observed so far (about 0.13 accuracy), and it splits the remaining configurations into two large groups. Settling it with a single-variable comparison should save more budget than refining encoders or fusion, which can be tested next in whichever profile setting proves better.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 kept the multiprofile multimodal setup from llm_summary_004 (pca_n2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, concat fusion) and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer, to test whether mean pooling explained the multiprofile drop. Validation accuracy was 0.5321 (F1 0.5172), only slightly above avgpool (0.5191 / 0.4797) and still well below single-profile multimodal (0.6530 / 0.6283) and image-only ResNet50 (0.6352 / 0.6183). Because aggregation was the only change, this single-run comparison suggests that avgpool alone does not account for most of the roughly 0.12 to 0.13 accuracy gap, which points toward multiprofile input, as handled in this setup, being harmful here; the somewhat larger F1 gain (about +0.037) may hint that learned aggregation helps per-class balance modestly. It remains uncertain whether the transformer aggregator was adequately tuned or trained, whether the multiprofile penalty holds for image-only, RNA-only, or other encoder and fusion choices, and how large run-to-run variance is. Still, the evidence so far favors prioritizing single-profile configurations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Image features carry most of the signal so far (image-only ResNet50 scored 0.635, RNA-only PCA 0.485). Adding PCA RNA with concat fusion gave a small gain to 0.653. Two multiprofile runs dropped to about 0.52-0.53, whether pooled by avgpool or a transformer, so single-profile currently looks better. The image encoder has not been varied yet, and since images dominate performance it is likely the most important untested choice. 2) Test: This run keeps the current best setup (multimodal, single-profile, pca_n2000, concat) and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Any difference can then be attributed to the image encoder alone. 3) Why now: It extends the best-performing direction and answers a key design question in one run. If ViT-L helps, later RNA-encoder and fusion comparisons can build on the stronger backbone. If it does not, ResNet50 is confirmed and the budget can shift to the RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT) or to weighted fusion.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: multimodal, single-profile, pca_n2000 RNA, concat fusion) and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy fell to 0.5907 (F1 0.5727), below ResNet50 multimodal (0.6530 / 0.6283) and also below image-only ResNet50 (0.6352 / 0.6183). Because the encoder was the only change, this single-run comparison is initial evidence that ViT-L features, as used here, are worse than ResNet50 in this setup (about -0.062 accuracy, -0.056 F1), so ResNet50 remains the preferred backbone for now. It is still uncertain whether the drop comes from the ViT-L backbone itself or from setup factors such as preprocessing, input resolution, feature dimensionality relative to the PCA RNA features under concat, or training and tuning. It is also unknown whether the result holds for image-only models, and run-to-run variance has not been measured. Natural next steps are RNA-encoder (scVI, scGPT) or fusion-method comparisons on the ResNet50 single-profile setup.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_016 (multimodal, single-profile, pca_n2000 RNA plus ResNet50, concat fusion), at 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Its gain over image-only ResNet50 is small (about +0.018 accuracy, single runs). Multiprofile runs (avgpool and transformer) and ViT-L each did clearly worse, so single-profile ResNet50 is the backbone to build on. RNA representation is the largest untested factor. PCA RNA alone is weak (0.485), so the RNA branch may be adding little because its features are poor. 2) This test: keep config_016 fixed and swap only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200. That isolates whether a learned RNA representation strengthens the RNA contribution to fusion. It may also change how the two modalities are balanced under concat, since scVI gives far fewer dimensions than PCA. 3) Why now: it is a one-variable change on the current best setup, so it is both exploitative (it could raise the top score) and informative (it tests whether RNA encoder quality is what limits the multimodal gain). The outcome will guide whether to explore scGPT or move to fusion-method comparisons such as weighted fusion (config_017/029).
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration (llm_summary_003: multimodal, single-profile, ResNet50 image, concat fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, to test whether a learned RNA representation strengthens the multimodal gain. Validation accuracy fell to 0.5266 (F1 0.5104), well below PCA multimodal (0.6530 / 0.6283; about -0.126 accuracy, -0.118 F1) and also below image-only ResNet50 (0.6352 / 0.6183). Because the RNA encoder was the only change, this single run is initial evidence that the scvi_n200 swap, as configured here, hurts this concat setup, and that adding this RNA branch may degrade rather than complement the image signal. It is uncertain whether the drop reflects weaker scVI features, the much lower RNA dimensionality shifting modality balance under concat, or training and tuning factors; there is no RNA-only scVI baseline to separate these, and run-to-run variance is unmeasured, so scGPT or fusion-method comparisons (e.g., weighted fusion) remain open next steps.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_016 (multimodal, single-profile, pca_n2000 + ResNet50, concat fusion), at 0.6530 accuracy and 0.6283 F1. Its gain over image-only ResNet50 is small (+0.018) and comes from a single run. Several changes to this setup hurt performance: multiprofile with avgpool or transformer aggregation, the ViT-L image encoder, and the scVI RNA encoder. Fusion method is the one major design axis not yet tested. 2) Test: config_017 changes only concat to weighted fusion, keeping everything else from config_016. This isolates the effect of fusion. It also probes the open question from the ViT-L and scVI drops, where shifts in modality balance under concat were a suspected cause. 3) Why now: This is a one-variable extension of the best configuration, so it is both a chance to improve and a clean comparison. If weighted fusion helps, it shows how RNA should be combined with images and justifies retrying other RNA encoders with weighted fusion. If it does not help, concat stays the default and the next budget can go to scGPT.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 kept the best configuration (llm_summary_003: multimodal, single-profile, pca_n2000 RNA + ResNet50 image) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. Validation accuracy fell to 0.5121 (F1 0.4771), well below concat (0.6530 / 0.6283; about -0.141 accuracy, -0.151 F1) and image-only ResNet50 (0.6352 / 0.6183), and only modestly above RNA-only PCA (0.4849 / 0.4639). Because fusion was the only change, this single run is initial evidence that weighted fusion, as implemented here, is clearly worse than concat in this setup, so concat stays the default; the near-RNA-only level may hint that the learned weighting under-uses the image signal, but this is untested. It remains uncertain whether the drop reflects the weighted-fusion design itself or its implementation, initialization, or tuning, whether weighted fusion would behave differently with other RNA or image encoders, and how large run-to-run variance is. The earlier hypothesis that modality-balance fixes would rescue scVI or ViT-L gets no support from this run, which points next toward scGPT under concat.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is single-profile multimodal with pca_n2000 RNA, ResNet50 image and concat fusion (config_016: 0.6530 accuracy / 0.6283 F1). Every one-factor change from it has hurt, each by a single run. These were multiprofile input (both aggregators), ViT-L, scVI and weighted fusion. Its gain over image-only ResNet50 is small (+0.018 accuracy). So whether RNA truly adds complementary signal depends on the RNA representation, and scGPT is the only RNA encoder not yet tested. 2. Test: config_040 changes only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scGPT, keeping single-profile, ResNet50 and concat fixed. It asks whether a pretrained RNA representation can widen the multimodal gain over image-only, or whether learned RNA encoders generally hurt here as scVI did. 3. Why now: This is the last untested one-factor neighbor of the current best, so it has a plausible chance of improving accuracy. It also resolves a key open question about the RNA representation. Under a limited budget, it is more useful than further multiprofile or ViT-L runs, which current evidence disfavors.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 kept the best configuration (llm_summary_003: multimodal, single-profile, ResNet50 image, concat fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from pca_n2000 to scGPT, the last untested one-factor neighbor of the current best. Validation accuracy fell to 0.5251 (F1 0.4979), well below PCA multimodal (0.6530 / 0.6283; about -0.128 accuracy, -0.130 F1) and image-only ResNet50 (0.6352 / 0.6183), and close to the scvi_n200 swap (0.5266 / 0.5104, llm_summary_007). Because the RNA encoder was the only change, this single run is initial evidence that scGPT, as configured here, hurts this concat setup. Together with scVI, it suggests that the learned RNA encoders tried so far degrade rather than complement the image signal, and that pca_n2000 RNA is the only RNA representation tested that adds signal over image-only, and only a small amount. It remains uncertain whether the drops reflect weaker learned-encoder features, dimensionality or modality-balance effects under concat, or embedding extraction and tuning choices. There are no RNA-only scVI/scGPT baselines to separate these explanations, and run-to-run variance is unmeasured; the several runs clustering near 0.51 to 0.53 may also warrant checking for a shared failure mode. Since every one-factor neighbor of llm_summary_003 has now underperformed it, further gains may require multi-factor changes, seed replicates of the current best, or RNA-only learned-encoder baselines.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Multiprofile input has only been tested in the multimodal PCA+ResNet50 concat setup. There it cut accuracy by about 0.12 to 0.13 with both avgpool (0.519) and transformer aggregation (0.532), compared with single-profile (0.653). It is unclear whether multiprofile itself is harmful or whether it interacts badly with RNA concat fusion, since several multimodal variants collapse to about 0.51 to 0.53. 2. Test: Image-only ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, compared directly with image-only single-profile ResNet50 (config_010, 0.635). Transformer aggregation is used because it was the better aggregator before. This shows whether the multiprofile penalty holds for the strongest single modality without any fusion. 3. Why now: Profile setting covers about half the remaining search space. Learning whether it is harmful in general, or only within multimodal fusion, decides whether that space can be pruned or deserves more budget. That is more informative than another encoder swap around a best configuration whose one-factor neighbors have all underperformed.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 tested whether the multiprofile penalty seen in multimodal concat runs (llm_summary_004/005, about 0.52 to 0.53 vs 0.653 single-profile) also appears without RNA or fusion, using image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation. Validation accuracy was 0.5420 (F1 0.4833), well below image-only single-profile ResNet50 (llm_summary_002: 0.6352 / 0.6183; about -0.093 accuracy, -0.135 F1) and close to the multimodal multiprofile runs. This is initial single-run evidence that the multiprofile drop is not just an interaction with RNA concat fusion, and that multiprofile input as currently handled appears harmful in general, so deprioritizing that half of the search space looks reasonable. The comparison changes profile setting and aggregation together, so it cannot fully separate multiprofile input from the transformer aggregator, although llm_summary_005 found aggregation choice mattered little. It also remains uncertain whether the aggregation pipeline is adequately tuned or has a shared failure mode (many runs cluster near 0.51 to 0.54), whether RNA-only multiprofile behaves the same, and how large run-to-run variance is.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, cheapest reference point. It sets a baseline accuracy and F1 that every later change can be compared against, one factor at a time: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting (avgpool or transformer aggregation), image modality, and fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, a simple anchor makes later results interpretable and avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better. Starting with a complex configuration would mix several design choices together, so a good or bad result could not be attributed to any one of them.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest reference configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4106 (F1 0.3785). Because this is the first completed experiment, there is no comparison yet, so the result is only an initial baseline. It does not show whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image features, or fusion would help. It also remains unknown how much the result varies across random seeds or splits, so later single-factor changes should be compared against this anchor with that variance in mind.

selection_reason: 1) The only evidence so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001): accuracy 0.4106, F1 0.3785. No design factor has been varied yet, so every factor's effect is still unknown. 2) config_002 changes exactly one factor: it moves from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregator (avgpool), keeping the PCA RNA encoder and RNA-only setting. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps, separate from any effect of the aggregator design, encoder choice, or image fusion. 3) Profile setting is a major structural choice that applies across RNA-only, image-only, and multimodal branches. Getting a clean read on it early will guide many later choices, such as whether to test the transformer aggregator or focus on single-profile encoder comparisons. One limitation: seed variance is unknown, so a small difference from the baseline should be treated as tentative.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 changed one factor relative to the RNA-only, single-profile PCA (n=2000) baseline (llm_summary_001). It switched to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation and kept the RNA-only setting with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.4106 to 0.5305, and F1 rose from 0.3785 to 0.5152. This suggests that pooling multiple profiles may substantially benefit the RNA-only PCA setting, although because multiprofile and avgpool were introduced together, the gain cannot be attributed to multiprofile input separately from the aggregator choice. It remains uncertain how large seed or split variance is, whether the gain holds for other RNA encoders, image-only, or multimodal branches, and whether alternative aggregators (e.g., transformer) would perform better than avgpool.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool raised accuracy from 0.411 to 0.530 and F1 from 0.378 to 0.515. This is the strongest signal so far. But it comes from a single run, and the aggregator has only been tested as avgpool, so it is unclear how much of the gain depends on how profiles are pooled. 2. Test: config_003 keeps everything from the current best (config_002: RNA-only, PCA n2000, multiprofile) and changes only the aggregator to a transformer. This isolates the aggregation choice and shows whether learned attention over profiles beats simple averaging. 3. Why now: it is a clean single-factor follow-up to the most promising direction. It also exploits the best setting found so far. The answer will guide aggregator choice for later encoder, image and fusion experiments, so that later multiprofile runs are not confounded by a poorly chosen aggregator.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile PCA (n=2000) setup of llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to a transformer, isolating the aggregation choice. Validation accuracy dropped from 0.5305 to 0.5070 and F1 from 0.5152 to 0.4548, so in this single-run comparison transformer aggregation did not outperform simple averaging. Both multiprofile runs still exceed the single-profile baseline (0.4106 accuracy), which suggests the multiprofile benefit is not unique to avgpool. Uncertainty remains: each configuration was run once with unknown seed or split variance, the transformer's hyperparameters and capacity were not explored, and it is untested whether the ranking holds for other RNA encoders, image, or fusion settings, so avgpool is a reasonable but provisional default aggregator for later multiprofile experiments.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: All three completed runs use RNA with a PCA encoder. Multiprofile input with avgpool is the best so far (0.5305 accuracy, 0.5152 F1). It beat the single-profile baseline (0.4106) and transformer aggregation (0.5070). The image modality is completely untested, and it is the largest open question. Without it, no multimodal result can be interpreted, because a fusion gain or loss could not be attributed to the image features. 2. What this tests: config_011 is an image-only model using ResNet50 with the current best profile and aggregation setting (multiprofile, avgpool). It measures how informative image features are on their own. It can be compared directly with config_002 (RNA-only, same settings) to see how the two modalities rank. It also checks whether the multiprofile benefit extends beyond RNA. ResNet50 is the simpler image encoder, so it gives a reasonable anchor before trying ViT-L. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: Testing a new modality shapes later decisions more than another RNA-encoder swap. It tells us whether multimodal fusion configs are worth exploring and which image encoder to favour. It also changes only the modality relative to the best known setup, so the result stays interpretable.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested the image modality for the first time with an image-only, multiprofile model using a ResNet50 image encoder and avgpool aggregation, with no RNA encoder or fusion. It differs from the best RNA-only run (llm_summary_002) only in modality. It reached 0.4224 validation accuracy (F1 0.4051), well below the RNA-only PCA counterpart (0.5305 accuracy, 0.5152 F1) and only slightly above the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.4106). This is an initial single-run observation suggesting that ResNet50 image features alone are less informative than PCA RNA features under these settings, though they carry non-trivial signal. Several questions remain open: seed and split variance is unknown; there is no single-profile image-only run, so it is untested whether multiprofile pooling helps images as it did for RNA; ViT-L or other image encoders could perform differently; and it is unknown whether fusing image with RNA would add complementary information or dilute the stronger RNA signal.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: multiprofile avgpool clearly helps RNA-only PCA (0.531 vs 0.411 accuracy), and avgpool beat transformer (0.531 vs 0.507 accuracy, F1 0.515 vs 0.455). Image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool carries real but weaker signal (0.422). The biggest open question is whether adding images to RNA helps or dilutes the stronger RNA signal. 2) config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA + ResNet50, avgpool, concat fusion) changes one factor from the best run (config_002): it adds the ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion. It also combines the two components already tested alone (config_002 and config_011), so the result directly shows whether the modalities are complementary. 3) This is the best use of the budget because fusion is a central design question that no run has addressed yet, and this test builds on the strongest configuration, so it is also a reasonable bet for improving accuracy. Concat is the simplest fusion baseline; weighted fusion, ViT-L images, and alternative RNA encoders can be compared against it in later runs.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested the first multimodal configuration. It added a ResNet50 image branch with simple concat fusion to the best RNA-only setup (llm_summary_002: multiprofile, PCA n=2000, avgpool), so it differs from that run only in the added image branch and fusion. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5305 to 0.4849 (F1 from 0.5152 to 0.4639), though it stayed above the image-only run (0.4224) and the single-profile RNA baseline (0.4106). In this single-run comparison, naive concatenation of ResNet50 image features did not add complementary information and may have diluted the stronger RNA signal. It remains uncertain whether this reflects the modalities themselves or the fusion choice, for example feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between the 2000-dim PCA and ResNet50 embeddings, or the lack of weighting or regularization. Seed and split variance is unknown, and weighted or other fusion strategies, ViT-L image features, and alternative RNA encoders remain untested against this concat baseline.

selection_reason: Evidence: multiprofile avgpool is the strongest direction so far (RNA-only PCA, 0.5305 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 image features with concat fusion lowered accuracy to 0.4849, even though image-only features carry real signal (0.4224). It is unclear whether this drop means images add nothing useful, or whether naive concat let the weaker or mismatched image features dilute the RNA signal. This experiment keeps everything identical to config_018 (multiprofile, PCA n=2000, ResNet50, avgpool) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. That isolates the fusion choice. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds the RNA-only result, multimodal integration is viable and the remaining fusion configs are worth exploring. If it still underperforms, that suggests ResNet50 image features add little here, and the budget should shift toward RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or ViT-L. It is the most direct single-factor test of the main open question about whether, and how, fusion helps.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the llm_summary_005 multimodal setup (multiprofile, PCA n=2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, avgpool) and changed only concat fusion to weighted fusion, isolating the fusion choice. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.4849 to 0.2266 (F1 from 0.4639 to 0.1907), well below the RNA-only avgpool run (0.5305), the image-only run (0.4224) and the single-profile RNA baseline (0.4106). In this single-run comparison, weighted fusion as implemented performed much worse than concat and did not recover the RNA-only result, so it provides no evidence yet that multimodal integration with ResNet50 features helps here. Because performance dropped below either modality alone, the result may reflect an optimization or implementation problem with the weighted fusion (e.g., degenerate or poorly initialized modality weights) rather than the intrinsic value of image features; seed and split variance, the learned weights, and other fusion strategies, image encoders (ViT-L), and RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) all remain unexamined.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The strongest result so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n=2000 with avgpool (0.5305 accuracy, 0.5152 F1). Multiprofile pooling helped RNA. Avgpool beat transformer aggregation in one comparison. Image-only ResNet50 was weaker (0.4224), and both fusion attempts lowered accuracy (concat 0.4849, weighted 0.2266). The RNA encoder is the dominant signal source, yet it is still completely untested: only PCA has been run. 2. What this tests: config_008 keeps the best setup (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder from PCA to scGPT. This directly measures whether a pretrained RNA representation improves on PCA in the most reliable setting we have. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: It is a clean single-factor comparison on the most important unexplored axis, with a realistic chance of a new best. The result will also guide later multimodal runs, since an RNA baseline that cannot beat PCA would make the scGPT fusion configurations less promising. Further fusion runs with the current weak image features seem less informative until the RNA representation question is settled. If scGPT underperforms, scVI (config_005) is the natural follow-up.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup from llm_summary_002 and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA (n=2000) to pretrained scGPT, which isolates the encoder choice. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5305 to 0.5856 and F1 from 0.5152 to 0.5745, making this the best result so far. In this single-run comparison, the scGPT representation outperformed PCA under these settings, which strengthens the view that the RNA representation is a key lever. Uncertainty remains: seed and split variance is unknown, so the size of the roughly 5.5-point gain is not yet confirmed. It is untested whether scGPT's advantage holds with single-profile input or transformer aggregation, how scVI compares, and whether scGPT-based multimodal fusion would avoid the drops seen when ResNet50 image features were combined with PCA (concat 0.4849, weighted 0.2266).

selection_reason:
1. Evidence and uncertainty: The RNA encoder looks like the strongest lever so far. In the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setting, scGPT scored 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1, against 0.531 and 0.515 for PCA. scVI is the only RNA encoder not yet tested. Adding images has hurt in both tries (concat 0.485, weighted 0.227). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation in the one comparison run.
2. What this tests: config_005 keeps the best setting (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps in scVI (n=200) as the only change. This completes the three-way encoder comparison under one setting. It shows whether a compact, task-agnostic latent model can match or beat pretrained scGPT, and whether PCA's lower score comes from dimensionality or from the type of representation.
3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Settling the encoder ranking first means later multimodal and aggregation runs build on the strongest RNA backbone. It also avoids changing several factors at once. The run has a reasonable chance of a new best result, and even a weak scVI result would tell us something useful.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup from llm_summary_002 and llm_summary_007 and changed only the RNA encoder to scVI (n=200), which completes a single-run, three-way encoder comparison under one setting. Validation accuracy was 0.6186 (F1 0.6103), the best result so far, above scGPT (0.5856 accuracy, 0.5745 F1) and PCA n=2000 (0.5305, 0.5152), with F1 following the same ranking. This suggests that, under these settings, the compact scVI latent representation is at least competitive with pretrained scGPT and that RNA encoder choice remains the strongest lever observed, making scVI a reasonable provisional RNA backbone. Uncertainties remain: seed and split variance is unknown, so the roughly 3.3-point margin over scGPT may not be robust. Because scVI differs from PCA in both dimensionality (200 vs 2000) and representation type, this run cannot separate those explanations for PCA's lower score. It is also untested whether scVI's advantage holds under single-profile input, transformer aggregation, or multimodal fusion, which previously hurt performance with PCA (concat 0.4849, weighted 0.2266).

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA encoder choice is the strongest lever so far. scVI multiprofile avgpool reached 0.619, versus 0.586 for scGPT and 0.531 for PCA. Images have only been tested with ResNet50, which was weak alone (0.422). Adding ResNet50 to PCA hurt: concat gave 0.485 and weighted fusion gave 0.227. Most of the remaining budget space is multimodal, and it is unclear whether that weakness comes from the image modality itself or from the ResNet50 representation. 2) This run changes only the image encoder relative to config_011 (image-only, multiprofile, avgpool), from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It isolates whether a stronger image representation carries more signal. 3) Why now: the result decides which image backbone to pair with scVI or scGPT in later fusion tests. If ViT-L is clearly better, scVI+ViT-L fusion becomes the logical next test. If it is also weak, the evidence favors RNA-only models and saves budget on many multimodal runs. Either way, one cheap single-factor run cuts uncertainty about half of the untested multimodal space.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the image-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup of llm_summary_004 and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, isolating the image backbone choice. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.4224 to 0.2239 (F1 from 0.4051 to 0.1843), making it the worst result so far, slightly below even the failed weighted-fusion run (0.2266) and far below scVI RNA-only (0.6186). In this single-run comparison, ImageNet ViT-L features did not provide a stronger image representation than ResNet50, and neither image backbone has yet come close to RNA-only performance, which provisionally favors RNA-centric models and ResNet50 as the default image encoder for any future fusion tests. Because the drop is so large, it may reflect a setup problem rather than the backbone's intrinsic value, for example preprocessing or resolution mismatch, embedding scale or dimensionality, or optimization settings poorly suited to ViT-L features. Seed and split variance is also unknown, and it is untested whether either image encoder adds complementary signal when fused with scVI or scGPT.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA encoder choice is the strongest lever observed so far. The best run is RNA-only multiprofile scVI with avgpool (0.6186 acc, 0.6103 F1). Multimodal fusion has only been tested with the weaker PCA encoder, where concat lowered accuracy (0.5305 to 0.4849) and weighted fusion collapsed. So it is still unclear whether image features are unhelpful in general or only hurt the PCA setup, for example because of scale or dimensionality imbalance. 2. What this tests: config_030 adds ResNet50, the better image encoder, with concat fusion to the best scVI setup, so modality is the only change. It shows whether image features add complementary signal on top of a stronger, compact RNA representation. It also checks whether the earlier fusion drop carries over across RNA encoders. 3. Why it is the best next run: whether multimodality helps is a central design question in this study, and this is the cleanest single-factor test of it against the current best anchor. If accuracy improves, it opens a high-performing direction to exploit. If it drops again, it gives strong evidence for RNA-centric models and lets the remaining budget skip much of the multimodal space. Transformer aggregation and single-profile scVI matter less, since transformer already underperformed avgpool and multiprofile clearly beat single-profile with PCA.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 added a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the best RNA-only setup (llm_summary_008: multiprofile, scVI n=200, avgpool), so it differs from that anchor only in the added image branch and fusion. Validation accuracy collapsed from 0.6186 to 0.2079 (F1 from 0.6103 to 0.1718). That is far below the scVI RNA-only run, the image-only ResNet50 run (0.4224) and the earlier PCA concat run (0.4849), and comparable to the failed weighted-fusion (0.2266) and ViT-L image-only (0.2239) runs. In this single-run comparison, naive concat fusion with ResNet50 features did not help with the stronger scVI encoder either, and the drop was far larger than with PCA. This provisionally strengthens the case for RNA-centric models. However, because performance fell below either modality alone, the result likely reflects an optimization, scaling or implementation problem rather than the intrinsic value of image features. One candidate is imbalance between the compact 200-dim scVI latent and the ResNet50 embeddings. The causes of this collapse and of the other near-0.21 to 0.23 results remain undiagnosed, as do seed and split variance and whether normalized, projected or regularized fusion would recover RNA-only performance.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest configuration available. It sets a reference baseline that later changes can be compared against one factor at a time: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting and aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image modality, and fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, a cheap and easy-to-interpret anchor is the best first step. It lets us judge whether added complexity actually helps rather than assuming it does, and makes it possible to build the next comparisons by changing one variable at a time.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest available configuration as a reference baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA encoder with 2000 components, and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.7207, the primary metric, and a validation F1 of 0.6815. The F1 being lower than accuracy may mean performance is uneven across classes, but this is not confirmed. Because there are no prior experiments to compare against, this result is only an initial baseline. It says nothing yet about whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multi-profile aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image inputs, or fusion would help or hurt. Those effects should be tested by changing one factor at a time against this anchor, and run-to-run variance is also still unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001). It reached 0.7207 accuracy and 0.6815 F1. We do not yet know the effect of any other factor. 2) Test: config_002 changes one thing, moving from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). Encoder and modality stay fixed. This directly measures whether pooling information across profiles helps. Profile setting runs through about two-thirds of the remaining space, including every multiprofile RNA, image and multimodal option. 3) Why now: knowing the multiprofile effect early tells us which part of the large multiprofile space is worth exploring. Using avgpool rather than the transformer gives a clean, low-complexity first comparison against the anchor. One limitation: run-to-run variance is unknown, so a small difference between the two runs should not be read as conclusive. Encoder and modality comparisons (scVI, scGPT, image-only) are natural next steps once this factor is better understood.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 changed one factor from the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) baseline (llm_summary_001): it moved from single-profile to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation, keeping the encoder and modality fixed. Validation accuracy (primary metric) rose slightly from 0.7207 to 0.7250 (+0.0043), and validation F1 moved in the same direction, from 0.6815 to 0.6847. Because this is one run per configuration and run-to-run variance is unknown, this small gain is only a tentative sign that average-pooling across profiles may help a little. It is not yet a reliable effect. It remains untested whether a stronger aggregator (transformer), other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image inputs, or fusion would change the multiprofile picture, and repeated seeds would help establish whether differences of this size are meaningful.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: We have only an RNA-only PCA anchor (0.7207 accuracy / 0.6815 F1) and a one-factor change to multiprofile avgpool (0.7250 / 0.6847). That +0.004 gain is small, comes from single runs, and is not yet reliable. The biggest open question is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all. Most of the remaining search space (36 of 49 configurations) involves image encoders, and we have no image evidence yet. 2) What this tests: An image-only, single-profile ResNet50 run with no aggregation or fusion gives a clean image baseline. It is directly comparable to the RNA-only single-profile anchor (config_001), differing only in modality. It shows whether images alone are competitive with, weaker than, or complementary to RNA, which is a prerequisite for interpreting any later fusion results. 3) Why now: Refining aggregation (transformer) or swapping RNA encoders would mostly fine-tune within the RNA-only region. Establishing image-only performance first reduces uncertainty about whether to invest the limited budget in multimodal and image configurations or to concentrate on RNA variants. ResNet50 single-profile is the simplest and cheapest image reference point.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 set up the first image-only reference point: a ResNet50 image encoder with single-profile input and no aggregation or fusion, compared against the RNA-only single-profile PCA (n=2000) anchor (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5321 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.5172, about 0.19 accuracy below the RNA anchor (0.7207 / 0.6815). This gap is much larger than the +0.004 multiprofile difference seen earlier, so on this single run, images processed this way look substantially weaker than RNA alone. Because modality and encoder change together (ResNet50 vs. PCA), the comparison cannot say whether the gap comes from the image modality itself or from this encoder choice, and run-to-run variance is still unknown. It also remains untested whether other image encoders, multiprofile image aggregation, or fusion with RNA could add signal beyond the RNA baseline.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA is the strongest anchor so far (single-profile 0.7207 accuracy; multiprofile avgpool 0.7250, a small and uncertain gain). Image-only ResNet50 is much weaker (0.5321). The central question for multimodal profiling is still untested: does image information add anything on top of RNA, or does it dilute it? 2. What this tests: config_016 adds ResNet50 image features to the config_001 baseline (single-profile, PCA n2000) with simple concat fusion. Modality is the only factor that changes, so any difference can be attributed to adding images. This is not true of options like a multiprofile multimodal run, which would also change aggregation. The accuracy and F1 differences will show whether images carry complementary signal even though they are weak alone. 3. Why now: the result determines whether the large multimodal portion of the search space deserves budget. If concat fusion gives no gain or hurts, effort can shift to RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation. If it helps, fusion type and the image encoder become worthwhile next tests.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 tested whether image information adds to RNA by adding ResNet50 image features to the RNA-only single-profile PCA (n=2000) anchor (llm_summary_001) using simple concat fusion, with modality as the only changed factor. Validation accuracy (primary metric) fell sharply from 0.7207 to 0.4106, and validation F1 fell from 0.6815 to 0.3785. Both values are also well below the image-only ResNet50 run (0.5321 / 0.5172), so in this setup adding images via concat hurt rather than helped, and the drop is far larger than the ~0.004 multiprofile difference seen earlier.
