Because the fused model underperforms even its weaker unimodal component, the result may reflect a problem with this concat fusion setup (for example, feature scale or dimensionality imbalance, or optimization issues) rather than images carrying no complementary signal; this is a single run with unknown run-to-run variance, and other fusion types, normalization, or image encoders remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA is the strongest result so far (about 0.721 accuracy single-profile, 0.725 with multiprofile avgpool). Image-only ResNet50 is much weaker at 0.532. Concat fusion of the two collapsed to 0.411 accuracy and 0.378 F1, below even the weaker image-only model. That points to a problem with the concat fusion setup, such as feature scale or dimensionality imbalance, rather than proof that images add nothing. It is the biggest open question in the search. 2. What this tests: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 fixed (multimodal, single-profile, PCA n2000, ResNet50) and changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted. This isolates whether the multimodal collapse comes from the fusion mechanism. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: if weighted fusion recovers to near or above the RNA baseline, the many multimodal configurations stay worth exploring, and weighted fusion becomes the preferred way to combine modalities. If it also fails, that is strong evidence to deprioritize multimodal configurations and spend the limited budget on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and aggregation. Either outcome prunes a large part of the search space with one controlled experiment.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted, relative to the multimodal single-profile PCA (n=2000) + ResNet50 run (llm_summary_004), to test whether the multimodal collapse was specific to concat fusion. Validation accuracy (primary metric) rose from 0.4106 to 0.5121 (+0.10), and F1 rose from 0.3785 to 0.4771. Because fusion was the only changed factor, this suggests weighted fusion is less harmful than concat in this setup, though it is a single run with unknown variance. However, weighted fusion still falls well short of the RNA-only anchor (0.7207 / 0.6815) and slightly below even image-only ResNet50 (0.5321 / 0.5172), so neither tested fusion method has shown any benefit from adding images. Since the fused model still underperforms both of its unimodal components, a broader multimodal setup issue (for example, feature scaling or normalization, optimization, or how fusion weights are learned) remains a plausible but untested explanation; other fusion types, image encoders, and multiprofile multimodal settings are also untested, so multimodal configurations currently look low-priority relative to RNA encoder and aggregation exploration.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA is clearly the strongest modality so far. RNA-only PCA reached about 0.72 accuracy, compared with 0.53 for image-only and 0.41–0.51 for both multimodal runs. Multiprofile avgpool gave only a small, uncertain gain (+0.004). The RNA encoder, which likely drives most of the performance, has only been tested with PCA (n=2000). 2. What this tests: config_004 swaps PCA for scVI (n=200) and keeps everything else matched to the anchor config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion). Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the encoder alone. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: the encoder question is the largest open question on the best-performing modality and could plausibly produce bigger gains than tuning aggregation. The result also tells us which RNA encoder to carry forward into multiprofile and multimodal tests. Multimodal configurations stay low priority until a better RNA base, or a fix for the fusion collapse, is identified.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 changed only the RNA encoder from PCA (n=2000) to scVI (n=200) relative to the RNA-only single-profile anchor (llm_summary_001), keeping modality, profile setting, aggregation, and fusion fixed. Validation accuracy (primary metric) dropped sharply from 0.7207 to 0.5070 (-0.21), and F1 dropped from 0.6815 to 0.4548. This makes the scVI run the weakest unimodal result so far, below image-only ResNet50 (0.5321 / 0.5172), and the drop is far larger than the ~0.004 multiprofile difference. Because the encoder was the only changed factor, this single run suggests that scVI with 200 dimensions, as configured here, is substantially worse than PCA (n=2000) in this pipeline, so PCA remains the RNA encoder to carry forward. It is uncertain whether the gap reflects scVI itself, the much smaller latent dimensionality (200 vs. 2000, which changes together with the method), or setup issues such as scVI training, latent normalization, or downstream classifier fit. Run-to-run variance is unknown, and scGPT, other scVI latent sizes or settings, and scVI under multiprofile aggregation remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: PCA (n=2000) is the strongest RNA encoder so far, at 0.7207 single-profile and 0.7250 multiprofile with avgpool. scVI (n=200) scored far lower (0.5070), so the encoder choice changed accuracy by about 0.21. Aggregation changed it by only about 0.004, which may be run-to-run noise. scGPT is the only RNA encoder not yet tested, and RNA is clearly the dominant modality. 2) What this tests: running scGPT RNA-only, single-profile, against the config_001 anchor changes only the encoder. It shows whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding can match or beat PCA, or whether PCA's lead holds across encoder families. 3) Why this is the best use of budget: the encoder has had the largest effect of any factor so far, and its result determines which encoder all later aggregation and fusion experiments should build on. Testing transformer aggregation on PCA (config_003) is still valuable, but past aggregation effects were small, so it can follow once the encoder choice is settled.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 changed only the RNA encoder from PCA (n=2000) to scGPT, relative to the RNA-only single-profile anchor (llm_summary_001), keeping modality, profile setting, aggregation, and fusion fixed. Validation accuracy (primary metric) dropped from 0.7207 to 0.5305 (-0.19), and F1 dropped from 0.6815 to 0.5152. scGPT therefore lands slightly above scVI (0.5070 / 0.4548) and close to image-only ResNet50 (0.5321 / 0.5172). Because the encoder was the only changed factor, this single run suggests that, as configured here, neither pretrained or learned RNA embedding tested so far (scVI, scGPT) matches PCA in this pipeline, so PCA remains the RNA encoder to carry forward into aggregation (e.g., transformer) and fusion experiments. It is uncertain whether the gap reflects scGPT itself or setup factors that change along with the encoder, such as embedding dimensionality, gene vocabulary or preprocessing mismatch, lack of fine-tuning, embedding normalization, or downstream classifier fit. Run-to-run variance is also unknown, and scGPT under multiprofile aggregation or with alternative extraction settings remains untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: RNA-only PCA (n=2000) is clearly the strongest branch so far, at 0.721 accuracy single-profile and 0.725 multiprofile with avgpool. The other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), the image-only model and both multimodal fusions all fell about 0.19 to 0.31 below it. Avgpool gave only a small, uncertain gain (+0.004 accuracy, with F1 moving the same way), and no learned aggregator has been tested. 2. Question: this run changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, keeping the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA setup fixed. It tests whether learned attention across profiles extracts more signal than simple averaging. It also helps judge whether multiprofile input really matters: a clear gain would support it, while a similar or lower score would suggest the profile setting has little effect. 3. Why now: it extends the best-performing direction and isolates a single design factor, aggregation, that has not been tested. That makes it informative whatever the result, and it is the most likely run to set a new best. The image encoder alternative (ViT-L) is the main open exploration question, but given how weak the image and multimodal results have been, the aggregation question on the strongest backbone is the better use of this run.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 changed only the aggregation from avgpool to transformer, relative to the best configuration so far (llm_summary_002: RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n=2000). Validation accuracy, the primary metric, fell from 0.7250 to 0.6390 (-0.086), and F1 fell from 0.6847 to 0.6197. The run also lands below the single-profile PCA anchor (0.7207 / 0.6815), though it remains well above the scVI, scGPT, image-only and multimodal runs (about 0.41 to 0.53). Because aggregation was the only changed factor, this single run suggests the transformer aggregator, as configured here, is worse than simple averaging, so avgpool multiprofile PCA remains the best setup. It is uncertain whether the drop reflects learned attention itself or setup factors such as transformer size, training budget, regularization or overfitting, or the number of profiles per sample. Run-to-run variance is still unknown, so this result neither confirms nor rules out the small (+0.004) multiprofile benefit seen with avgpool.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA PCA (n=2000) is clearly the strongest encoder (about 0.72 accuracy), well ahead of scVI and scGPT (about 0.51 to 0.53). Avgpool multiprofile gives at most a tentative +0.004 gain, and transformer aggregation hurt. Image-only ResNet50 reached only 0.532, and both multimodal ResNet50 fusions (concat 0.411, weighted 0.512) scored below their weaker unimodal component. The image encoder is the one major design factor not yet varied, so we cannot tell whether images are weak in general or ResNet50 features are simply poor here. 2) What this tests: config_013 swaps ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L in the image-only single-profile setting and changes nothing else. Comparing it directly with config_010 isolates the effect of the image representation. 3) Why this is the best next run: the outcome decides whether any of the large multimodal space (roughly half of the remaining configurations use ViT-L) is worth budget. If ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50, PCA + ViT-L fusion becomes a principled next step. If it does not, the evidence that images add little supports concentrating the remaining budget on RNA PCA variants. It is a clean one-factor comparison with high decision value.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, relative to the image-only single-profile run (llm_summary_003), keeping modality, profile setting, aggregation, and fusion fixed. Validation accuracy (primary metric) rose from 0.5321 to 0.6352 (+0.10), and F1 rose from 0.5172 to 0.6183. Because the encoder was the only changed factor, this single run suggests that ResNet50 features were a major reason images looked weak, not only the image modality itself. ViT-L image-only is still below the RNA PCA runs (0.7207 single-profile, 0.7250 avgpool multiprofile) and roughly level with transformer-aggregated PCA (0.6390). It is uncertain whether ViT-L features add signal that complements RNA, since PCA + ViT-L fusion is untested and both earlier ResNet50 fusions underperformed their weaker unimodal component, possibly because of fusion setup issues. Run-to-run variance is unknown, and other image encoders and multiprofile image aggregation also remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: PCA (n=2000) is the clear RNA encoder, with 0.7207 single-profile and 0.7250 with avgpool multiprofile. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L raised image-only accuracy from 0.5321 to 0.6352. Both multimodal runs so far used ResNet50 and fell below their weaker unimodal part. Weighted fusion (0.5121) did better than concat (0.4106). The main open question is whether stronger image features add signal beyond RNA, or whether fusion itself is the problem in this pipeline. 2) This run changes only the image encoder relative to config_017 (PCA + ResNet50, single-profile, weighted fusion). It directly tests whether ViT-L features rescue multimodal performance. It also compares against two anchors: RNA-only PCA (0.7207) and ViT-L image-only (0.6352). Single-profile keeps aggregation out of the picture. 3) Multimodality is the largest untested lever with real upside, and this is the cleanest one-factor test of it. If the run beats or matches 0.72, multiprofile avgpool fusion with ViT-L becomes the logical next step. If it still falls below both unimodal parts, that points to a systematic fusion problem and justifies spending the remaining budget on RNA-side and image aggregation experiments.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, relative to the multimodal single-profile PCA (n=2000) weighted-fusion run (llm_summary_005), to test whether stronger image features rescue multimodal performance. Validation accuracy (primary metric) fell sharply from 0.5121 to 0.2239 (-0.29), and F1 fell from 0.4771 to 0.1843. This is the worst result so far and far below both unimodal parts, RNA-only PCA (0.7207 / 0.6815) and ViT-L image-only (0.6352 / 0.6183). Because a stronger image encoder that improved image-only accuracy by about 0.10 made the fused model much worse, this single run strengthens the earlier suspicion of a systematic problem in this fusion pipeline, such as feature scale or dimensionality imbalance (ViT-L features may differ in size or scale from ResNet50), normalization, optimization, or how fusion weights are learned, rather than evidence that images carry no complementary signal. The specific cause is not isolated, run-to-run variance is unknown, and a possible implementation or training failure cannot be ruled out. Further multimodal runs look low-value unless the fusion setup is diagnosed or changed (for example, feature normalization or late or ensemble-style fusion); otherwise, avgpool multiprofile PCA (0.7250) remains the best configuration.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest baseline in the space. It gives a reference point for accuracy and F1 that later experiments can each change along one axis. Examples: switching to multiprofile avgpool (config_002) tests the profile setting, swapping to scVI or scGPT (config_004/007) tests the RNA encoder, and adding images with concat fusion (config_016) tests multimodality. 3) Under a limited budget, starting with the simplest baseline makes every later comparison easier to interpret. It also guards against assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models are necessarily better.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001, corresponding to config_001) tested the simplest configuration in the search space: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA-2000 RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5856 (F1 0.5745). Because this is the only completed experiment, it should be treated as an initial baseline reference point and not as evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. It remains uncertain whether alternative RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, or adding image features would improve on this baseline. Single-axis comparisons against this configuration are needed to attribute any differences to specific design choices.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: only one baseline exists, config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000), at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. Nothing is yet known about any design axis. 2) This experiment changes one factor from the baseline: single-profile becomes multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), keeping the RNA-only setting and PCA-2000 encoder fixed. It tests whether aggregating several profiles helps at all, independent of encoder or modality effects. Testing avgpool before the transformer means any gain can be credited to multiprofile input rather than a more complex aggregator. 3) Profile setting splits the search space roughly in half (most configurations are multiprofile), so an early answer about it shapes many later choices. Encoder (scVI, scGPT) and modality comparisons are equally valid single-axis steps and can follow next. A single run will not settle the question, but it gives the first directional evidence on a high-impact axis at low cost.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an RNA-only model with the PCA-2000 RNA encoder, as in the baseline llm_summary_001, but switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with average-pooling aggregation. Validation accuracy fell to 0.4710 (F1 0.4419), compared with the baseline's 0.5856 (F1 0.5745), a drop of about 0.11 accuracy and 0.13 F1. This is initial directional evidence that multiprofile input with avgpool underperforms single-profile input in the RNA-only PCA setting. Because the profile setting and the aggregator changed together and each configuration was run only once with no variance estimate, it remains uncertain whether multiprofile input itself is unhelpful or whether avgpool is a poor aggregator (e.g., one that dilutes profile-level signal). It is also unknown whether this pattern holds with other aggregators (e.g., transformer), other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or added image features.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The single-profile RNA PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.586 accuracy. Moving to multiprofile with avgpool (config_002) dropped accuracy to 0.471 and F1 by a similar margin. Because profile setting and aggregator changed together, we cannot tell whether multiprofile input is unhelpful or whether avgpool is simply a weak aggregator that dilutes profile-level signal. 2) Test: config_003 keeps RNA-only, PCA-2000 and multiprofile fixed and changes only the aggregator to transformer. This directly isolates the aggregation effect. If it recovers to the baseline or beats it, avgpool was the problem and multiprofile remains viable. If it stays near 0.47, multiprofile itself likely hurts in this setting. 3) Value: Most of the remaining search space (over half the configurations) is multiprofile with either avgpool or transformer. Settling this question with a single controlled comparison will let us prune or prioritize a large part of the space before spending budget on encoder or modality comparisons.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 (config_003) held the RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile setup fixed and changed only the aggregator from avgpool (llm_summary_002) to transformer, giving a validation accuracy of 0.5203 (F1 0.4982), compared with 0.4710 (F1 0.4419) for avgpool. Because this comparison isolates the aggregator, it is initial evidence that transformer aggregation outperforms avgpool in this multiprofile setting, by about 0.05 accuracy and 0.06 F1. Multiprofile with transformer still fell about 0.065 accuracy (0.076 F1) short of the single-profile baseline (0.5856 / 0.5745), so the result lands between the two outcomes the experiment was designed to distinguish: avgpool appears to explain part of the earlier drop, and multiprofile input has not yet matched single-profile. Uncertainties remain: each configuration was run once with no variance estimate, transformer hyperparameters were not explored, and it is unknown whether the remaining gap persists with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or with added image features. Multiprofile settings therefore should not yet be pruned, but transformer looks like the stronger aggregator to prioritize over avgpool.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: All three experiments so far are RNA-only with PCA-2000. They give initial evidence that single-profile (0.586) beats multiprofile, and that transformer aggregation beats avgpool within multiprofile. Each was run only once. The image modality is completely untested, even though most of the remaining search space (multimodal configs 016–051) depends on images adding useful signal. 2. What this tests: An image-only, single-profile model with ResNet50 sets an image baseline in the setting that has done best so far. Comparing it with config_001 isolates the effect of modality (RNA vs. image) with profile setting held fixed. It also shows whether image features alone carry enough signal to make fusion worth pursuing. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: Learning whether images are informative reduces uncertainty about the largest branch of the search space. Testing an alternative RNA encoder such as scVI matters too, but it would refine one axis within RNA-only. This experiment tells us whether to prioritize multimodal configurations or keep refining RNA-only ones.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 tested the first image-only configuration, a single-profile ResNet50 image encoder with no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.2266 (F1 0.1907), far below the RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.5856 / 0.5745), a gap of about 0.36 accuracy and 0.38 F1. With profile setting held fixed, this is initial evidence that ResNet50 image features alone carry much less class-discriminative signal than PCA-2000 RNA features in this setting. Because modality and encoder change together, the gap cannot be attributed to modality alone rather than to the ResNet50 choice. Each configuration was run once with no variance estimate, chance-level performance is not given, and no other image encoders or hyperparameters were tried. Most importantly, weak standalone image performance does not rule out images adding complementary signal when fused with RNA, so multimodal configurations should be tested directly (e.g., RNA PCA-2000 plus ResNet50 single-profile fusion versus config_001) before that branch is deprioritized.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 (config_001: 0.586 acc / 0.574 F1) is the best result so far. Image-only ResNet50 is far weaker (config_010: 0.227 acc). In the multiprofile setting, transformer aggregation beat avgpool, but both still trailed single-profile. The biggest open question is whether images add complementary signal when fused with RNA. That answer decides whether most of the search space, the multimodal configurations, deserves budget. 2. What this tests: config_016 keeps everything from config_001 (single-profile, PCA-2000) and adds ResNet50 image features with concat fusion. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be credited to adding the image modality, using the simplest fusion and the image encoder already characterized in config_010. 3. Why now: this result guides the rest of the budget. A gain would justify exploring fusion type (weighted) and stronger image encoders (ViT-L). No gain or a drop would be initial evidence for focusing on RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) instead. Either way it reduces more uncertainty than another within-RNA comparison, though one run without a variance estimate should not settle the question.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 (config_016) kept the RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.5856 acc / 0.5745 F1) fixed and added ResNet50 image features with concat fusion, reaching only 0.2596 validation accuracy (F1 0.2217). That is a drop of about 0.33 accuracy and 0.35 F1 from the baseline, and only slightly above image-only ResNet50 (llm_summary_004: 0.2266 / 0.1907). Because this comparison isolates adding the ResNet50 image branch via concat, it is initial evidence that this particular multimodal setup substantially hurts performance rather than adding complementary signal. The fact that it lands near image-only performance is consistent with, but does not demonstrate, the fused model being dominated by or destabilized by the image features. It remains uncertain whether the drop reflects images being inherently uninformative or reflects the concat fusion, feature scaling or imbalance, or training choices, since this was a single run with no variance estimate. Weighted fusion, stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), and other RNA encoders were not tested. A modest check of an alternative fusion may still be warranted before pruning multimodal configurations entirely, but current evidence favors prioritizing RNA-encoder exploration (scVI, scGPT).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is the RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (0.586 acc / 0.574 F1). Multiprofile input was worse with both aggregators, though transformer beat avgpool. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion fell sharply (0.260), close to image-only (0.227). The RNA encoder is the main design axis not yet tested, even though RNA carries most of the signal seen so far. 2. Test: Changing only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, with everything else matching config_001, isolates the encoder's effect on the strongest branch. 3. Why now: This single-axis comparison has a real chance of beating the current best, and it shows whether encoder choice is a major lever before budget goes to multiprofile or multimodal variants built on it. A modest weighted-fusion check remains a reasonable later experiment, but RNA-encoder uncertainty is currently the most important gap.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 held the RNA-only single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001, config_001) fixed and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. It reached 0.6352 validation accuracy (F1 0.6183), about 0.05 accuracy and 0.04 F1 above PCA-2000 (0.5856 / 0.5745), making it the new best configuration so far. Because this comparison isolates the encoder, it is initial evidence that scVI-200 outperforms PCA-2000 in this setting and that RNA encoder choice is a meaningful lever. Uncertainties remain: each configuration was run once with no variance estimate, scGPT and other scVI settings are untested, and it is unknown whether scVI's advantage carries over to multiprofile (e.g., transformer aggregation) or multimodal configurations, or whether it changes the earlier weak results for those branches.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA encoder choice is the strongest positive lever so far. scVI-200 (0.635 acc / 0.618 F1) beat PCA-2000 (0.586 / 0.574) in the RNA-only single-profile setting, which is the best setting tested. The third RNA encoder, scGPT, has not been tested at all. The other branches look weaker: multiprofile trailed single-profile even with transformer aggregation, and adding ResNet50 images hurt badly. 2) What this tests: config_007 keeps the best setting fixed (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion) and changes only the encoder to scGPT. This gives a clean three-way comparison with config_001 and config_004. It shows whether the scVI gain reflects learned or foundation-model embeddings generally, and whether scGPT could be an even stronger base. 3) Why this is the best use of the budget: picking the strongest RNA encoder first lets later multiprofile and multimodal experiments build on the best base and avoids spending runs on combinations with a weaker encoder. It is also a single-axis change in the highest-performing setting, so it is efficient for both exploration and exploitation.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 kept the best setting so far fixed (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder to scGPT. It reached 0.6878 validation accuracy (F1 0.6585), about 0.05 accuracy and 0.04 F1 above scVI-200 (llm_summary_006: 0.6352 / 0.6183) and about 0.10 accuracy and 0.08 F1 above PCA-2000 (llm_summary_001: 0.5856 / 0.5745), making it the new best configuration. Because this is a single-axis comparison, it is initial evidence for the ordering scGPT > scVI-200 > PCA-2000 in this setting, consistent with learned or foundation-model embeddings helping and with RNA encoder choice being the strongest lever tested so far. The ordering is still uncertain: each configuration was run once with no variance estimate, and scGPT hyperparameters were not explored. It is also unknown whether scGPT's advantage carries over to multiprofile settings (e.g., transformer aggregation, which trailed single-profile with PCA) or to multimodal fusion (where ResNet50 plus concat hurt badly), so scGPT is the natural base for testing those branches next.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: scGPT is the strongest RNA encoder so far (single-profile, 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1), ahead of scVI-200 and PCA-2000. Multiprofile input is still unresolved. With PCA, transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.05, but it still trailed single-profile by about 0.065. It is unclear whether that gap reflects multiprofile input itself or the weaker PCA representation. 2. What this tests: config_009 keeps the best setting fixed (RNA-only, scGPT) and switches only to multiprofile input with the transformer aggregator. This shows whether the multiprofile penalty persists with a richer encoder or whether multiprofile can match or beat single-profile. The result can be read directly against config_007, and against the PCA multiprofile/single-profile pair as an encoder-by-profile check. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: it combines exploitation (the best encoder with the better aggregator) with resolving a major design axis that governs half the remaining space. If multiprofile still underperforms with scGPT, that is stronger grounds to deprioritize multiprofile configurations, including the multimodal multiprofile ones. If it helps, scGPT multiprofile becomes the base for later fusion tests. Multimodal weighted-fusion checks remain important but can follow once the profile question is clearer.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 kept the best configuration so far fixed (RNA-only, scGPT encoder; llm_summary_007: 0.6878 acc / 0.6585 F1) and switched to multiprofile input with transformer aggregation, reaching only 0.5121 validation accuracy (F1 0.4771). That is a drop of about 0.18 accuracy and 0.18 F1 from scGPT single-profile, and slightly below PCA-2000 multiprofile with transformer (llm_summary_003: 0.5203 / 0.4982). This is initial evidence that the multiprofile penalty persists with a stronger encoder, and grows from about 0.065 with PCA to about 0.18 with scGPT, so scGPT's single-profile advantage did not carry over and multiprofile results look roughly encoder-independent near 0.51–0.52. Because profile setting and aggregation change together (single-profile uses no aggregator), each configuration was run once with no variance estimate, and transformer hyperparameters were not explored, it remains uncertain whether multiprofile input itself is harmful or whether the aggregation pipeline fails to use richer embeddings; even so, current evidence supports deprioritizing multiprofile configurations, including multimodal multiprofile ones, in favor of single-profile scGPT as the base for further tests such as alternative fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA encoder choice is the strongest lever so far (scGPT 0.688 > scVI 0.635 > PCA 0.586). Multiprofile input has underperformed single-profile across encoders, so it can be deprioritized. The multimodal branch has only one test, config_016 (PCA-2000 + ResNet50 with concat fusion). It collapsed to 0.260, close to image-only, which suggests concat let weak image features dominate or destabilize the model. That run does not show whether images are useless or concat is the problem. 2) Test: config_017 keeps config_016 identical and changes only fusion from concat to weighted. Weighted fusion can learn to down-weight a weak modality, so this cleanly measures the effect of fusion type. If it recovers to near or above the PCA-only baseline (0.586), the earlier collapse was a fusion artifact and multimodal scGPT plus weighted fusion becomes a strong next candidate. If it stays near 0.26, the multimodal branch with ResNet50 can be pruned with more confidence. 3) Value: fusion is the only untested design axis. One controlled experiment decides whether a large part of the remaining search space (multimodal single-profile configs) is worth spending budget on. That is more useful than further tweaks to the already deprioritized multiprofile branch.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 (config_017) kept the multimodal single-profile PCA-2000 + ResNet50 setup of llm_summary_005 fixed and changed only the fusion from concat to weighted. It reached 0.5176 validation accuracy (F1 0.4837), about 0.26 accuracy and 0.26 F1 above concat (0.2596 / 0.2217) but still about 0.07 accuracy and 0.09 F1 below the RNA-only PCA-2000 baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.5856 / 0.5745). Because fusion type is the only change, this is initial evidence that weighted fusion outperforms concat here and that much of the earlier collapse was tied to concat fusion; however, adding ResNet50 images still did not beat RNA alone, so there is no evidence yet that these image features add complementary signal. Uncertainties remain: each configuration was run once with no variance estimate, the learned modality weights were not reported (so it is unknown whether the model simply down-weighted images), and it is untested whether weighted fusion with a stronger RNA encoder (scGPT, current best at 0.6878) or a different image encoder could match or exceed the corresponding RNA-only result.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: scGPT RNA-only single-profile (config_007) is the best result so far at 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. Multiprofile with a transformer fell to about 0.51 even with scGPT, so that branch looks weak. On the multimodal side, weighted fusion recovered most of the concat collapse with PCA plus ResNet50 (0.518 vs 0.260 accuracy), but it still trailed PCA RNA-only by about 0.07. The open question is whether that gap reflects uninformative images or a weak RNA base. 2. What this tests: config_041 keeps the best setup (scGPT, single-profile) and adds ResNet50 through weighted fusion, the better fusion found so far. Compared against config_007, it isolates the effect of adding image features to a strong RNA encoder. Compared against config_017, it shows whether the encoder ranking (scGPT > PCA) holds under multimodal fusion. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: it is a logical extension of the strongest evidence and tests a key unresolved design choice, whether images add complementary signal. It also has a real chance of producing a new best, and either outcome guides how many of the remaining multimodal configurations are worth testing. If it still falls short of RNA-only, a natural follow-up is a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) to see whether ResNet50 was the limitation.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 (config_041) took the best configuration so far, RNA-only single-profile scGPT (llm_summary_007: 0.6878 acc / 0.6585 F1), and added ResNet50 image features through weighted fusion, the only change. It reached 0.5191 validation accuracy (F1 0.4797), a drop of about 0.17 accuracy and 0.18 F1 from scGPT RNA-only, and almost identical to PCA-2000 + ResNet50 with weighted fusion (llm_summary_009: 0.5176 / 0.4837). Because only the image branch was added, this is initial evidence that adding ResNet50 through weighted fusion hurts performance even with a strong RNA encoder. The scGPT > PCA advantage (about 0.10 accuracy RNA-only) disappeared under this fusion, so multimodal results so far sit near about 0.52 regardless of RNA encoder, which suggests the image branch or fusion pipeline is limiting performance rather than RNA quality (and resembles the about 0.51–0.52 multiprofile plateau). It remains uncertain whether this reflects uninformative ResNet50 features or a fusion or training issue that overrides the RNA signal: learned modality weights were not reported, each configuration was run once with no variance estimate, and stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) are untested, so a ViT-L check may still be worthwhile before deprioritizing multimodal configurations relative to single-profile scGPT RNA-only.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run yet. We do not know how well any modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice performs. 2. What this tests: config_001 is the simplest configuration: RNA-only, single-profile, PCA (n=2000) encoder, with no aggregation or fusion. It sets a reference point. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time against it: encoder (scVI or scGPT), profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), modality (image-only, multimodal), and fusion. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Under a limited budget, starting from a simple, interpretable baseline lets each later comparison isolate a single design choice. It also avoids assuming that complex multimodal or multiprofile models will help. If more complex configurations cannot beat this baseline, that is itself an important result.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration as a reference baseline: RNA-only, single-profile, with a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.512 (primary metric), with a validation F1 of 0.477 as supporting evidence. No other experiments have been completed, so this is only an initial observation and cannot yet be judged good or poor relative to other encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings, image-only, or multimodal fusion. The number of classes, the chance-level baseline, and run-to-run variance are unknown, so later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons against this baseline are needed to show which design choices matter.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: Only one result exists, an RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline with accuracy 0.512 and F1 0.477. The biggest open question is whether the image modality carries useful signal on its own. That answer determines whether the large multimodal half of the search space (configs 016-051) is worth much budget. 2) What this tests: config_010 runs image-only, single-profile with a ResNet50 encoder and no aggregation or fusion. Comparing it with config_001 isolates the effect of modality (RNA vs. image) at the simplest setting, since both are single-profile with no aggregation or fusion. 3) Why now: One run gives a reference point for image-alone performance and indicates whether imaging could add complementary information in fusion. It sets up a later direct multimodal test (config_016, PCA+ResNet50 concat) to check whether fusion beats both single-modality baselines. ResNet50 is chosen over ViT-L as the simpler image baseline; the encoder comparison can follow. This is more informative early than refining RNA encoders or aggregation, which only matter within one modality.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile configuration with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, as a reference point for image-alone signal. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.519 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.480. These are nearly identical to the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) baseline from llm_summary_001 (0.512 accuracy, 0.477 F1), which suggests the image modality carries useful signal on its own, roughly comparable to the RNA baseline at this simplest setting. The ~0.007 accuracy gap is small, and run-to-run variance, the number of classes, and chance level are unknown, so this should not be read as image outperforming RNA. The comparison also changes both modality and encoder type (PCA vs. ResNet50), so it does not cleanly isolate modality. It remains untested whether the two modalities are complementary under fusion (e.g., the planned PCA+ResNet50 concat), and whether other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) or multiprofile aggregation would change image-only performance.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the two single-profile unimodal baselines perform almost the same. RNA-only PCA reached 0.512 accuracy and 0.477 F1. Image-only ResNet50 reached 0.519 accuracy and 0.480 F1. Each modality therefore carries some signal, but we don't know whether that signal is shared or complementary. 2) Test: config_016 fuses exactly these two encoders (PCA n2000 + ResNet50) by simple concatenation in the single-profile setting. Encoders and profile setting stay fixed, so any change in accuracy or F1 relative to both baselines can be attributed cleanly to adding a second modality. 3) Value: whether multimodality helps is the highest-impact open question, because about two-thirds of the remaining search space is multimodal. A clear gain would justify exploring fusion variants, encoders, and multiprofile aggregation within multimodal models. No gain would redirect the budget toward unimodal encoder or aggregation choices. Concat is the simplest fusion and gives a reference point for later tests of weighted fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a single-profile multimodal model that concatenates the same two encoders used in the unimodal baselines: PCA (n=2000) for RNA and ResNet50 for images, with no aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.629 (primary metric) and a validation F1 of 0.599. That is about 0.11 accuracy and 0.12 F1 above both the RNA-only baseline (0.512/0.477) and the image-only baseline (0.519/0.480). Because encoders, profile setting, and aggregation were held fixed, this comparison mainly isolates adding the second modality, and it suggests the two modalities carry at least partly complementary signal under simple concat fusion. Several points remain uncertain. Each configuration has a single run, so run-to-run variance is unknown. The number of classes and chance level are unknown. The multimodal model may also differ in input dimensionality or capacity. It is untested whether other fusion methods (e.g., weighted), other encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT, ViT-L), or multiprofile aggregation would add further gains on top of this concat reference point.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Single-profile RNA-only (0.512 accuracy) and image-only (0.519) baselines perform about the same. Concat fusion of PCA_n2000 and ResNet50 raised accuracy to 0.629 and F1 to 0.599, a large gain that points to complementary signal. The profile setting is the main design axis not yet explored at all, and it is a natural extension of the best configuration so far. 2. What this tests: config_018 keeps the encoders (PCA_n2000, ResNet50) and the fusion method (concat) identical to config_016. It changes only the profile setting from single-profile to multi-profile, using the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether aggregating multiple profiles improves on the current best model. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It exploits the strongest direction found so far while answering a high-level structural question. That answer will decide whether the rest of the budget should focus on multi-profile variants, such as transformer aggregation or other encoders, or stay with single-profile models. Fusion type (weighted vs. concat) is likely a smaller, second-order choice, so it can be tested afterwards.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best configuration so far (multimodal PCA n=2000 + ResNet50 with concat fusion, from llm_summary_003) and changed it from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.224 (primary metric), with F1 at 0.184, compared with 0.629/0.599 for the single-profile counterpart. That is also well below the RNA-only (0.512) and image-only (0.519) single-profile baselines, so this multiprofile+avgpool setup is clearly unfavorable as configured. The comparison changes the profile setting and introduces aggregation together, so it cannot separate whether the drop comes from multiprofile input itself, from avgpool washing out profile-level signal, or from a setup or implementation issue (the size of the collapse makes a pipeline problem worth checking). With a single run, unknown variance, and unknown chance level, it remains untested whether other aggregators (e.g., transformer), multiprofile unimodal models, or a verified pipeline would recover or exceed single-profile performance.

selection_reason: Evidence: single-profile PCA+ResNet50 concat is the best result so far (0.629 acc / 0.599 F1). Switching that setup to multiprofile with avgpool (config_018) collapsed accuracy to 0.224, well below both unimodal baselines. That run changed the profile setting and added aggregation at the same time, so we cannot tell whether multiprofile input is harmful in itself or whether avgpool washes out profile-level signal. This matters because about half of the remaining search space is multiprofile. Test: config_020 keeps everything from config_018 fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, concat) and changes only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the effect of aggregation. If accuracy recovers to near or above 0.629, multiprofile stays viable and transformer aggregation becomes a priority. If it also collapses, multiprofile is likely unfavorable (or the pipeline has a problem), and we can deprioritize most multiprofile configs and focus on single-profile fusion and encoder choices. Why now: a single-factor experiment that resolves the largest open uncertainty is the most budget-efficient next step, because its outcome guides pruning of many remaining configurations. Tweaking fusion or encoders first would yield smaller, less decisive information.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 isolated the aggregator in the multiprofile multimodal setup. It kept multimodal, multiprofile, PCA (n=2000), ResNet50 and concat fusion fixed from llm_summary_004 and changed only avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy recovered from 0.224 to 0.530 (primary metric), with F1 rising from 0.184 to 0.515. This suggests avgpool was a major contributor to the earlier collapse and that multiprofile input is not inherently catastrophic. However, the result is still about 0.10 below the single-profile concat model (0.629/0.599) and only roughly on par with the unimodal single-profile baselines (0.512 RNA, 0.519 image). So multiprofile has not yet shown a benefit, and the remaining gap may reflect the profile setting itself, transformer capacity or training, or a lingering pipeline issue. Uncertainties include single runs with unknown variance and unknown chance level. Other aggregators, multiprofile unimodal models, and alternative fusion or encoders under multiprofile remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is single-profile multimodal PCA(n=2000)+ResNet50 with concat fusion (0.629 accuracy / 0.599 F1). It beats both unimodal baselines (about 0.51-0.52) by roughly 0.11, so the two modalities appear complementary. Multiprofile has not helped: with avgpool it collapsed to 0.224, and with a transformer aggregator it only recovered to 0.530, still below single-profile. Fusion method has only been tested with concat, so whether fusion design matters is still unknown. 2) Test: config_017 keeps the best configuration fixed (single-profile, PCA n=2000, ResNet50, no aggregation) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. This isolates the effect of fusion method. 3) Why now: it builds on the strongest evidence in a one-factor comparison, and it answers a question that affects every later multimodal configuration. If weighted fusion helps, it becomes the default for later encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L). If it does not, concat is supported and the budget can move to encoder or multiprofile diagnostics. This is cheaper and easier to interpret than changing encoders or profile settings together.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 isolated the fusion method. It kept the best configuration from llm_summary_003 fixed (multimodal, single-profile, PCA n=2000 + ResNet50, no aggregation) and changed only concat fusion to weighted fusion. Validation accuracy dropped from 0.629 to 0.527 (primary metric), and F1 fell from 0.599 to 0.510. That puts weighted fusion roughly level with the unimodal baselines (0.512 RNA, 0.519 image), so in this single run it recovered none of the multimodal gain that concat produced, and concat remains the preferred default. With single runs, unknown variance and unknown chance level, it is uncertain whether this reflects weighted fusion being inherently worse, a poorly tuned or degenerate weighting (e.g., collapsing onto one modality, which the unimodal-level score hints at but does not show), or an implementation issue. Whether weighted fusion would behave differently with other encoders (scVI, scGPT, ViT-L) or under multiprofile settings is also untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Single-profile concat fusion of PCA n=2000 and ResNet50 (config_016) is clearly best so far, at 0.629 accuracy and 0.599 F1. It beats both unimodal baselines (about 0.51-0.52), multiprofile aggregation (0.224 with avgpool, 0.530 with transformer) and weighted fusion (0.527). Profile setting, aggregation and fusion have each been probed at least once. The encoders, however, have never been varied: every run has used PCA for RNA and ResNet50 for images. 2) What this tests: config_022 keeps the winning setup fixed (multimodal, single-profile, no aggregation, concat, PCA n=2000) and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Since it is a one-factor change, it directly measures whether a larger pretrained image representation improves the fused model. Because no other factor moves, any change in accuracy or F1 can be attributed to the encoder. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: It exploits the strongest direction found so far, so it has a good chance of setting a new best. It also opens the untested encoder dimension, and the image encoder is the simplest place to start because it has only two options. The result will tell us whether encoder choice matters before we spend runs on scVI or scGPT variants of the same configuration (config_028 and config_040), or return to the multiprofile settings that have underperformed.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 isolated the image encoder. It kept the best configuration from llm_summary_003 fixed (multimodal, single-profile, PCA n=2000 RNA, no aggregation, concat fusion) and changed only ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.629 to 0.421 (primary metric), with F1 dropping from 0.599 to 0.412. That is well below both unimodal baselines (0.512 RNA-only, 0.519 image-only ResNet50), so in this single run the larger pretrained ViT-L representation not only failed to help but appears to have degraded the fused model, and ResNet50 remains the preferred image encoder. Because the score falls below RNA-only, ViT-L features may be adding noise or hurting optimization under concat. Possible causes include feature dimensionality or scale imbalance relative to PCA, preprocessing or resolution mismatch, insufficient tuning, or a pipeline issue. A ViT-L image-only run would help distinguish poor ViT-L features from a fusion interaction. Single runs, unknown variance and unknown chance level remain caveats, and the scVI and scGPT RNA encoder variants are still untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: the best result is single-profile multimodal PCA n=2000 + ResNet50 with concat fusion (0.629 accuracy, 0.599 F1). One-factor changes to that model have each hurt it: weighted fusion gave 0.527, ViT-L in place of ResNet50 gave 0.421, and multiprofile gave 0.224 with avgpool and 0.530 with transformer. So concat, ResNet50 and single-profile are tentatively the best choices. The RNA encoder is the main design dimension still untested, because every run so far used PCA. 2) This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed and swaps only PCA n=2000 for scVI n=200. That isolates whether a learned, lower-dimensional RNA representation improves or degrades the fused model. The 200-dimensional embedding also tests whether a more balanced feature scale relative to ResNet50 helps concat fusion. 3) Why this is the best use of the budget: it is an exploitation step on the strongest configuration, and it also explores the largest remaining source of uncertainty. Either outcome narrows the search. A gain would point to scVI-based models as the next direction. A loss would strengthen PCA as the default and leave scGPT (config_040) as the final RNA encoder check.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 isolated the RNA encoder. It kept the best configuration from llm_summary_003 fixed (multimodal, single-profile, ResNet50 image encoder, no aggregation, concat fusion) and replaced PCA n=2000 with scVI n=200. Validation accuracy fell from 0.629 to 0.523 (primary metric), and F1 fell from 0.599 to 0.508. That leaves the scVI model roughly level with the unimodal baselines (0.512 RNA-only PCA, 0.519 image-only ResNet50), so in this single run it recovered little or none of the multimodal gain. PCA n=2000 therefore remains the preferred RNA encoder, and the hypothesis that a lower-dimensional, more scale-balanced RNA embedding would help concat fusion was not supported. Several points remain uncertain. It is unclear whether the drop reflects weaker scVI features or the lower dimensionality (200 vs. 2000), since both change together. It could also reflect scVI training or tuning choices, or a fusion interaction; an scVI RNA-only run would help separate these. Single runs, unknown variance and unknown chance level remain caveats, and scGPT is still the untested RNA encoder.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: the best result so far is single-profile multimodal PCA n=2000 + ResNet50 with concat fusion (0.629 accuracy, 0.599 F1). Every one-factor change from that model has lowered accuracy to about 0.42–0.53. Those changes were weighted fusion, ViT-L as the image encoder, scVI as the RNA encoder, and multiprofile with avgpool or transformer aggregation. The main design axis still untested is the scGPT RNA encoder. 2. Test: config_040 keeps the best setup fixed and swaps only PCA for scGPT. This shows whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding beats PCA under concat fusion. It also helps tell a general weakness of learned, lower-dimensional embeddings (as scVI showed) apart from a weakness specific to scVI. 3. Why now: this is a clean single-factor comparison against the current best. It closes the last unexplored encoder option, and it is the most plausible remaining way to beat 0.629. A scGPT RNA-only run (config_007) would be useful later, but this one serves both exploration and exploitation under the limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 isolated the RNA encoder by keeping the best configuration from llm_summary_003 fixed (multimodal, single-profile, ResNet50 image encoder, no aggregation, concat fusion) and swapping PCA n=2000 for scGPT. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.653 (primary metric) and an F1 of 0.628, up from 0.629/0.599. This makes it the new best configuration and the first one-factor change from the reference to improve rather than lower accuracy, unlike scVI (0.523), ViT-L (0.421), weighted fusion (0.527) and multiprofile variants. It also suggests the scVI drop was not a general weakness of learned RNA embeddings. The gain is modest (~0.024 accuracy, ~0.029 F1) and comes from single runs with unknown variance and chance level, so it may not be robust. It is also unclear whether it reflects better scGPT features or a fusion interaction, because no scGPT RNA-only run exists yet (e.g., config_007). Whether scGPT also helps under other fusion methods, image encoders or multiprofile settings remains untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scGPT + ResNet50 concat (config_040) is the new best at 0.653 accuracy / 0.628 F1. It is only about 0.024 above PCA + ResNet50 concat (config_016), from single runs. It is the only one-factor change so far that improved on the reference; scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion and multiprofile variants all scored lower. With no scGPT RNA-only run, we cannot tell whether the gain comes from stronger scGPT RNA features or from a fusion interaction. That uncertainty also covers scVI, whose multimodal drop (0.523) was never checked unimodally. 2) What it tests: config_007 changes only the RNA encoder relative to the RNA-only PCA baseline (config_001, 0.512 / 0.477). This cleanly isolates the representation effect within one modality. If scGPT RNA-only clearly beats 0.512, the representation gain is supported and scGPT should anchor later multiprofile and fusion tests (e.g., config_044). If it is near 0.512, the small multimodal gain is more likely noise or an interaction, which argues for caution before building on it. 3) Why now: it adds independent support for the most promising design choice with a single-factor change. By contrast, extending scGPT to multiprofile has weak prior support, since the multiprofile transformer was about 0.10 below single-profile, and weighted fusion has already underperformed. This makes config_007 the most informative next experiment under a limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 isolated the RNA representation within the RNA-only, single-profile setting by swapping PCA n=2000 (llm_summary_001, 0.512 accuracy / 0.477 F1) for scGPT, with no image encoder, aggregation or fusion. It reached 0.721 validation accuracy (primary) and 0.681 F1, a gain of about 0.21 accuracy that strongly supports scGPT features carrying much more class signal than PCA. It is now the best configuration overall, about 0.068 accuracy above the scGPT + ResNet50 concat model (0.653 / 0.628), so adding ResNet50 through concat appears to have lowered performance relative to scGPT alone rather than complementing it, unlike the PCA case where concat added about 0.11. Remaining uncertainties: these are single runs with unknown variance and unknown chance level; it is unclear why fusion hurt here (e.g., dilution or scale/dimensionality imbalance under concat, optimization, or tuning); and it remains untested whether other fusion schemes, multiprofile scGPT, or an scVI RNA-only comparison would change the picture.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so we know nothing about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matters, and there is no reference point to judge later results against. 2. What this tests: config_001 is the simplest setup: RNA-only, a single profile, PCA features, and no aggregation or fusion. It gives a low-complexity baseline. Later experiments can then change one factor at a time against it: scVI or scGPT for the encoder (config_004/007), multiprofile with avgpool (config_002), image-only (config_010), or multimodal concat (config_016). 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Without a simple baseline, any gain from a complex multimodal or multiprofile model cannot be attributed to a specific design choice, and we should not assume the more complex models win. Starting here anchors controlled comparisons for the rest of the search.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration as a baseline: an RNA-only model on single profiles with PCA features (pca_n2000), and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.471 and a validation F1 of 0.442, which sets the first reference point for later controlled comparisons. No other experiments have been run, so it is not yet known whether this is weak or strong for the task. It is also unknown whether swapping the encoder (scVI, scGPT), using multiple profiles with aggregation, adding images, or fusing modalities would change performance. Because there is a single run, the variability of this baseline is also uncharacterized.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one experiment has been run. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline reached 0.471 accuracy and 0.442 F1. We do not yet know how much signal the image modality carries, and that unknown shapes about two-thirds of the search space (the image-only and multimodal configurations). 2. What this tests: config_010 (image-only, single-profile, ResNet50) keeps the simplest setting: single profile, no aggregation, no fusion. The only change is the modality. This gives a clean RNA-versus-image comparison under matched conditions. 3. Why it is the best next use of the budget: Knowing whether images are weaker than, comparable to, or stronger than RNA tells us whether multimodal fusion is worth exploring, and which modality's encoders to prioritize. Encoder or aggregation variants within RNA-only would refine only one branch. The multiprofile and encoder questions can be tested afterward on whichever modality looks more promising.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only model on single profiles with a ResNet50 image encoder and no aggregation or fusion, matching the simple setup of the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001) apart from the input modality. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.573 and a validation F1 of 0.573, versus 0.471 and 0.442 for the RNA-only baseline. This initial observation suggests the image modality carries substantial signal, and it supports exploring image-based and multimodal configurations. Uncertainties remain: modality and encoder change together (ResNet50 vs. PCA), so the gap cannot be attributed to modality alone; each configuration has only one run, so variability is unknown; and it is untested whether other encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT for RNA), multiprofile aggregation, or fusion would change the ranking.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there are two single-profile runs. Image-only with ResNet50 reached 0.573 accuracy and 0.573 F1. RNA-only with PCA reached 0.471 and 0.442. Images seem to carry more signal, but we do not know whether the two modalities are complementary or whether RNA only adds noise. Each result is a single run, so small gaps should not be overread. 2) Test: config_016 fuses exactly the two encoders already tested (PCA and ResNet50) with simple concat fusion, still on single profiles. Comparing it with both baselines isolates the effect of adding a second modality, with no change in encoder, profile setting or aggregation. 3) Why now: whether multimodality helps is the most important open question, because most of the remaining search space is multimodal. A gain over 0.573 would justify exploring fusion types, aggregation and encoders within multimodal models. No gain would point the budget toward image-only refinements, such as ViT-L or multiprofile aggregation. Concat is the simplest fusion and gives a clean reference before testing weighted fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a multimodal single-profile model that concatenates the two encoders already evaluated alone, PCA (pca_n2000) for RNA and ResNet50 for images, with no aggregation. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.532 and a validation F1 of 0.516. That is below the image-only ResNet50 baseline (0.573 / 0.573) and above the RNA-only PCA baseline (0.471 / 0.442). This initial observation suggests that simple concat fusion did not add value over images alone in this setting, and may have diluted the image signal with weaker RNA features. Each configuration has only one run, so variability is unknown and the roughly 0.04 accuracy gap may not be robust. The result does not show whether other fusion strategies (e.g., weighted fusion), other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), stronger image encoders, or multiprofile aggregation would make multimodality beneficial, so it should be read as a concat-fusion reference point rather than evidence against multimodality in general.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: image-only ResNet50 single-profile (config_010) is the best result so far at 0.573 accuracy and 0.573 F1. It beats the RNA-only PCA baseline (0.471) and PCA+ResNet50 concat fusion (0.532). No multiprofile configuration has been tested yet, so the effect of profile setting and aggregation is completely unknown. That axis touches most of the remaining configurations. 2) What this tests: config_011 changes only the profile setting from single to multiprofile, with avgpool aggregation, on the strongest configuration found so far. It shows whether pooling multiple profiles improves the image signal. Avgpool is the simplest aggregator, so it gives a clean reference point before trying the transformer. 3) Why it is the best use of the next experiment: it exploits the most promising direction (images) while resolving a major design question with a single-variable change. The result will guide many later choices: whether to prioritize multiprofile variants across image-only and multimodal models, and whether a transformer aggregator is worth testing. Switching to ViT-L or weighted fusion is also informative, but each answers a narrower question.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 changed only the profile setting of the previous best configuration, the image-only ResNet50 single-profile model (llm_summary_002), from single to multiprofile, with avgpool aggregation (aggregation is inherent to the multiprofile setting). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.721 and a validation F1 of 0.681, versus 0.573 and 0.573 for llm_summary_002, making it the strongest result so far (RNA-only PCA: 0.471; PCA+ResNet50 concat: 0.532). Because this is a near single-variable comparison, it is reasonable initial evidence that pooling multiple profiles helps the image model, though the gain could be partly sensitive to the avgpool choice, and F1 now trails accuracy, which may mean the improvement is uneven across classes. Uncertainties remain: each configuration has only one run, so variability is unknown; it is untested whether a transformer aggregator would do better than avgpool; and it is unknown whether multiprofile aggregation gives similar gains for RNA-only or multimodal models, or with other encoders and fusion strategies.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The strongest result so far is image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool (config_011), at 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Its single-profile counterpart reached 0.573. Each configuration has only one run, so this is initial rather than conclusive evidence that pooling profiles helps. We do not yet know whether the gain depends on the aggregator, and F1 trailing accuracy hints that the improvement may be uneven across classes. 2) Test: This run changes only avgpool to a transformer aggregator, keeping image-only, ResNet50 and multiprofile fixed. It isolates whether learned attention-based aggregation improves over simple mean pooling. 3) Value: Aggregation choice affects every remaining multiprofile configuration, including RNA-only and multimodal ones, so resolving it now guides many later choices. It also directly exploits the most promising direction found so far, without changing several design choices at once.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 changed only the aggregator of the best configuration so far, image-only ResNet50 multiprofile (llm_summary_004), from avgpool to a transformer. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.540 and F1 of 0.524, a large drop from 0.721 / 0.681 with avgpool and below even the single-profile image-only baseline (0.573 / 0.573). As a controlled single-variable comparison, this is initial evidence that in this setup transformer aggregation performed worse than simple mean pooling, so the multiprofile gain seen earlier appears sensitive to the aggregator choice. Each configuration has only one run, so variability is unknown and the gap may partly reflect training instability (e.g., hyperparameters, data size, or optimization of the attention aggregator) rather than an inherent limitation of transformer aggregation. It is also untested whether this ranking holds for RNA-only or multimodal multiprofile models.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool (0.721 acc, 0.681 F1). Moving from single to multiprofile gave a large gain. A transformer aggregator performed much worse, and adding PCA RNA via concat fusion hurt in the single-profile setting. The image encoder, a major design choice, has never been varied; every image result so far uses ResNet50. 2) This experiment swaps ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L and keeps everything else in the best configuration fixed (image-only, multiprofile, avgpool). That is a clean single-variable test of whether the image representation is limiting performance. 3) Images are clearly the dominant modality, and the encoder choice affects every later image and multimodal configuration. Resolving it now both exploits the strongest direction and removes a key uncertainty, so later fusion and RNA-encoder comparisons can be built on the stronger image backbone.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the image encoder of the best configuration so far (image-only, multiprofile, avgpool; llm_summary_004) from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.224 and F1 of 0.184, a drop from 0.721 / 0.681 with ResNet50 that puts it below every prior run, including the RNA-only PCA baseline (0.471 / 0.442). Because this is a controlled single-variable comparison, it is initial evidence that ViT-L, as used here, performed far worse than ResNet50, so ResNet50 remains the reference image backbone. The collapse is severe enough that it may reflect a pipeline or compatibility problem (e.g., input resolution or normalization mismatch, feature extraction, or optimization) rather than the representation itself. With only one run per configuration, variability is unknown, and it is untested whether other image encoders or a corrected ViT setup would match or beat ResNet50.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool (0.721 accuracy / 0.681 F1). Moving from single to multiprofile gave a large gain for images, from 0.573 to 0.721. Single-profile PCA+ResNet50 concat fusion (0.532) fell below single-profile image-only (0.573), but that is one run in the weaker single-profile setting. It is unknown whether RNA adds value once profiles are pooled. 2) What this tests: config_018 differs from config_016 only in the profile setting (multiprofile with avgpool). It also differs from the best config_011 only by adding PCA RNA through concat fusion. It therefore shows whether the multiprofile avgpool gain carries over to the multimodal model, and whether adding RNA to the strongest setup helps or hurts. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: It builds on the strongest direction (multiprofile avgpool with ResNet50) and changes only one variable relative to two existing reference runs. It also settles the central question of whether multimodality helps before spending budget on fusion type (weighted) or other RNA encoders. It avoids the transformer aggregator and ViT-L, both of which underperformed.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 tested a multimodal multiprofile model (PCA pca_n2000 RNA + ResNet50 images, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion), which differs from the single-profile multimodal run (llm_summary_003) only in the profile setting and from the best image-only multiprofile run (llm_summary_004) only in adding PCA RNA through concat fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.520 and F1 of 0.479, slightly below llm_summary_003 (0.532 / 0.516) and far below llm_summary_004 (0.721 / 0.681), and also below single-profile image-only (0.573). As initial controlled evidence, the large multiprofile avgpool gain seen for images did not carry over to the concat multimodal model, and adding PCA RNA via concat to the strongest image setup was associated with a large drop, consistent with the earlier single-profile observation that concat fusion with PCA RNA underperformed images alone. Each configuration has only one run, so variability is unknown, and the failure may be specific to concat fusion, the PCA RNA features (e.g., scale or dimensionality imbalance swamping image features), or training and optimization of the fused model rather than evidence against multimodality in general; weighted fusion and other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) remain untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool (0.721 accuracy / 0.681 F1). Adding PCA RNA through concat fusion dropped performance sharply, to 0.520 / 0.479. Concat also underperformed images alone in the single-profile setting (0.532 vs 0.573). It is unclear whether the fault lies with concat fusion, for example weak or badly scaled RNA features swamping the image signal, or with the RNA representation itself. Weighted fusion is untested. 2. Test: config_019 differs from config_018 only in fusion (concat to weighted), keeping PCA, ResNet50, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above 0.721, concat was the bottleneck and multimodality may still help. If it stays near 0.52, the problem more likely lies with the PCA RNA features, which would point next to the scVI or scGPT encoders. 3. Why now: this is a single-variable comparison on the strongest backbone and aggregation, so it isolates the fusion choice. It also has a plausible chance of producing a new best, which balances learning about the design with exploiting the current lead.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 changed only the fusion method of the multiprofile multimodal model (PCA pca_n2000 RNA + ResNet50 images, avgpool) from concat (llm_summary_007) to weighted. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.579 and F1 of 0.563, up from 0.520 / 0.479 with concat but still far below the best image-only multiprofile ResNet50 avgpool run (0.721 / 0.681). This is controlled initial evidence that the fusion choice matters, with weighted fusion only partially recovering performance. Adding PCA RNA still coincided with a large drop relative to images alone, so neither of the pre-stated outcomes held cleanly: concat was not the sole bottleneck, and the PCA RNA features (e.g., weak signal or scale imbalance) or the training of the fused model remain plausible causes. Each configuration has only one run, so variability and the robustness of the roughly 0.06 gain are unknown, and it is untested whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) with weighted fusion would let multimodality match or beat images alone.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: the best result so far is image-only multiprofile ResNet50 with avgpool (0.721 accuracy / 0.681 F1). Adding PCA RNA has hurt in every case. With concat it fell to 0.520, and weighted fusion only partly recovered it to 0.579. The most likely remaining cause is the PCA RNA representation itself, either weak signal or high-dimensional (2000) features that crowd out the image signal. PCA is also the only RNA encoder tested so far. 2. What this tests: config_031 changes only the RNA encoder of config_019, from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200, keeping multiprofile, ResNet50, avgpool and weighted fusion fixed. This cleanly asks whether a compact, learned RNA representation makes multimodal fusion competitive with, or better than, images alone. If it helps clearly, PCA was the bottleneck. If it still trails 0.721, that strengthens the case that RNA adds little here under this setup, though one run cannot settle it. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: it targets the largest open question, whether multimodality can help at all. It also has real upside, since it builds on the best-known aggregation and fusion choices, and it avoids changing several design choices at once.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 changed only the RNA encoder of the weighted-fusion multiprofile multimodal model (ResNet50 images, avgpool; llm_summary_008) from PCA (pca_n2000) to scVI (scvi_n200). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.422 and F1 of 0.405, below PCA with weighted fusion (0.579 / 0.563), far below the best image-only multiprofile ResNet50 avgpool run (0.721 / 0.681), and even below the RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline (0.471 / 0.442). As controlled initial evidence, swapping in this compact learned RNA representation did not rescue multimodality and was associated with a further drop, so PCA does not appear to be the sole bottleneck, and every multimodal configuration tested so far has trailed images alone. Uncertainties remain. scVI has never been run RNA-only, so it is unknown whether its features are weak or whether this fusion setup handles them poorly. The drop is large enough that a pipeline, scaling, or optimization problem cannot be ruled out. Each configuration has only one run, so variability is unknown, and other RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT) and fusion variants remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile avgpool pooling strongly helped the image-only ResNet50 model (0.573 to 0.721). Every multimodal run has trailed images alone, including PCA+ResNet50 with concat (0.520) or weighted fusion (0.579) and scVI with weighted fusion (0.422). RNA has only been tested once on its own, as single-profile PCA (0.471). So it is unclear whether the multimodal drops come from weak RNA features, from RNA not benefiting from profile pooling, or from the fusion step. 2) What this tests: config_002 changes only the profile setting of the RNA-only PCA baseline (config_001), from single to multiprofile with avgpool. It shows whether the multiprofile gain is image-specific or general. A large RNA gain would point to fusion or optimization as the bottleneck in the multiprofile multimodal runs. Little or no gain would suggest the RNA branch adds noise to a strong image signal. 3) Why now: this is a clean single-variable comparison on an untested part of the space, the RNA branch under the best-performing aggregation. Its result guides whether further multimodal runs (e.g., scGPT with weighted fusion) are worth the budget. That makes it more informative than another multimodal variant that changes several factors at once.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 changed only the profile setting of the RNA-only PCA (pca_n2000) baseline (llm_summary_001), from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, to test whether the large multiprofile gain seen for ResNet50 images (0.573 to 0.721) also applies to RNA. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.227 and F1 of 0.191, a sharp drop from 0.471 / 0.442 single-profile and near the lowest result so far (comparable to the ViT-L collapse, 0.224). As controlled initial evidence, multiprofile avgpool did not help and was associated with a large loss for PCA RNA, so the pooling benefit appears not to be general across modalities. This is consistent with a weak or degraded RNA branch under multiprofile pooling contributing to the multimodal multiprofile runs trailing images alone (concat 0.520, weighted 0.579). However, it does not show that fusion is not also a bottleneck, and the severity of the drop means a pipeline, profile-alignment, scaling, or optimization problem in RNA multiprofile handling cannot be ruled out.
