Each configuration has only one run, so variability is unknown, and it is untested whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) behave similarly under multiprofile pooling or would hold up better single-profile.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so nothing is known about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2. What it tests: config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest and cheapest baseline. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that every later change can be compared against one factor at a time. From here, single-step changes are possible: swap the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), switch to multiprofile with avgpool or transformer aggregation, use an image-only model, or add image fusion. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: Starting with a complex multimodal model would mix several design choices together and make any result hard to attribute. Starting from a simple, interpretable baseline keeps later comparisons clean, which matters most when the budget is limited.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established a first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA encoder with 2000 components, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.7207, with a validation F1 of 0.6815 as supporting evidence. Because no other experiments have been completed, this is only an initial reference point and says nothing yet about whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only models, or image fusion would help or hurt. The somewhat lower F1 than accuracy may mean performance is uneven across classes, but this is unconfirmed, and the run-to-run variability of this result is unknown.

selection_reason: 1) The only evidence is a single baseline: RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 at 0.7207 accuracy and 0.6815 F1. We do not yet know how sensitive performance is to any design choice, and the gap between F1 and accuracy hints that some classes may be handled worse than others. 2) config_002 keeps the modality and encoder fixed and changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregator (avgpool). This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps, a question that applies to every RNA, image and multimodal branch of the search space. 3) It is a clean one-factor comparison against the baseline using the lowest-complexity aggregator, so any change can be attributed to multiprofile input itself rather than to a transformer's added capacity. That makes it a cheap, interpretable way to decide early whether multiprofile designs deserve budget. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) and image-only baselines are strong next candidates. One run cannot separate a real effect from run-to-run noise, so small differences should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup from baseline llm_summary_001 and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input pooled with avgpool (no image encoder or fusion). Validation accuracy fell from 0.7207 to 0.6530 (about -0.068), and validation F1 fell from 0.6815 to 0.6283 (about -0.053), so multiprofile input with simple average pooling did not help in this configuration and appears worse. Because multiprofile input and avgpool were introduced together, the drop cannot be attributed to multiprofile input itself rather than to the aggregation method. It is unknown whether a more expressive aggregator (e.g., a transformer), a different encoder, or an image or multimodal setting would change this. Each configuration has only one run with unknown run-to-run variance, so the size and reliability of the gap are uncertain, though it is large enough to treat avgpool multiprofile as a weak candidate for now.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile baseline (config_001) reached 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. Switching to multiprofile with avgpool (config_002) dropped this to 0.653 accuracy and 0.628 F1. Because multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation were introduced together, we cannot tell whether multiprofile input itself is unhelpful or simple average pooling is discarding useful per-profile information. 2) Test: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 and changes only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. If accuracy recovers to or above the single-profile baseline, the earlier drop was mainly due to avgpool. If it stays low, multiprofile input itself looks weak, at least with PCA features. 3) Why now: multiprofile settings with avgpool or transformer aggregation make up most of the remaining search space, including most multimodal configurations. Resolving this aggregation question with a single-variable change tells us whether to keep exploring multiprofile/transformer options or to focus the budget on single-profile encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) and image or fusion settings. This is a more decisive use of one experiment than changing the encoder or modality now.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000 setup from llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. This was meant to test whether avgpool explained the earlier drop below the single-profile baseline. Validation accuracy fell further, to 0.5729 (about -0.080 vs avgpool's 0.6530 and about -0.148 vs the single-profile baseline's 0.7207), and validation F1 fell to 0.5730 (vs 0.6283 and 0.6815). So the avgpool-related drop was not recovered, and in this single-variable comparison the transformer aggregator performed worse than avgpool. Together with llm_summary_002, this suggests multiprofile input with PCA features is weak under both aggregators tried so far, but each configuration has only one run with unknown variance, and the transformer's hyperparameters, capacity and training adequacy were not explored, so it remains uncertain whether multiprofile input is inherently unhelpful or these aggregators are simply poorly suited or undertuned here. It is also unknown whether this pattern holds with other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) or with image and fusion settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Three RNA-only PCA-2000 runs show single-profile (0.721 acc / 0.681 F1) beating multiprofile with avgpool (0.653) and with transformer (0.573). This points to single-profile as the stronger setting for now, though each result is a single run. The image modality is completely untested. Yet 42 of the 48 remaining configurations use images (image-only or multimodal), so whether images carry useful signal is the largest open uncertainty. 2) What this tests: config_010 is an image-only, single-profile ResNet50 baseline with no aggregation or fusion. It mirrors the strongest RNA setting, so it can be compared directly with the single-profile RNA baseline. It shows how much signal images carry on their own before fusion is tried. 3) Why it is the best next step: one clean image baseline tells us whether the many multimodal configurations are worth exploring and gives a reference for judging later fusion gains. Testing alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) matters too, but it only affects a smaller part of the space and can follow next.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 set the first image-only baseline: a single-profile ResNet50 image encoder with no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, chosen to mirror the strongest RNA setting (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4710 and a validation F1 of 0.4419, well below the RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (0.7207 / 0.6815; about -0.250 accuracy and -0.240 F1). This suggests that images alone, with this encoder, carry weaker discriminative signal than RNA in this setup. However, modality and encoder differ together in this comparison, so the gap cannot be attributed to the image modality itself rather than to ResNet50 or its training setup. It is also unknown how 0.47 compares with chance, since the class count is not given, and each result is a single run with unknown variance. Whether image features add complementary signal when fused with RNA, or behave differently in multiprofile settings or with other image encoders, remains untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 (0.721 acc / 0.681 F1). Both multiprofile variants scored lower: avgpool reached 0.653 and transformer 0.573. Image-only ResNet50 single-profile was much weaker (0.471 / 0.442). What we still don't know is whether image features add complementary signal to RNA, even though images are weak on their own. That is the central question for multimodal profiling. 2. Test: config_016 adds the ResNet50 image branch to the best RNA setup with simple concat fusion. It keeps PCA-2000, single-profile and no aggregation, so adding the image modality is the only change from config_001. This directly tests whether fusion helps, hurts or is neutral, without confounding from the multiprofile settings that have looked weak. 3. Why now: Both components are already characterized individually, so the result is easy to interpret either way. A gain points toward exploring fusion further (weighted fusion, ViT-L). No gain suggests focusing the remaining budget on RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) in single-profile mode. Concat is the simplest fusion and sets the reference point for later fusion comparisons.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 added a ResNet50 image branch, fused by simple concatenation, to the best RNA setup (single-profile PCA-2000, no aggregation), so image addition was the only change from the RNA-only baseline llm_summary_001. Validation accuracy fell from 0.7207 to 0.6287 (about -0.092), and validation F1 fell from 0.6815 to 0.5993 (about -0.082), though it stayed above image-only ResNet50 (0.4710 / 0.4419). In this configuration, concat fusion with ResNet50 image features did not add complementary signal and appears to hurt relative to RNA alone. Each configuration has only one run with unknown variance, and concat is the simplest fusion option, so it remains uncertain whether the drop reflects images being uninformative, ResNet50 features, or the fusion method (e.g., unbalanced feature dimensions or a lack of modality weighting); weighted fusion, other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), and other RNA encoders in multimodal settings are untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA is clearly the strongest signal so far. RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 reached 0.7207 accuracy and 0.6815 F1. Every added complexity has hurt in single runs: multiprofile avgpool, multiprofile transformer, image-only ResNet50 and concat fusion. The RNA encoder, however, has never been varied; every RNA result uses PCA-2000. That makes representation the largest untested design choice for the dominant modality. 2) Test: config_004 swaps PCA-2000 for scVI-200 and keeps everything else as in the best baseline (RNA-only, single-profile, no aggregation, no fusion). This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. 3) Value: it is a one-variable comparison against the current best, so it can either improve the best result directly or show that PCA is a solid choice. Either way, the answer shapes which RNA encoder to carry into later multiprofile and fusion experiments. Testing weighted fusion or ViT-L before knowing the best RNA representation risks spending budget on a weaker backbone.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the RNA encoder of the best baseline (llm_summary_001), from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, keeping the RNA-only, single-profile setting with no aggregation or fusion. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.7207 to 0.5070 (about -0.214), and validation F1 fell from 0.6815 to 0.4548 (about -0.227). That puts scVI-200 well below PCA-2000 and only slightly above the image-only ResNet50 baseline (0.4710 / 0.4419), so in this one-variable comparison PCA-2000 remains the stronger RNA representation and the best configuration overall. Each result is a single run with unknown variance, and scVI hyperparameters (latent size, training length, preprocessing) were not explored, so it is unclear whether scVI is inherently weaker here or just undertuned; the 200- vs 2000-dimension difference is also bundled with the encoder change, and other RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT) remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA is clearly the strongest modality so far. RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 is best (0.721 acc / 0.681 F1). Changing a single choice from that baseline has hurt every time: multiprofile with either aggregator, adding a ResNet50 image branch by concat, and swapping in scVI-200 (0.507). Within RNA representations, only scGPT remains untested, so it is unknown whether PCA's lead reflects a real advantage or just a weak scVI setup. 2) This run changes only the RNA encoder of the best baseline, from PCA-2000 to scGPT. It tells us whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding beats or matches PCA. 3) The RNA representation is the factor that most limits performance, and it determines which encoder to carry into the multiprofile and fusion experiments. One clean experiment can either find a new best configuration or confirm PCA as the anchor, which makes it a better use of budget than fusion variants built on the uncertain image branch.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 changed only the RNA encoder of the best baseline (llm_summary_001) from PCA-2000 to scGPT, keeping the RNA-only, single-profile setting with no aggregation or fusion. This tested whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding could beat or match PCA. Validation accuracy fell from 0.7207 to 0.5191 (about -0.202), and validation F1 fell from 0.6815 to 0.4797 (about -0.202). That leaves scGPT far below PCA-2000 and only marginally above scVI-200 (0.5070 / 0.4548), so in these one-variable comparisons PCA-2000 is the strongest RNA representation tried and remains the anchor configuration. Each result is a single run with unknown variance, and how scGPT was used (frozen vs fine-tuned embeddings, preprocessing and gene-vocabulary matching, embedding dimension) was not explored, so it is unclear whether pretrained encoders are inherently weaker here or just poorly configured. Because both learned encoders landed near each other well below PCA, a shared factor in the downstream setup or in dimensionality may also be involved, but this is untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 (config_001, 0.721 acc / 0.682 F1) is the best result so far. Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_016) dropped accuracy to 0.629 and F1 to 0.599. That drop could come from uninformative images or from naive concatenation, for example unbalanced feature dimensions and no modality weighting. Every result is a single run, so the size of each gap is uncertain. 2) Test: config_017 changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, keeping the best RNA encoder, the single-profile setting and ResNet50. This isolates whether the fusion design caused the multimodal drop. If weighted fusion recovers or beats the RNA-only baseline, the image branch can add signal when fused properly. If it stays below 0.72, that supports images (at least ResNet50 features) adding little here. 3) Why now: it is a clean one-variable comparison anchored on the strongest configuration, and it settles an important design choice before spending budget elsewhere. It informs every remaining multimodal configuration, since about half use weighted fusion. It also has a realistic chance of matching or improving the best accuracy, so it balances learning and exploitation better than testing ViT-L or more multiprofile variants, which have so far underperformed.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 changed only the fusion method of the multimodal single-profile PCA-2000 + ResNet50 setup (llm_summary_005) from concat to weighted, to test whether naive concatenation explained the multimodal drop below the RNA-only baseline. Validation accuracy fell further, to 0.5305 (about -0.098 vs concat's 0.6287 and about -0.190 vs RNA-only PCA-2000's 0.7207), and validation F1 fell to 0.5152 (vs 0.5993 and 0.6815), though both stayed above image-only ResNet50 (0.4710 / 0.4419). So in this one-variable comparison weighted fusion did not recover the drop and performed worse than concat; neither fusion method tried so far lets ResNet50 image features add value over RNA alone, and RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 remains the best configuration. Each result is a single run with unknown variance, and the weighted-fusion details (how weights are learned or initialized, feature normalization, training adequacy) were not explored, so it remains uncertain whether images are inherently uninformative here, whether ResNet50 features are the limitation, or whether this fusion implementation is poorly suited (e.g., over-weighting the weaker image branch); other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) and other fusion variants remain untested.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 is the best result so far (0.721 / 0.682 F1). Image-only ResNet50 is weak (0.471). Adding ResNet50 features hurt the multimodal model under both concat (0.629) and weighted fusion (0.530). The image encoder is the only major design axis not yet varied, so we cannot tell whether images lack useful signal here or ResNet50 features are the bottleneck. 2) What this tests: Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L in the image-only single-profile setting changes one variable relative to config_010. That isolates the effect of the image encoder. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: This cheap diagnostic decides whether the many ViT-L multimodal configurations are worth pursuing. If ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50, testing PCA-2000 + ViT-L fusion (config_022) next becomes well motivated. If it does not, we have stronger evidence that images add little and can focus the remaining budget on the RNA-only side.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 changed only the image encoder of the image-only, single-profile baseline (llm_summary_004) from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, with no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. The goal was to test whether ResNet50 features, rather than the image modality, explained the weak image results. Validation accuracy rose sharply from 0.4710 to 0.7250 (about +0.254), and validation F1 rose from 0.4419 to 0.6847 (about +0.243). That puts image-only ViT-L marginally above the previous best, RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 (0.7207 / 0.6815), making it nominally the best configuration so far. In this one-variable comparison, the encoder swap suggests ResNet50 features were a major bottleneck and that images carry substantial signal here. This makes ViT-L multimodal configurations (e.g., PCA-2000 + ViT-L with concat or weighted fusion) well motivated. However, every result is a single run with unknown variance, so the roughly 0.004 accuracy edge over RNA-only PCA-2000 should be treated as a tie rather than a real ranking. It also remains untested whether ViT-L and PCA-2000 features are complementary when fused, given that both fusion methods hurt with ResNet50. ViT-L behavior in multiprofile settings and the reasons for its advantage (architecture, pretraining, feature dimension) are likewise unexplored.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The two strongest unimodal models are effectively tied. Image-only ViT-L scored 0.7250 accuracy / 0.6847 F1, and RNA-only PCA-2000 scored 0.7207 / 0.6815. Fusing PCA with ResNet50 lowered accuracy with both concat (0.6287) and weighted fusion (0.5305). But ResNet50 alone was weak (0.4710), so those runs mostly show that fusing in a weak image branch hurts. We do not yet know whether two strong, possibly complementary modalities help when combined. 2. Test: Concat PCA-2000 + ViT-L, single-profile. Relative to config_016, the only change is the image encoder, ResNet50 to ViT-L. Comparing against both unimodal ViT-L and PCA-2000 shows directly whether multimodal fusion adds value once the image features are strong. Concat is chosen over weighted fusion because it was clearly the better fusion method with ResNet50. Single-profile is chosen because multiprofile aggregation has hurt so far. 3. Why now: Fusion with a strong image encoder is the most important untested design question. It also has the highest expected immediate payoff. If it fails, that is strong evidence that the simpler unimodal models should be preferred, and it would focus the remaining budget on unimodal ViT-L or PCA variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 concatenated two individually strong branches, RNA PCA-2000 and image ImageNet ViT-L, in a single-profile multimodal model with no aggregation. Its only change from llm_summary_005 (PCA-2000 + ResNet50 concat, 0.6287 / 0.5993) was the image encoder. Validation accuracy collapsed to 0.2239 (F1 0.1843), roughly 0.50 below both image-only ViT-L (0.7250) and RNA-only PCA-2000 (0.7207), and about 0.40 below the ResNet50 concat run, so in this setup concat fusion clearly did not combine the two strong modalities usefully. Because the result is far worse than either branch alone and worse than fusing with the much weaker ResNet50, it looks more like a possible optimization or implementation failure than reliable evidence that the modalities conflict, for example from feature-scale or dimension imbalance between ViT-L and PCA features, lack of normalization, or training collapse. This is a single run with unknown variance, so it remains unresolved whether PCA-2000 + ViT-L fusion is inherently unhelpful; the anomaly should be checked (e.g., with feature normalization, the training logs, or weighted fusion) before multimodal fusion is ruled out in favor of the tied unimodal leaders.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference baseline for accuracy and F1 that every later change can be measured against. 3) Starting here is the best use of the first experiment because later runs can each change one factor at a time: single vs multiprofile (config_002), PCA vs scVI or scGPT (config_004/007), RNA vs image (config_010), and unimodal vs multimodal (config_016). Each result can then be attributed to a specific design choice rather than to a tangle of changes, and we avoid assuming that more complex models are better.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) tested the simplest configuration in the search space as a reference baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA encoder (2000 components) and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.520 and a validation F1 of 0.479, which should be read only as an initial baseline, since no other configurations have been run to compare against. The modest F1 relative to accuracy may mean performance is uneven across classes, but the data available here cannot confirm that. It remains unknown whether multiprofile inputs, alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-based models, or multimodal fusion would do better or worse. Planned one-factor-at-a-time comparisons against this baseline are needed before attributing any difference to a specific design choice.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far, an RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.520, F1 0.479). We do not yet know how informative imaging is compared with RNA. That is the main uncertainty, because it bears on all 36 multimodal configurations and the 6 image-only ones. 2) This experiment runs an image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model with no aggregation or fusion, so it adds no further complexity. It shows whether the image modality alone is weaker than, comparable to, or stronger than RNA. 3) Why this is the best next use of budget: it is one controlled step that tests the highest-level design choice, modality. That tells us whether image encoders and fusion deserve further budget before we spend runs on finer choices such as the RNA encoder or multiprofile aggregation. Encoder and aggregation comparisons can be run afterwards against well-defined single-profile baselines for both modalities.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no aggregation or fusion, as a counterpart to the RNA-only PCA (n=2000) single-profile baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.632 and a validation F1 of 0.607, compared with 0.520 and 0.479 for the RNA-only baseline. This is an initial observation that this image configuration outperformed this RNA configuration, so the image modality looks at least competitive and justifies further budget for image-based and multimodal runs. The comparison changes modality and encoder at the same time (ResNet50 vs. PCA), and each result comes from a single run with no variance estimate, so the gap cannot be attributed to modality alone. It also remains unknown whether stronger RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), other image encoders, multiprofile aggregation, or fusion would change this ordering.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Two single-profile runs exist. Image-only ResNet50 (acc 0.632, F1 0.607) beat RNA-only PCA (acc 0.520, F1 0.479). Each is a single run, and that comparison changed modality and encoder together. It is still unknown whether RNA adds information beyond images. 2. Test: config_016 combines exactly these two tested components (PCA-2000 RNA and ResNet50 image), keeps the single-profile setting, and adds only simple concat fusion. Comparing it against both unimodal baselines isolates whether multimodal fusion helps, is neutral, or hurts. 3. Why now: Whether the weaker RNA modality adds anything beyond images determines whether multimodal configurations deserve budget. The answer sets the priority for most of the remaining search space (configs 016–051). The alternatives (image multiprofile aggregation, ViT-L, or other RNA encoders) each matter, but they refine a single modality and can follow. Using the simplest fusion with already-measured encoders avoids changing several factors at once.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested a multimodal, single-profile model that joins the two already-measured encoders, PCA-2000 RNA and ResNet50 image, with simple concat fusion and no aggregation, to check whether RNA adds information beyond images. It reached validation accuracy 0.519 and F1 0.480, essentially identical to the RNA-only baseline (0.520 / 0.479) and well below image-only ResNet50 (0.632 / 0.607). This is an initial observation that this concat fusion did not just fail to add value but lost the image-only advantage, so the fused model behaved as if the image signal contributed little or nothing. The near-exact match to RNA-only could reflect RNA features dominating the concatenation (e.g., feature scale or dimensionality imbalance), optimization issues, or a pipeline problem with the image branch, and these single runs with no variance estimates cannot tell these apart or show that multimodal fusion is inherently unhelpful; checks of the fused model's image pathway, feature normalization, or alternative fusion methods are needed before deprioritizing multimodal configurations.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only ResNet50 (0.632 acc / 0.607 F1) clearly beat RNA-only PCA (0.520 / 0.479). However, concat fusion of the same two encoders (config_016) collapsed to RNA-only performance (0.519 / 0.480). That points to a fusion-specific problem, such as RNA features dominating the concatenation or the image signal being ignored, rather than to multimodality being inherently unhelpful. Each result is a single run, so none of this is settled. 2. What this tests: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 the same (single-profile, PCA-2000, ResNet50) and changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds image-only accuracy, the concat result was a fusion artifact and multimodal configurations deserve more budget. If it also collapses to RNA-only levels, that suggests a broader problem with the multimodal image pathway or that RNA adds noise, which would justify shifting budget toward image-only extensions (multiprofile aggregation, ViT-L). 3. Why now: This answers the most consequential open question, whether to keep investing in the largest part of the search space (multimodal configurations, 35 of the 48 remaining), with a clean one-factor change. That makes it more informative than exploring a new axis while the multimodal anomaly is still unexplained.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the llm_summary_003 multimodal single-profile setup (PCA-2000 RNA + ResNet50 image, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted, to test whether the earlier collapse to RNA-only performance was specific to concat fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.518 and F1 0.484, again essentially matching RNA-only (0.520 / 0.479) and concat fusion (0.519 / 0.480), and well below image-only ResNet50 (0.632 / 0.607). This initial observation suggests the problem is not specific to concat: two different fusion methods with these encoders both lose the image-only advantage, which is consistent with a broader issue in the multimodal image pathway (e.g., image features being ignored, scale or normalization imbalance, or a pipeline or integration bug) or with RNA features dominating, rather than with any one fusion method. All results are single runs without variance estimates, and the near-identical scores across the three RNA-containing configurations make a pipeline issue in the multimodal image branch worth checking directly (e.g., image-branch contribution, feature normalization) before concluding that multimodality is inherently unhelpful or shifting the remaining multimodal budget toward image-only extensions.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: image-only ResNet50 (0.632 acc / 0.607 F1) clearly beats RNA-only PCA-2000 (0.520 / 0.479). Both multimodal runs that pair PCA-2000 with ResNet50 fall back to RNA-only levels (concat 0.519, weighted 0.518). Because the result does not depend on the fusion method, the likely cause is the RNA side. One plausible explanation is that the 2000-dimensional PCA features swamp the image features through scale or dimensionality imbalance. The other is a problem with the image branch inside the multimodal pipeline. 2) Test: config_028 keeps config_016 fixed (single-profile, ResNet50, concat) and changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to the compact 200-dimensional scVI. If accuracy rises to or above the image-only level, the collapse is specific to PCA-2000 and multimodal fusion is still viable. If it again matches an RNA-like level, that points more strongly to a general image-branch or integration problem. 3) Why now: most of the remaining search space is multimodal, so deciding whether fusion can work at all is the highest-value uncertainty. The result will tell us whether to keep spending budget on multimodal configurations or move it to image-only extensions such as multiprofile aggregation and ViT-L. One limit: scVI has no RNA-only reference yet, so an RNA-like result here is partly confounded with scVI's own quality. Running config_004 would resolve that if needed.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the llm_summary_003 multimodal single-profile setup (ResNet50 image encoder, concat fusion, no aggregation) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to the 200-dimensional scVI. The goal was to test whether the earlier collapse to RNA-only performance was specific to the high-dimensional PCA features. It reached validation accuracy 0.471 and F1 0.442, which is below image-only ResNet50 (0.632 / 0.607) and also below the PCA-2000 multimodal runs (concat 0.519, weighted 0.518) and the PCA-2000 RNA-only baseline (0.520 / 0.479). This initial observation suggests that shrinking the RNA input to 200 dimensions did not restore the image-only advantage, so the failure does not appear specific to PCA-2000 dimensionality. Across three multimodal runs, the fused model seems to track the RNA side rather than benefit from the image features, which is consistent with a general image-branch, normalization, or integration problem, though not proven. A key uncertainty is that scVI-n200 has no RNA-only reference (e.g., config_004), so the score cannot yet be separated from scVI's own quality, and all results are single runs without variance estimates. Directly checking the image pathway's contribution inside the multimodal pipeline, or running scVI RNA-only, would be needed before deciding to shift budget away from multimodal configurations toward image-only extensions.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only ResNet50 (0.632 acc / 0.607 F1) clearly beats RNA-only PCA-2000 (0.520 / 0.479). All three multimodal runs lose the image advantage. The two PCA-2000 fusions match RNA-only almost exactly. The scVI-n200 concat run (0.471 / 0.442) dropped further, but it has no RNA-only scVI reference. So we cannot tell whether fused models simply track the RNA branch or whether scVI fusion is degraded for some other reason. 2. What this tests: Running config_004 (scVI-n200 RNA-only, single-profile) changes only the encoder relative to config_001. It also gives the missing reference for config_028. If it scores about 0.47, the pattern that multimodal performance equals RNA-only performance is confirmed across two RNA encoders. That would strongly suggest the image branch is effectively ignored in the fusion pipeline. If it scores clearly above 0.471, fusion is actively harmful in a different way. Either result also tells us how scVI compares with PCA as an RNA encoder. 3. Why now: Multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space (34 of 46 configs). Resolving whether they are systematically capped at RNA-only performance decides whether to prune them and shift budget toward image-only extensions (multiprofile aggregation, ViT-L). This single cheap, one-factor run therefore reduces more uncertainty than an immediate image-only exploit.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 tested an RNA-only, single-profile model with the 200-dimensional scVI encoder, changing only the RNA encoder relative to the PCA-2000 RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001). It also supplied the missing RNA-only reference for the scVI-n200 + ResNet50 concat run (llm_summary_005). It reached validation accuracy 0.532 and F1 0.516, slightly above PCA-2000 RNA-only (0.520 / 0.479), with a larger F1 gap that may indicate more balanced class performance. It remained well below image-only ResNet50 (0.632 / 0.607) and clearly above its scVI concat fusion counterpart (0.471 / 0.442), so the earlier pattern that multimodal performance simply equals RNA-only performance does not hold for scVI. Instead, this initial observation suggests fusion can actively degrade performance below either single modality, which is consistent with, but does not prove, a general problem in the multimodal integration or image pathway (e.g., normalization, optimization, or pipeline issues) rather than the image branch merely being ignored. All results are single runs without variance estimates, so the small scVI-vs-PCA difference (about 0.012 accuracy) may not be meaningful, and the cause of the fusion degradation remains untested; directly diagnosing the multimodal pipeline is still needed before pruning the remaining multimodal configurations in favor of image-only extensions.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Image-only ResNet50 single-profile (config_010, 0.632 acc / 0.607 F1) is clearly the best result so far. RNA-only runs sit around 0.52-0.53. Three multimodal runs either matched RNA-only or fell below it, which suggests an integration problem rather than useful fusion. Profile setting and aggregation have never been tested in any modality, so multiprofile versus singleprofile is the largest untested design choice. 2) What this tests: config_011 keeps the strongest setup (image-only, ResNet50) and changes only singleprofile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. Any difference in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to multiprofile inputs and aggregation, not to modality or encoder. 3) Why this is the best next run: it exploits the most promising direction while settling a design choice that applies to every modality and to future multimodal runs. Avgpool is the simplest aggregator, so it gives a clean baseline before trying transformer aggregation (config_012) or the ViT-L image encoder (config_013). It also avoids spending more budget on multimodal configurations that keep failing for reasons not yet understood.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the strongest prior setup, image-only with a ResNet50 encoder (llm_summary_002), and changed only the profile setting from singleprofile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. This was the first test of profile setting and aggregation in any modality. It reached validation accuracy 0.688 and F1 0.659, up from 0.632 / 0.607 for single-profile image-only, and is now the best result so far, well above RNA-only (0.520–0.532) and all multimodal runs (0.471–0.519). Because only the profile setting changed, this initial observation suggests that multiprofile input with avgpool helps the image-only ResNet50 model, though profile setting and aggregation were introduced together and cannot be separated. The result also comes from a single run without a variance estimate. It remains untested whether the gain carries over to RNA-only or multimodal configurations, whether other aggregators (e.g., transformer) or encoders (e.g., ViT-L) improve further, and whether the still-unexplained multimodal integration problem would also affect multiprofile fusion runs.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool (0.688 acc / 0.659 F1). It beats single-profile image-only (0.632), all RNA-only runs (0.520–0.532) and all multimodal runs (0.471–0.519). Multimodal fusion has failed three times, for reasons still unexplained. Aggregation has only ever been tested as avgpool, so the multiprofile gain cannot yet be separated from the choice of aggregator. 2) Test: This run keeps the best setup fixed (image-only, ResNet50, multiprofile) and changes only avgpool to transformer. It isolates whether a learned aggregator adds value beyond simple pooling. 3) Why now: This exploits the strongest direction with a clean one-factor comparison. Aggregation affects most of the remaining search space, since many untested configs are multiprofile, so the answer helps prune both avgpool and transformer variants for later image-only and multimodal runs. It is more decisive than adding more multimodal runs while the fusion problem remains undiagnosed. Testing ViT-L (config_014) is a natural follow-up once the better aggregator is known.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best prior setup, image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile input (llm_summary_007), fixed and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer, to test whether a learned aggregator adds value beyond simple pooling. It reached validation accuracy 0.494 and F1 0.453. That is far below multiprofile avgpool (0.688 / 0.659) and single-profile image-only (0.632 / 0.607), and even below the RNA-only runs (0.520–0.532), placing it near the weakest multimodal results (0.471–0.519). Because this was a clean one-factor change, the initial observation is that the transformer aggregator, as configured here, performed much worse than avgpool. A drop this large, below even the single-profile result, suggests the transformer may have failed to train well (e.g., optimization, hyperparameter, data-size, or implementation issues) rather than revealing a basic limit of learned aggregation. This is a single run without a variance estimate, so it is untested whether a tuned transformer would recover or exceed avgpool, how this aggregator behaves with other encoders (e.g., ViT-L), RNA-only, or multimodal settings, and whether its failure shares a cause with the unexplained multimodal degradation. For now, avgpool remains the better-supported aggregator for multiprofile runs.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool is clearly the best result so far (0.688 acc / 0.659 F1). It beats single-profile image-only (0.632), all RNA-only runs (0.520–0.532), all multimodal runs (0.471–0.519) and the transformer aggregator (0.494). The image encoder has not been varied at all, so it is unknown whether ResNet50 is a good choice or a bottleneck. 2) Test: config_014 keeps the best setup fixed (image-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. This cleanly isolates the effect of the image representation within the strongest pipeline found so far. 3) Why now: it is both exploitation and exploration. It could raise the best accuracy, and it answers an important open design question with a single-factor comparison. Its result will also guide later runs. If ViT-L helps, ViT-L variants of the single-profile and multimodal configurations become higher priority. If it does not, ResNet50 stays the reference encoder, and the remaining budget can go to diagnosing multimodal fusion under multiprofile avgpool (e.g., config_018).
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the best prior setup fixed (image-only, multiprofile, avgpool; llm_summary_007 at 0.688 acc / 0.659 F1) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, to test whether the image representation was a bottleneck. It reached validation accuracy 0.411 and F1 0.378, far below ResNet50 multiprofile avgpool and single-profile ResNet50 (0.632 / 0.607). This is now the lowest result so far, below the RNA-only runs (0.520–0.532), all multimodal runs (0.471–0.519), and the transformer-aggregator run (0.494). Because this was a clean one-factor change, the initial observation is that ViT-L, as configured in this pipeline, performed much worse than ResNet50, so ResNet50 remains the reference image encoder. A drop this large for a typically strong encoder suggests possible feature-extraction, preprocessing or resolution mismatch, normalization, or downstream-training issues rather than a basic limit of ViT-L representations. This single run has no variance estimate. It remains untested whether a corrected or tuned ViT-L pipeline would recover, and whether this failure shares a cause with the unexplained multimodal and transformer-aggregator degradations. This lowers the priority of ViT-L variants of other configurations until the encoder pipeline is checked.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is image-only ResNet50 with multiprofile avgpool (0.688 acc / 0.659 F1). It improved on single-profile image-only (0.632 / 0.607) in a clean one-factor change. Profile setting has only been tested for images, so it is unknown whether the multiprofile gain is general or image-specific. Among RNA encoders, scVI-n200 is slightly the strongest (0.532 / 0.516 vs PCA 0.520 / 0.479), though that gap is small. Multimodal runs consistently fall to or below RNA-only levels. The transformer aggregator and ViT-L both performed poorly, so neither is a good choice for a clean test. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes only the profile setting, from singleprofile to multiprofile avgpool, relative to scVI RNA-only (config_004). It shows whether multiprofile avgpool also helps the RNA modality. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean, low-risk test of whether profile setting matters broadly, using the aggregator that has worked. It also provides the RNA-only multiprofile reference needed to interpret later multiprofile multimodal runs (e.g., config_030 or config_031). Given that fusion appears to track or degrade toward the RNA side, that reference is needed before spending budget on multimodal multiprofile configurations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the scVI-n200 RNA-only setup (llm_summary_006, 0.532 acc / 0.516 F1) and changed only the profile setting from singleprofile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation, to test whether the multiprofile gain seen for image-only ResNet50 also applies to RNA. It reached validation accuracy 0.721 and F1 0.681, a large improvement over single-profile scVI RNA-only and now the best result so far, above multiprofile image-only ResNet50 avgpool (0.688 / 0.659). Because this was a clean one-factor change and both modalities improved under the same change, the initial observation is that multiprofile input with avgpool helps beyond the image modality and is not image-specific, though profile setting and aggregation were introduced together and cannot be separated. The gain here (about +0.19 accuracy) is much larger than for images (about +0.06), which is notable and worth confirming. Each result is a single run with no variance estimate, so the small RNA-vs-image multiprofile gap (about 0.033) may not be meaningful. It remains untested whether multiprofile multimodal fusion (e.g., scVI + ResNet50 avgpool) would beat either single modality or still show the unexplained fusion degradation, and whether the PCA RNA encoder gains similarly. This run now serves as the RNA-only multiprofile reference for those comparisons.

selection_reason: 1. No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet on whether modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matter. 2. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, cheapest reference point. Every more complex choice can be compared against it with one change at a time: a learned RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT), adding images, moving to multiprofile with avgpool or transformer, or adding fusion. 3. Spending the first experiment on this baseline gives a lower bound for accuracy and F1. It also keeps later comparisons interpretable, so we do not have to start with a complex multimodal model whose result could not be attributed to any single design decision.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first reference point with the simplest configuration: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA-2000 RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.5907 (primary metric), with a validation F1 of 0.5727 as supporting evidence. Because no other experiments have been completed, this is only a baseline and does not show whether modality, encoder type, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion affect performance. Future single-change comparisons against this setup, such as a learned RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT), adding images, multiprofile with avgpool or transformer aggregation, or fusion, are needed to judge the impact of each design choice, and variance across runs or seeds is also still unknown.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA-2000 baseline (acc 0.5907, F1 0.5727). We do not yet know the effect of any design choice. 2) Test: config_002 changes one factor, the profile setting. It moves from singleprofile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool) and keeps the same RNA-only PCA-2000 setup. This isolates whether pooling information across multiple profiles helps. 3) Why now: Profile setting cuts across every modality and encoder in the search space, so this result informs a large share of the remaining configurations. Avgpool is the lowest-complexity aggregation, which gives a clean read on the multiprofile effect before testing transformer aggregation, other encoders, images, or fusion. A gain here would point the search toward multiprofile variants; no gain would steer the budget toward encoder or modality changes.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA-2000 setup from the llm_summary_001 baseline and switched from single-profile to multiprofile input with avgpool aggregation, using no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6390 (+0.048, primary metric), and validation F1 rose from 0.5727 to 0.6197 (+0.047) as supporting evidence. This suggests that multiprofile input with simple mean pooling may help in the RNA-only PCA setting. However, multiprofile and avgpool were introduced together, so their separate contributions cannot be told apart, and each configuration was evaluated only once, so run-to-run or seed variance is unknown and the gain may be partly noise. It also remains untested whether the benefit carries over to learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image or fused modalities, or a more expressive aggregator such as a transformer, so multiprofile variants are a promising direction rather than an established improvement.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Moving from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool (config_001 to config_002) raised validation accuracy from 0.591 to 0.639, and F1 rose by a similar amount. That makes multiprofile the most promising direction so far. However, each setup was run only once, and the aggregation method has not been varied. 2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from the current best (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether a more expressive aggregator adds value beyond simple mean pooling. It also checks whether the multiprofile gain holds up under a different aggregator. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: It extends the strongest evidence while changing exactly one design choice, so the result is easy to interpret. The avgpool-versus-transformer choice recurs in every multiprofile configuration (RNA-only, image-only and multimodal), so resolving it early informs many later experiments. Encoder and modality questions can follow once aggregation is better understood.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile setup from llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, with no image encoder or fusion. Validation accuracy rose from 0.6390 to 0.6530 (+0.014, primary metric; +0.062 over the single-profile baseline llm_summary_001), and validation F1 rose from 0.6197 to 0.6283 (+0.009) as supporting evidence. Because only aggregation differed, this is a direct comparison, and it suggests transformer aggregation may give a modest benefit over mean pooling in this setting. Each configuration was run only once and seed or run-to-run variance is unknown, so this small gain may fall within noise; it also remains untested whether the transformer advantage holds with learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only, or multimodal fused configurations.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the RNA-only PCA-2000 series suggests multiprofile input helps (+0.048 accuracy). Transformer aggregation adds a smaller gain (+0.014), with F1 moving the same way. Each result comes from a single run, so the aggregation gain may be noise. The image modality, the defining question of multimodal profiling, has not been tested at all. 2) This experiment keeps the current best setup fixed (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile, transformer; config_003). It only adds ResNet50 image features with the simplest fusion, concat. Comparing against config_003 directly tests whether adding images improves accuracy and F1 beyond RNA alone. Concat is the minimal fusion choice, so weighted fusion can be compared in a later experiment. 3) Whether to use images at all is the largest open design decision and determines which half of the remaining search space deserves budget. Swapping the RNA encoder (scVI or scGPT) would only refine a single axis within the modality already tested. Building on the strongest known configuration also keeps this a reasonable exploitation step while it serves as an exploration step.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best RNA-only configuration fixed (llm_summary_003: PCA-2000, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and added ResNet50 image features with concat fusion, the first test of the image modality. Validation accuracy dropped sharply from 0.6530 to 0.5399 (-0.113, primary metric), and validation F1 fell from 0.6283 to 0.5245 (-0.104) as supporting evidence. This multimodal result is also below the single-profile RNA-only baseline (llm_summary_001, 0.5907), so in this setup, adding images through plain concatenation clearly hurt rather than helped. Because the image encoder and concat fusion had to be introduced together, the evidence cannot tell whether the image features carry little useful signal or whether the fusion itself is the problem (for example, imbalance between the two feature sets). The result comes from a single run with unknown seed variance, and untested options include weighted fusion, an image-only configuration, and other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), so the value of the image modality remains open rather than ruled out.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Multiprofile input helped RNA-only PCA (0.591 to 0.639), and transformer aggregation added a modest gain (0.653). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion (config_020) dropped accuracy sharply to 0.540, with F1 falling similarly. Because the image encoder and fusion were introduced together, we cannot tell whether the image features lack signal or plain concatenation is the problem, for example the image features swamping the RNA features. 2. Test: config_021 is identical to config_020 except that it uses weighted fusion instead of concat. This single-change comparison isolates the effect of fusion. If accuracy recovers to near or above 0.653, concat was the bottleneck and multimodal fusion remains viable. If it stays well below the RNA-only result, the ResNet50 image features themselves are probably unhelpful or harmful here. 3. Why now: Multimodal settings make up most of the remaining search space. Learning whether fusion choice can rescue the image modality decides whether those configurations deserve budget, so this experiment is worth more than an incremental RNA-encoder test. Encoder swaps (scVI, scGPT) and image-only checks remain natural follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 repeated the multimodal llm_summary_004 configuration (PCA-2000 RNA, ResNet50 images, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) but changed only the fusion, from concat to weighted, which isolates the effect of fusion choice. Validation accuracy recovered from 0.5399 to 0.6501 (+0.110, primary metric), and validation F1 rose from 0.5245 to 0.6275 (+0.103) as supporting evidence. This suggests concat fusion, not the presence of image features alone, was responsible for the earlier drop. However, the result is essentially tied with the best RNA-only setup (llm_summary_003: 0.6530 accuracy, 0.6283 F1; -0.003 accuracy here), so there is no evidence yet that ResNet50 images add useful signal. Weighted fusion may simply be down-weighting the image branch, but the learned weights were not inspected, image-only performance is untested, and each configuration was run once with unknown seed variance. Multimodal configurations therefore remain viable but unproven, and natural next steps are an image-only check, inspecting the fusion weights, and trying learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) under weighted fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile input with transformer aggregation is the best RNA-only setup so far (0.653 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 images hurt badly with concat fusion (0.540). With weighted fusion it only tied RNA-only (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). So it is still unclear whether the ResNet50 image features carry any useful signal, or whether weighted fusion is simply down-weighting the image branch. 2. What this tests: an image-only model with the same multiprofile transformer setup, swapping only the modality relative to config_003. This isolates how much predictive signal the image branch carries by itself. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: About half the remaining configurations are multimodal. If images alone perform near chance, effort should shift to RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and image fusion can be deprioritized. If images are reasonably strong, the tie suggests the fusion is under-using them, which justifies trying ViT-L and other fusion variants. Either outcome sharply narrows the search, so it is a better use of budget than further multimodal guesses.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 was the first image-only test. It used the multiprofile transformer setup from llm_summary_003 (ResNet50 image encoder, no RNA, no fusion), so modality was the only change. Validation accuracy was 0.5793 (primary metric), with F1 0.5631 as supporting evidence. That is clearly below the RNA-only counterpart (0.6530 accuracy, -0.074; F1 -0.065), slightly below the single-profile RNA baseline (0.5907), and above the concat multimodal model (0.5399), which suggests ResNet50 images carry some predictive signal but less than PCA RNA features in this setup. Because the image-only model outscored the concat model that also had RNA, the evidence is consistent with concat fusion actively interfering rather than images being useless. However, the number of classes and the chance level are not given, so how much image signal exists beyond chance is unclear. It also remains unresolved whether the weighted-fusion tie (llm_summary_005) reflects down-weighting of images or images being redundant with RNA, since fusion weights were not inspected. Every result comes from a single run with unknown seed variance, and stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) and learned RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) are untested.

selection_reason: 1) Existing evidence: RNA is the strongest modality so far. RNA-only PCA multiprofile with transformer aggregation (config_003) scored 0.653 accuracy, versus 0.579 for image-only. Weighted fusion with ResNet50 images only tied that result (0.650), and concat fusion hurt it. Multiprofile and transformer aggregation look beneficial. The biggest untested design choice is the RNA representation, because every run with RNA so far used PCA-2000. 2) What this tests: config_009 keeps the best setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer) and swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT. This directly shows whether a pretrained foundation-model representation improves on PCA. 3) Why now: since RNA drives performance and image gains are unproven, the RNA encoder is the dimension most likely to raise the ceiling. A single-change comparison against config_003 is clean. The result also decides which RNA encoder to carry into later multimodal weighted-fusion runs, which is more informative than further image or fusion variants built on PCA.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_003 fixed (multiprofile input, transformer aggregation, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.6530 to 0.4106 (-0.242, primary metric), and validation F1 fell from 0.6283 to 0.3785 (-0.250) as supporting evidence. This is the lowest result so far, below the image-only run (0.5793) and the concat multimodal run (0.5399), and because only the encoder changed, it suggests that scGPT embeddings as used here are much worse than PCA-2000 in this pipeline, so PCA remains the better RNA encoder to carry into weighted-fusion runs for now. It remains unclear whether the drop reflects scGPT's representation itself or how it was applied (for example, frozen versus fine-tuned embeddings, gene-vocabulary or preprocessing mismatch, or aggregator hyperparameters tuned for PCA); the result also comes from a single run with unknown seed variance, chance level is not given, and scVI is still untested, so learned RNA encoders are not ruled out in general.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA is the strongest modality so far. The best result is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation (0.6530 accuracy / 0.6283 F1). Weighted fusion with ResNet50 images only tied it (0.6501), and image-only scored lower (0.5793). So the RNA representation appears to drive performance. Among RNA encoders, scGPT dropped accuracy sharply (0.4106), while scVI is still untested. It is unclear whether learned RNA encoders fail in general or only scGPT as applied here. 2) Test: config_006 keeps config_003 fixed and swaps only PCA-2000 for scVI-200. This directly isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. It shows whether a compact learned latent space can beat or match PCA, and whether the scGPT result reflects learned encoders broadly. 3) Value: the RNA encoder is the choice with the largest observed effect, and the result decides which encoder to carry into the many remaining multimodal and weighted-fusion configurations. Resolving it now, with one clean comparison, avoids spending budget on scVI multimodal runs that would confound encoder and fusion effects. Testing ViT-L images is a reasonable later step, but images currently add little.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_003 fixed (multiprofile input, transformer aggregation, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI with a 200-dimensional latent. Validation accuracy rose from 0.6530 to 0.7150 (+0.062, primary metric), and validation F1 rose from 0.6283 to 0.6872 (+0.059) as supporting evidence. This is the best result so far, well above the weighted-fusion multimodal run (0.6501) and far above scGPT (0.4106). Because only the encoder changed, it suggests scVI-200 is a stronger RNA representation than PCA-2000 in this pipeline, and that the poor scGPT result does not mean learned RNA encoders fail in general, which makes scVI the leading encoder to carry into weighted-fusion multimodal runs. It remains uncertain whether the gain comes from scVI's learned latent space itself or from factors such as its much lower dimensionality interacting with transformer hyperparameters originally used with PCA. All results are single runs with unknown seed variance, chance level is not given, and it is untested whether ResNet50 or stronger image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) add signal on top of scVI under weighted fusion.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: scVI-200 with multiprofile transformer aggregation (config_006) is the clear leader at 0.7150 accuracy and 0.6872 F1. That is +0.062 over PCA-2000 in an otherwise identical setup. Separately, weighted fusion recovered from the large concat drop, but it only tied PCA RNA-only (0.6501 vs 0.6530). The image-only ResNet50 run (0.5793) shows images carry some signal, so whether they add value on top of RNA is still unresolved. 2. Test: config_033 changes one factor from the best configuration, adding ResNet50 images through weighted fusion while keeping scVI, multiprofile input and transformer aggregation fixed. It asks whether images add complementary signal to a stronger RNA representation, or whether the PCA tie reflects image features being redundant or down-weighted. 3. Why now: this is a single-variable extension of the best model, so it exploits the strongest evidence while answering the key open question of whether multimodality is worth pursuing. If it clearly beats 0.715, it justifies testing ViT-L images next. If it ties or falls short, the budget can shift toward refining the RNA-only scVI setup, such as aggregation and profile ablations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 took the best configuration (llm_summary_008: scVI-200 RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation) and added ResNet50 image features through weighted fusion, testing whether images add complementary signal on top of the stronger RNA representation. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.7150 to 0.5420 (-0.173, primary metric), and F1 fell from 0.6872 to 0.4833 (-0.204) as supporting evidence. This result is below the PCA-2000 weighted-fusion run (0.6501), below image-only ResNet50 (0.5793), and close to the failed PCA concat run (0.5399), so in this setup adding images to scVI clearly hurt, and the run gives no support for moving on to ViT-L images. It suggests the budget should favor refining RNA-only scVI, but it is unclear why weighted fusion tied with PCA yet degraded with scVI: possible explanations include scale or dimensionality imbalance between the 200-d scVI latent and ResNet50 features, fusion-weight behavior (weights were not inspected), or hyperparameters tuned for other setups. The result is also a single run with unknown seed variance, so it does not rule out multimodality in general.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: scVI-200 RNA-only with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation is clearly the best configuration so far (0.715 accuracy, 0.687 F1). Adding ResNet50 images to scVI hurt badly (0.542), so the RNA-only scVI direction deserves exploitation. Within that direction, the aggregation choice is the least settled. Transformer beat avgpool by only +0.014 accuracy with PCA in a single run, which may be noise, and that comparison has never been made with scVI. scVI's much smaller 200-d latent could change how the two aggregators behave. 2. What this tests: config_005 changes only the aggregation (transformer to avgpool) on the best scVI multiprofile setup. It isolates whether transformer aggregation actually helps, or whether simpler mean pooling performs as well or better with the stronger encoder. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: it is a single-variable comparison in the most promising region of the search space. It has a real chance of matching or beating the current best, and either outcome sharpens the aggregation conclusion. Testing the single-profile scVI setup (config_004) would ask about profile setting, which already had the more robust effect (+0.048 with PCA). Further image or multimodal runs currently have weak support.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the best configuration fixed (llm_summary_008: scVI-200 RNA-only, multiprofile, no image encoder or fusion) and changed only the aggregation, from transformer to avgpool, to test whether the small transformer advantage seen with PCA (+0.014, llm_summary_002 vs 003) also holds with scVI. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.7150 to 0.5729 (-0.142, primary metric), and F1 fell from 0.6872 to 0.5730 (-0.114) as supporting evidence. The result is also below PCA-2000 with avgpool (0.6390) and even the single-profile PCA baseline (0.5907). Because only aggregation changed, this suggests transformer aggregation matters much more with scVI than with PCA, and that scVI's advantage over PCA depends on the aggregator, so scVI plus transformer remains the configuration to build on. It is unclear why mean pooling hurts scVI so much. Possible explanations include mean pooling washing out information in the compact 200-d latent, or hyperparameters suited to other setups, but neither has been tested. All results come from single runs with unknown seed variance, and the single-profile scVI setting is still untested.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run yet, so we have no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest, most interpretable baseline. Many later experiments can be compared against it by changing one factor at a time: the RNA encoder (config_004 for scVI, config_007 for scGPT), the profile setting and aggregation (config_002 for multiprofile avgpool), the modality (config_010 for image-only), and adding fusion (config_016 for multimodal). 3) With a limited budget, a cheap, low-variance reference point is the most efficient first experiment. It sets a performance floor and avoids confounding several design choices, so it should be run before testing more complex multimodal or multiprofile models.
experiment_summary: This first experiment (llm_summary_001) established a baseline using an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA encoder (2000 components) and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.519, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.480, which gives an initial reference point for later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons (e.g., scVI or scGPT RNA encoders, multiprofile avgpool, image-only, multimodal fusion). Because no other configurations have been evaluated, it is unknown whether this performance is strong or weak relative to alternatives, and no conclusions can yet be drawn about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. Run-to-run variance is also uncharacterized, so small future differences from this baseline should be interpreted cautiously.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001) reached 0.519 accuracy and 0.480 F1. We do not yet know how much the image modality contributes, and that is the largest open question because it determines whether the many multimodal and image configurations are worth testing. 2) Test: config_010 is the image-only, single-profile ResNet50 model, with no aggregation or fusion. Against config_001 it changes only the modality, so it directly measures how informative images are compared with RNA. 3) Why now: knowing the strength of the image modality alone sets the reference point for later fusion experiments. If images are weak, the search can focus on RNA encoders and profile settings. If they are comparable or stronger, multimodal fusion becomes a more promising direction. This is the most useful uncertainty to reduce with the next experiment. Comparing RNA encoders (scVI or scGPT) or adding multiprofile pooling are natural follow-ups after that.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.532 (F1 0.516), slightly above the RNA-only PCA baseline from llm_summary_001 (accuracy 0.519, F1 0.480). This is an initial sign that images alone are at least comparable to RNA alone, with a somewhat larger margin on F1. Because modality and encoder changed together (PCA vs ResNet50), the comparison reflects these specific encoders rather than the modalities in general. The roughly 1.3-point accuracy gap is small and run-to-run variance is uncharacterized, so it remains uncertain whether either modality is truly stronger. The result does make multimodal fusion and alternative RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) reasonable next comparisons.

selection_reason: Evidence: the two single-profile baselines are close. RNA-only PCA reached 0.519 accuracy (F1 0.480) and image-only ResNet50 reached 0.532 (F1 0.516). This suggests the two modalities are roughly comparable, though variance is uncharacterized. The biggest open question is whether combining them adds complementary signal. Test: config_016 is single-profile multimodal with concat fusion, using exactly the PCA and ResNet50 encoders already tested. It therefore isolates the effect of fusion against both unimodal references, with no confound from encoder, profile setting or aggregation. Concat is the simplest fusion and gives a clean reference point for testing weighted fusion later. Why now: whether to fuse is a top-level decision for the rest of the search. A clear gain over 0.532 would point the budget toward multimodal extensions such as aggregation, weighted fusion and stronger encoders. No gain would point toward refining unimodal encoders and profile settings instead.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_003 tested a single-profile multimodal model that concatenates the same PCA (n=2000) RNA and ResNet50 image encoders used in the two unimodal baselines, with no aggregation, so fusion is the only change relative to those references. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.520 (F1 0.479), nearly identical to RNA-only (0.519, F1 0.480) and below image-only (0.532, F1 0.516). This is an initial sign that simple concat fusion adds no complementary signal here, and the near-exact match to RNA-only might hint that the fused model leans on RNA features, though that is a hypothesis the current evidence does not test. Because run-to-run variance is uncharacterized and only one fusion method was tried, it is unclear whether the shortfall versus image-only is real, or whether other fusion schemes (e.g., weighted fusion, feature normalization or balancing) or other encoders would let fusion help. For now, this result does not support prioritizing multimodal concat over refining unimodal encoders.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence so far: all three runs are single-profile. Image-only ResNet50 is slightly best (acc 0.532, F1 0.516). RNA-only PCA (0.519) and concat fusion (0.520) are nearly tied, and fusion gave no benefit. The profile-setting and aggregation axis is completely untested, even though it applies to every model type. 2) This run changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool, on the current best configuration (config_010). That isolates whether combining multiple profiles helps, using the simplest aggregation as the reference before trying transformer aggregation. 3) It explores an important unmeasured design axis while building on the strongest result so far. A clear gain would point the rest of the search toward multiprofile settings across modalities. No gain would let us drop many multiprofile configurations. That makes it more informative than tweaking fusion, which has already shown no benefit, or swapping encoders right now.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_004 tested the best configuration so far (image-only, ResNet50 from llm_summary_002) with one change: single-profile was switched to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy was 0.523 (F1 0.508), slightly below the single-profile image-only result (0.532, F1 0.516). This is an initial sign that combining profiles by simple average pooling does not help this image-only setup, but the roughly 0.9-point drop is small and run-to-run variance is uncharacterized, so it may be noise rather than a real decline. The result is specific to this configuration. It is unknown whether learned aggregation (e.g., a transformer) or multiprofile settings with RNA-only or multimodal models would behave differently, so it is premature to drop the multiprofile axis entirely.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Image-only ResNet50 single-profile is the best result so far (acc 0.532, F1 0.516). It is ahead of RNA-only PCA (0.519) and PCA+ResNet50 concat fusion (0.520), and multiprofile avgpool did not help (0.523). All gaps are about 1 point with unknown run-to-run variance. The encoder axis is completely unexplored for both modalities. 2) This experiment changes only the image encoder (ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L) and keeps the best setup otherwise: image-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion. It isolates whether representation quality, which may matter more than profile or fusion choices, can improve the strongest modality. 3) It exploits the current best direction while answering a key design question with a single controlled change. The answer also guides later multimodal choices: whether to pair RNA with ViT-L or ResNet50, and whether a stronger image encoder lets fusion add value. Testing RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) is a close alternative and a natural follow-up.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_005 kept the best configuration so far (image-only, single-profile, no aggregation or fusion, from llm_summary_002) and made one change, replacing the ResNet50 image encoder with an ImageNet ViT-L encoder. Validation accuracy fell sharply to 0.208 (F1 0.172), compared with 0.532 (F1 0.516) for ResNet50 and about 0.52 for every other configuration tested. This drop of about 32 points is far larger than the roughly 1-point gaps seen so far, so it is unlikely to be run-to-run noise, and because the encoder was the only setting changed, it indicates that this ViT-L setup performs much worse here than ResNet50. It is still unclear whether the cause is ViT-L's representations being poorly suited to these cell images, or an implementation or optimization problem specific to this run (e.g., preprocessing, input resolution, feature extraction, or training instability), so the result should be checked or debugged before ViT-L is ruled out, and ResNet50 remains the safer image encoder for multimodal follow-ups and RNA-encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT).

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Every working configuration so far sits near 0.52-0.53 accuracy, with image-only ResNet50 single-profile slightly best (0.532, F1 0.516). The ViT-L run collapsed to 0.208, so ResNet50 is the safer image encoder. RNA has only been tested with PCA, and concat fusion with PCA RNA matched RNA-only almost exactly. That leaves open whether PCA is a weak RNA representation that holds back both RNA-only and multimodal models. RNA encoder choice affects most of the remaining search space (scVI and scGPT appear in about two-thirds of the untested configurations), yet it is entirely unexplored. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scVI (n=200) relative to the config_001 baseline, keeping RNA-only, single-profile, and no aggregation or fusion. This isolates the effect of RNA representation. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: A clear scVI gain would point to better multimodal follow-ups, such as config_028 or config_029 with scVI and ResNet50. Another result near 0.52 would suggest that RNA representation is not the bottleneck and shift priority toward fusion type (e.g., config_017 weighted) or transformer aggregation. This one-factor change reduces uncertainty on a high-leverage design axis more than further tuning of the already-mapped image or concat-fusion settings.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_006 kept the RNA-only, single-profile baseline from llm_summary_001 and made one change, replacing the PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder with scVI (n=200). Validation accuracy dropped to 0.427 (F1 0.417), about 9 points below PCA (0.519, F1 0.480) and the roughly 0.52-0.53 range of all other working configurations. This is several times larger than the roughly 1-point gaps seen so far, so it is unlikely to be noise alone, and it is an initial sign that this scVI setup is a weaker RNA representation than PCA here, which offers no support for the hypothesis that PCA is the bottleneck. It remains unclear whether the drop comes from scVI itself or from this particular setup (e.g., the much smaller latent size of 200 vs 2000 PCA components, scVI training or preprocessing choices), and scGPT is still untested. Multimodal follow-ups using scVI (e.g., config_028/029) therefore look less promising for now, and fusion type (e.g., weighted fusion) or aggregation choices may be the better next axes to test.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The working configurations cluster around 0.52-0.53 accuracy. Image-only ResNet50 is best (0.532, F1 0.516).
