Concat fusion of PCA and ResNet50 (config_016) matched RNA-only (0.520, F1 0.479) and fell slightly below image-only. That suggests either the modalities are not complementary, or naive concat lets the fused model lean on the weaker RNA features. Only one fusion method has been tried, so this is the main open question about multimodal value. 2) Test: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 (single-profile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, no aggregation) and changes only concat to weighted fusion. If weighted fusion reaches or exceeds image-only, the problem was how the modalities were combined. If it stays near 0.52, that is stronger evidence that the RNA signal adds little and that unimodal image refinements or other RNA encoders such as scGPT deserve priority. 3) Why now: It is a clean one-factor test of the fusion axis, built on the best-supported encoders. It avoids the failed ViT-L and the weaker scVI, and its result tells us whether the remaining multimodal configurations are worth budget.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_007 kept the multimodal concat configuration from llm_summary_003 (single-profile, PCA n=2000 RNA, ResNet50 image, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted. Validation accuracy fell to 0.435 (F1 0.423), about 8.5 points below concat (0.520, F1 0.479) and about 10 points below image-only ResNet50 (0.532, F1 0.516). That gap is much larger than the roughly 1-point differences seen among working configurations, and fusion was the only setting changed, so this weighted-fusion setup appears to perform worse than concat here and gives no support to the hypothesis that the way modalities were combined was what held fusion below image-only. It remains unclear whether the drop reflects weighted fusion itself or this particular implementation or optimization (e.g., weight initialization or learning, feature scale imbalance between PCA and ResNet50 features, training instability), and run-to-run variance is uncharacterized. Across two fusion methods, multimodal models have not beaten image-only, which weakly suggests that unimodal image refinements or untested RNA encoders such as scGPT deserve priority over further PCA+ResNet50 fusion variants.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: Among working setups, ResNet50 image-only single-profile is best (0.532 acc, 0.516 F1). PCA RNA-only (0.519) and PCA+ResNet50 concat (0.520) are close behind. scVI (0.427), weighted fusion (0.435) and ViT-L (0.208) all fell clearly short. scGPT is the only RNA encoder not yet tested, and many remaining multimodal configurations (040-051) depend on it. 2) Test: Swap PCA for scGPT in the RNA-only single-profile baseline (config_001), with everything else unchanged. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA representation beats PCA. That would show whether the RNA side is the bottleneck that kept fusion from beating image-only. 3) Why now: It resolves the largest remaining uncertainty on the encoder axis with a clean one-factor change. If scGPT beats PCA, scGPT+ResNet50 fusion and multiprofile follow-ups become worth testing. If it does not, those 12+ configurations can be deprioritized in favor of refining image-only models, such as transformer aggregation in config_012.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_008 kept the RNA-only, single-profile baseline from llm_summary_001 and made one change, replacing the PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder with scGPT. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.586 (F1 0.574), about 6.7 points above PCA (0.519, F1 0.480) and about 5.4 points above the previous best, image-only ResNet50 (0.532, F1 0.516), so it is now the best configuration tested. Because the encoder was the only setting changed, and the gain is several times larger than the roughly 1-point gaps seen among working configurations, this is an initial sign that scGPT gives a stronger RNA representation than PCA here, and it is consistent with the hypothesis that the RNA representation limited the earlier PCA-based fusion. That hypothesis is not yet tested, since run-to-run variance is uncharacterized, scGPT has been run only once, and it is unknown whether scGPT's advantage carries over to multimodal fusion with ResNet50 (concat or weighted) or to multiprofile settings, so scGPT+ResNet50 fusion and scGPT multiprofile follow-ups are now the most informative next experiments.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: scGPT RNA-only is the best result so far (0.586 acc, F1 0.574). It beats PCA (0.519) and image-only ResNet50 (0.532) by margins well above the roughly 1-point noise seen among working configurations. Concat fusion of PCA with ResNet50 (0.520) matched PCA RNA-only and did not beat image-only. Weighted fusion did clearly worse (0.435). It is still untested whether fusion failed because the PCA representation was weak. 2) This experiment keeps the previously tested single-profile, ResNet50, concat fusion setup and swaps only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT. Two comparisons follow: against config_016 it isolates the RNA encoder's effect inside fusion, and against scGPT RNA-only (config_007) it shows whether adding ResNet50 image features adds complementary signal on top of the strongest RNA representation. 3) It is the best use of the budget because it can produce a new best configuration and also answer the main open question, whether multimodality helps at all. It uses concat, the better-behaved fusion method, and avoids confounding the result with multiprofile or aggregation changes. Those changes have shown no benefit so far and can be tested afterwards with config_008/009.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_009 kept the single-profile concat fusion setup from llm_summary_003 (ResNet50 image encoder, no aggregation) and changed only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.507 (F1 0.455), about 7.9 points below scGPT RNA-only (0.586, F1 0.574) and also below image-only ResNet50 (0.532, F1 0.516). Against PCA+ResNet50 concat (0.520, F1 0.479), it was about 1.3 points lower, which is near the roughly 1-point noise seen among working configurations. Because adding ResNet50 features through concat was the only change from scGPT RNA-only, and the drop is far larger than that noise, this is an initial sign that this concat fusion degrades rather than complements the strongest RNA representation. It also shows that the stronger RNA encoder did not rescue fusion, so it gives no support to the hypothesis that weak PCA features caused the earlier fusion shortfall. It remains unclear whether the cause is concat fusion itself or this implementation or optimization (e.g., feature-scale or dimensionality imbalance between scGPT and ResNet50 features, lack of normalization, or training dynamics). Each configuration has also been run only once. Across three fusion runs, no multimodal model has beaten its best unimodal component, so scGPT RNA-only remains the best configuration, and diagnosing or normalizing the fusion pipeline may matter more than further encoder swaps within it.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: scGPT RNA-only single-profile (config_007) is the clear best so far, at 0.586 accuracy and 0.574 F1. Three fusion attempts have not beaten their best unimodal component. Multiprofile has been tested only once, on image-only ResNet50 with avgpool, where it gave a small drop (0.532 to 0.523) that is within likely noise. So it is still unknown whether multiprofile helps RNA models, and in particular the strongest RNA encoder. 2) What this tests: config_008 changes only the profile setting of the best configuration, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. This isolates the profile and aggregation effect on scGPT RNA and checks whether the earlier image-only avgpool result carries over to RNA. 3) Why now: it exploits the strongest finding (scGPT) with one logical extension and could raise the best score. It also resolves an important, under-tested design axis. Avgpool is the simplest baseline aggregation, so it should come before the learned transformer variant (config_009). A gain would justify testing transformer aggregation next. A loss would strengthen the case that single-profile scGPT is the configuration to refine.
experiment_summary: llm_summary_010 kept the best configuration, scGPT RNA-only single-profile (llm_summary_008: accuracy 0.586, F1 0.574), and changed only the profile setting, switching to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy was 0.579 (F1 0.563), about 0.6 points lower in accuracy and 1.1 points lower in F1. That gap is within the roughly 1-point noise seen among working configurations, so it does not show a real decline, and scGPT single-profile remains the nominal best. Together with the similarly small drop for image-only ResNet50 (0.532 to 0.523), this is an initial, weak sign that avgpool multiprofile aggregation does not help in either modality, though neither drop clearly exceeds noise. Multiprofile and avgpool were changed together, so their effects cannot be separated. Each configuration has been run only once, and it remains untested whether learned aggregation (e.g., a transformer) or multiprofile in multimodal settings would behave differently, so the multiprofile axis is not ruled out, but it currently offers no evidence of gains over single-profile scGPT.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-complexity baseline. It sets a reference accuracy and F1 that later comparisons can build on one factor at a time: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), profile setting and aggregation (avgpool, transformer), image-only performance, and the added value of multimodal fusion. 3) With a limited budget, a simple anchor makes every later experiment interpretable as a single-factor change. It also guards against assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models will win, so it is the most informative first experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model with a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.678, with a validation F1 of 0.646. Because no other experiments have been completed, this result is a reference point only. It does not show whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only models, or multimodal fusion would do better or worse. Later single-factor comparisons are needed to find which design choices matter, and run-to-run variability around this baseline is still unknown.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: only one result exists, the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (acc 0.678, F1 0.646). We know nothing yet about which design factors matter. 2. Test: config_002 changes a single factor, single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool), and keeps the PCA RNA encoder. This isolates whether pooling several profiles per sample helps accuracy and F1. 3. Why now: profile setting affects every model family (RNA-only, image-only and multimodal), so learning its effect early will shape how much of the remaining budget goes to multiprofile versus single-profile configurations. Avgpool is the cleanest first test before trying transformer aggregation. Testing encoder or modality would be equally clean, but the profile effect has the broadest bearing on the rest of the search.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only PCA (2000-component) setup from baseline llm_summary_001 and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with simple average pooling (no image encoder or fusion). Validation accuracy fell from 0.678 to 0.653 (about -0.025), and validation F1 fell from 0.646 to 0.628 (about -0.018). This suggests that average-pooled multiprofile input did not help this RNA-only PCA model and may have hurt it. However, this is a single pair of runs with unknown run-to-run variability, and the effect cannot be attributed to multiprofile input in general rather than to avgpool aggregation specifically. It also remains unknown whether learned aggregation (e.g., a transformer), other RNA encoders, or image-only and multimodal models would respond differently to multiprofile input.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only RNA-only PCA models have been tested. Single-profile (0.678 accuracy) did better than avgpool multiprofile (0.653). Nothing is known yet about the image modality, even though most of the remaining search space (image-only and the 36 multimodal configurations) depends on how useful image features are. 2. What this tests: An image-only, single-profile ResNet50 baseline measures how much signal images carry by themselves. It uses the simplest setting, with no aggregation or fusion, so it is directly comparable to the RNA-only single-profile baseline (config_001). 3. Why it is the best next experiment: The result decides how to spend the rest of the budget. If images are weak, the search should focus on RNA encoders and aggregation. If images are competitive or complementary, multimodal fusion becomes a priority. Follow-ups that refine RNA (such as transformer aggregation in config_003 or scVI in config_004) answer narrower questions and can come after this broader uncertainty is reduced.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 tested the first image-only baseline: a single-profile model with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.619 and a validation F1 of 0.610, about 0.059 accuracy and 0.036 F1 below the RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.678 / 0.646). This suggests images carry real but weaker standalone signal than RNA in this setup, though the comparison changes both modality and encoder (PCA vs. ResNet50), so the gap cannot be attributed to modality alone. It is still unknown whether image features are complementary to RNA in multimodal fusion, whether other image encoders or multiprofile aggregation would change the picture, and how large run-to-run variability is, given that each setting is a single run.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The RNA-only single-profile PCA baseline is the best so far (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). Average-pooled multiprofile input lowered RNA-only performance by about 0.025 accuracy. The image-only ResNet50 single-profile model is weaker (0.619 / 0.610) but carries real signal. The main open question is whether that image signal adds to RNA or is redundant with it. 2. Test: config_016 joins the two already-tested single-profile components (PCA RNA and ResNet50 image) with simple concat fusion. Both parent baselines are known, so any change can be attributed to adding the image modality, without confounding from a new encoder, aggregation or fusion method. 3. Why now: Multimodal configurations make up most of the search space, so whether images help on top of RNA is the most important design question to settle early. A gain would justify exploring fusion types, image encoders and aggregation. No gain would point the budget toward RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT) and learned aggregation instead.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 tested the first multimodal configuration. It combined the two known single-profile components, a PCA (2000-component) RNA encoder and a ResNet50 image encoder, with simple concat fusion and no aggregation, to see whether image signal adds to RNA. Validation accuracy was 0.224 and validation F1 was 0.184. That is far below both unimodal parents: RNA-only llm_summary_001 reached 0.678 / 0.646 and image-only llm_summary_003 reached 0.619 / 0.610. A collapse this large, to well below the weaker single modality, looks more like a failure of this particular run or setup (for example, feature-scale mismatch between PCA and ResNet50 embeddings, optimization instability, or an implementation or pipeline issue) than evidence that images are merely redundant with RNA. It should therefore not yet be read as showing that multimodal fusion or concat fusion inherently hurts. This is a single run with unknown variability, and the cause has not been diagnosed. Whether image features are complementary to RNA remains unresolved, so verifying or rerunning this configuration (or trying a normalized or alternative fusion) is advisable before using it to redirect the budget away from multimodal models.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA single-profile is the best so far (0.678 accuracy / 0.646 F1), and image-only ResNet50 trails it (0.619 / 0.610). The first multimodal run (config_016, PCA+ResNet50, concat) collapsed to 0.224 / 0.184, far below either unimodal parent. That pattern points to a fusion or setup failure, such as feature-scale mismatch, rather than to images being redundant. It is currently the largest unresolved question in the study. 2) What this tests: config_017 keeps everything from config_016 (single-profile, PCA, ResNet50) and changes only the fusion method from concat to weighted. If weighted fusion recovers to at least unimodal-level performance, the collapse was specific to concat fusion, and multimodal models remain viable. If it also collapses, the problem likely lies in combining these encoders or in the multimodal pipeline itself. 3) Why now: the multimodal configurations make up most of the remaining search space. Diagnosing this failure with a clean single-factor change tells us whether to keep investing budget in multimodal models or shift it toward RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT). That makes it more valuable than an incremental unimodal test.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 repeated the collapsed multimodal setup from llm_summary_004 (single-profile, PCA 2000-component RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, no aggregation) and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. Validation accuracy recovered from 0.224 to 0.635 and F1 from 0.184 to 0.618. That is above the image-only baseline (llm_summary_003: 0.619 / 0.610) but still below the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001: 0.678 / 0.646). In this single-factor comparison the concat collapse did not recur with weighted fusion, so multimodal models look viable, but adding images has not yet beaten RNA alone. Each setting is a single run with unknown variability, and the concat failure was never diagnosed (e.g., feature-scale mismatch, instability, or a pipeline bug), so the recovery cannot be firmly attributed to weighted fusion. It also remains open whether normalized concat, other fusion methods, other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or multiprofile input would let multimodal models exceed the RNA-only baseline.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile PCA (config_001, 0.678 acc / 0.646 F1) is the best result so far. Single-profile setups have beaten avgpool multiprofile. Multimodal models have not yet exceeded RNA alone (weighted fusion 0.635; concat collapsed). The RNA encoder, which drives the strongest modality, has never been varied, so it is the largest untested design choice for the current best direction. 2. What this tests: config_004 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200, in the RNA-only single-profile baseline. This isolates whether a learned latent representation beats PCA. 3. Why this is the best use of the budget: the answer feeds directly into which RNA encoder to carry into later multiprofile and multimodal runs, which is better than spending runs on fusion or aggregation variants built on a possibly suboptimal encoder. It is also a low-risk, interpretable comparison against a known reference. The scGPT single-profile run (config_007) is the natural follow-up to finish the encoder comparison.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the RNA-only single-profile setup of the best baseline (llm_summary_001) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA (2000 components) to scVI (200 latent dimensions), with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. Validation accuracy fell sharply from 0.678 to 0.435 (about -0.24) and F1 from 0.646 to 0.423, which also puts it below image-only ResNet50 (0.619) and weighted multimodal fusion (0.635). In this single-factor comparison, the scVI-200 configuration as run was much worse than PCA-2000, so PCA remains the reference RNA encoder for later runs. However, this is one run with unknown variability, and the drop cannot be attributed to learned latents in general. It may instead reflect this scVI setup, such as latent size, scVI training or convergence, input preprocessing, or a pipeline issue, so whether a better-tuned scVI or another encoder (e.g., scGPT, config_007) could match or beat PCA remains unresolved.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only PCA-2000 single-profile (config_001: 0.678 acc / 0.646 F1) is still the best run. scVI-200 did much worse (0.435). Whether the RNA encoder choice favors PCA in general, or only PCA over this scVI setup, is unresolved. The third encoder, scGPT, is untested. 2. What this tests: config_007 changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scGPT, keeping the best RNA-only single-profile setup. This completes the single-factor RNA encoder comparison and shows whether a pretrained foundation-model embedding can match or beat PCA. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: RNA is the strongest modality so far, and the RNA encoder choice applies to roughly a third of the remaining multimodal and multiprofile configurations (all scGPT variants). Settling it now lets later aggregation and fusion experiments build on the best RNA representation. If scGPT also falls short, PCA is confirmed as the RNA backbone and many scGPT configurations can be deprioritized. This experiment is cleaner and more decision-relevant than adding further multiprofile or multimodal factors at this stage.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the RNA-only single-profile setup of the best baseline (llm_summary_001) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA (2000 components) to scGPT embeddings, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. This completes the single-factor RNA encoder comparison. Validation accuracy was 0.537 and F1 was 0.518. That is well below PCA-2000 (0.678 / 0.646) and above scVI-200 (0.435 / 0.423), and it also trails image-only ResNet50 (0.619) and weighted multimodal fusion (0.635). In this comparison, both learned encoders as run fell short of PCA, so PCA remains the reference RNA backbone, and scGPT-based configurations look like reasonable candidates for deprioritization. However, each setting is a single run with unknown variability. The gap cannot be attributed to pretrained foundation-model embeddings in general, since it may reflect this scGPT setup (e.g., checkpoint, embedding extraction, preprocessing or gene-vocabulary matching, or the downstream head). It also remains untested whether scGPT would behave differently in multiprofile or multimodal settings.

selection_reason:
1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only single-profile PCA-2000 is still the best result (0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). Moving to multiprofile with avgpool (config_002) lowered accuracy to 0.653, but that comparison cannot tell whether multiprofile input itself hurts or only simple average pooling does. Learned transformer aggregation has not been tested at all, and it appears in about half of the remaining configurations.
2. What this tests: config_003 keeps everything from config_002 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA-2000) and changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates the aggregation effect on the strongest backbone. If transformer aggregation recovers or beats 0.678, multiprofile stays a live direction across unimodal and multimodal settings. If it also falls short, that is stronger evidence to focus the budget on single-profile models.
3. Why it is the best use of the budget: it resolves an open design question that affects many downstream configurations. It also has a realistic chance of exceeding the current best, since it builds on the strongest encoder. It is a cleaner and more broadly useful comparison than another encoder or fusion variant right now. The image-encoder question (ViT-L, config_013) is a good candidate for the following experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the RNA-only multiprofile PCA-2000 setup of llm_summary_002 and changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, to test whether learned aggregation could make multiprofile input competitive with the single-profile best (llm_summary_001: 0.678 acc / 0.646 F1). Validation accuracy collapsed to 0.227 and F1 to 0.191, far below both avgpool multiprofile (0.653 / 0.628) and every unimodal baseline. The result is strikingly close to the concat-fusion collapse in llm_summary_004 (0.224 / 0.184), so it looks more like a training or setup failure (e.g., optimization instability, lack of normalization or tuning for the transformer, degenerate predictions, or a pipeline issue) than evidence that transformer aggregation or multiprofile input is inherently harmful. This is a single undiagnosed run with unknown variability, so the multiprofile question is still open; avgpool remains the only working multiprofile aggregation, and the transformer configuration should be verified or rerun before the budget is moved away from transformer-aggregated configurations.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA encoders have now been compared head to head, and PCA-2000 is best as run (0.678). Multiprofile avgpool slightly underperformed single-profile. Both concat fusion and transformer aggregation collapsed to about 0.22, which looks like a setup failure rather than a verdict on those methods. Weighted multimodal fusion with ResNet50 (0.635) sits between image-only and RNA-only. The image encoder is the one major design factor not yet tested at all: ImageNet ViT-L has never been run, and ResNet50 image-only reached 0.619. 2. What this tests: config_013 is the clean single-factor counterpart to config_010. It changes only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ViT-L, in the simple single-profile image-only setting, which avoids the unstable fusion and aggregation components. This shows whether a stronger image representation raises standalone image signal enough to make images more useful to RNA. 3. Why it is the best next use: The result decides which image encoder to carry into later weighted-fusion multimodal runs (e.g., config_023 vs. config_017). Those runs are the most plausible route to beating the RNA-only baseline. Testing the encoder in isolation first avoids confounding it with fusion or aggregation, and roughly half of the remaining configurations depend on this choice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the image-only single-profile setup of llm_summary_003 and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, with no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion. Validation accuracy fell from 0.619 to 0.519 (about -0.10) and F1 from 0.610 to 0.480. That puts it below RNA-only PCA-2000 (0.678 / 0.646) and weighted multimodal fusion with ResNet50 (0.635 / 0.618), and it is also below scGPT RNA-only (0.537), though it does not show the ~0.22 collapse seen with concat fusion or transformer aggregation. In this single-factor comparison, ViT-L as run gave weaker standalone image signal than ResNet50, so ResNet50 is the better-supported image encoder to carry into later weighted-fusion multimodal runs (e.g., favoring the ResNet50 counterpart over ViT-L configurations such as config_023 vs. config_017). However, this is one run with unknown run-to-run variability, and the drop cannot be attributed to ViT architectures or larger pretrained image models in general. It may reflect this ViT-L setup (e.g., input resolution or preprocessing, feature extraction layer or pooling, embedding dimensionality, or downstream head tuning). Whether ViT-L features could still add complementary signal to RNA in weighted fusion remains untested.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile input has only been tested in the RNA modality. With PCA-2000, avgpool gave a small drop (0.678 to 0.653), and transformer aggregation collapsed to 0.227, which looks like a training failure. ResNet50 is the best image encoder so far (0.619 image-only), and weighted fusion with PCA reaches 0.635. That is still below RNA alone, so it is open whether any multiprofile or multimodal direction can beat the RNA baseline. Whether multiprofile aggregation helps or hurts depends on modality is untested. Image features may benefit from pooling over several profiles even if RNA PCA features do not. 2. What this tests: config_011 changes only the profile setting relative to config_010 (image-only ResNet50, single-profile to multiprofile avgpool). It uses avgpool because that aggregation has trained stably so far, and it avoids the collapse-prone transformer and concat components. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: It is a clean single-factor test of whether the multiprofile effect is modality-specific. That bears directly on the large untested block of multiprofile multimodal configurations, such as config_019 and config_021. If multiprofile helps images, config_019 becomes a well-motivated exploit. If it hurts again, multiprofile can reasonably be deprioritized across modalities, with the caveat that each comparison is a single run.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the image-only ResNet50 setup of llm_summary_003 and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. The goal was to test whether the multiprofile effect seen in RNA depends on modality. Validation accuracy fell from 0.619 to 0.485 (about -0.13) and F1 from 0.610 to 0.464. In the RNA-only PCA-2000 pair, the same change gave a much smaller drop (0.678 to 0.653, llm_summary_002), so avgpool multiprofile input did not help in either modality tested and was clearly harmful here. The result is well above the ~0.22 collapses seen with concat fusion and transformer aggregation, so it does not look like a training failure, and it weakens the motivation for multiprofile multimodal configurations such as config_019 and config_021. However, each comparison is a single run with unknown variability, and the effect cannot be separated from avgpool itself, since transformer aggregation has never trained stably. It also remains untested whether other aggregations, normalization, or multimodal weighted fusion would change how multiprofile input behaves.

selection_reason: 1. No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, RNA encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion strategy matters. 2. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest configuration and serves as a baseline. Later experiments can each change one choice against it: the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), the profile setting and aggregation (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer), and the modality (image-only, multimodal). 3. Starting with a simple, low-variance reference uses the limited budget well, because the gain from added complexity can then be measured directly rather than assumed.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 established the first baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile configuration using a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.3316 (primary) and validation F1 0.3150 (supporting). The similar F1 suggests performance is roughly even across classes rather than driven by a few, though this is tentative. No other experiments have been run, so it is unknown whether this level is good or poor for the task, or whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multiprofile aggregation, image-only, or multimodal fusion would do better. Future experiments that change one choice at a time against this baseline would be needed to attribute any gain to a specific design choice; with a single run, variance across seeds is also uncharacterized.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: there is only one result so far. RNA-only, single-profile PCA reached 0.332 accuracy and 0.315 F1. We do not yet know which design dimension drives performance. Most of the remaining space (36 of 50 configs) is multiprofile, so the value of multiprofile input is a large open question. 2. What this tests: config_002 changes only the profile setting, from single to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation. Encoder (PCA) and modality (RNA-only) stay fixed. This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps, using the simplest aggregator rather than a transformer, so any gain is not confounded with aggregator complexity. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: this one-factor comparison against the baseline directly informs whether to prioritize the multiprofile part of the space, including later transformer and multimodal variants. If it gives no gain, we can redirect budget toward encoder choice (scVI, scGPT) or image modality instead.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an RNA-only configuration with a PCA (n=2000) encoder, changing only the profile setting from single-profile to multiprofile with simple avgpool aggregation (no image encoder or fusion). It reached validation accuracy 0.5203 (primary) and F1 0.4982 (supporting), up from the single-profile baseline's 0.3316 / 0.3150. Because this is a one-factor change, the roughly 0.19 accuracy gain is attributable to multiprofile input with avgpool in this setting, and it supports prioritizing the multiprofile part of the space. It remains uncertain whether the gain holds across seeds (each configuration has only one run), whether it transfers to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image or multimodal settings, and whether more complex aggregators such as transformers would add further benefit over avgpool.

selection_reason: Evidence: multiprofile input with avgpool clearly beat single-profile for RNA-only PCA (0.520 vs 0.332 accuracy, with F1 following the same pattern). That makes multiprofile/avgpool the current anchor. Nothing yet tells us whether the image modality adds value, even though most of the remaining search space (36 of 49 configurations) is multimodal. Question: config_018 keeps the best configuration (PCA n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) fixed and adds only a ResNet50 image branch with the simplest fusion (concat). Comparing it with config_002 isolates whether adding image features improves on RNA alone. Why now: the answer decides whether the budget should go to the large multimodal region or to refining RNA-only choices such as encoder and aggregator. It is also a reasonable exploit, since it extends the strongest configuration so far. A single run should be read cautiously, but a clear gain or loss here will narrow the search more than tuning the aggregator or encoder first.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the best configuration so far fixed (PCA n2000 RNA encoder, multiprofile input, avgpool aggregation) and changed one thing: it added a ResNet50 image branch fused by simple concatenation, so it is a direct comparison with llm_summary_002. Validation accuracy was 0.5200 (primary), essentially identical to the RNA-only 0.5203, and validation F1 was somewhat lower (0.4791 vs 0.4982). This suggests that adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion gave no accuracy gain over RNA alone in this setting, and may slightly worsen class balance, though the F1 gap is small. It remains uncertain whether this holds across seeds (one run each), and whether the image modality could add value with other fusion methods, image encoders, aggregators, or RNA encoders. Concat alone should not be taken as evidence that the whole multimodal region lacks benefit.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Switching from single-profile to multiprofile input with avgpool gave the largest effect so far (0.332 to 0.520 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion gave no accuracy gain (0.520) and slightly lower F1 (0.479 vs 0.498). So the multiprofile setting is the clearest lever. How to aggregate across profiles is still untested. 2. Test: config_003 keeps the best configuration fixed (RNA-only, PCA n2000, multiprofile) and changes only the aggregator from avgpool to transformer. Any difference can then be attributed to aggregation alone. 3. Why now: This exploits the strongest finding with a clean one-factor comparison. Aggregation also applies across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal settings, so the result will guide many later choices. Other questions, such as RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) and whether images carry standalone signal, are left for later experiments.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best RNA-only setup fixed (PCA n2000 encoder, multiprofile input, no image branch or fusion) and changed only the aggregator from avgpool to a transformer, making it a direct one-factor comparison with llm_summary_002. Validation accuracy rose to 0.5729 (primary) from 0.5203, and validation F1 rose to 0.5730 from 0.4982. The F1 is now on par with accuracy, which tentatively suggests more even performance across classes. Within this configuration, the roughly 0.05 accuracy gain is attributable to transformer aggregation, making it the new best setting so far. It remains uncertain whether the gain holds across seeds (one run per configuration), and whether it transfers to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), to image-only settings, or to multimodal settings, where transformer aggregation might also change the null result seen with ResNet50 and concat fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Multiprofile input (+0.19 accuracy over single-profile) and transformer aggregation (+0.05 over avgpool) both helped clearly. The best result so far is config_003 (PCA n2000, multiprofile, transformer), at 0.573 accuracy and 0.573 F1. Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion gave no gain. Every run so far used the PCA n2000 RNA encoder, so the effect of the RNA representation is completely unknown. Since RNA appears to carry most of the signal, that choice may matter a lot. 2) What this tests: config_006 changes only the RNA encoder, from PCA n2000 to scVI n200, while keeping the best multiprofile and transformer setup. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the RNA representation. 3) Why this is the best next experiment: It exploits the strongest setup found so far while exploring an untested design factor that affects every downstream RNA-only and multimodal configuration. The result will show whether the remaining budget should focus on PCA or shift to a learned encoder before spending more runs on fusion or image variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best setup so far fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile input, transformer aggregation, no image branch or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder, from PCA n2000 to scVI n200. This makes it a direct one-factor comparison with llm_summary_004. Validation accuracy fell to 0.4348 (primary) from 0.5729, and validation F1 fell to 0.4234 (supporting) from 0.5730, which suggests that in this configuration the scVI n200 representation performs clearly worse than PCA n2000. PCA n2000 therefore remains the preferred RNA encoder for now. It remains uncertain whether the roughly 0.14 accuracy gap holds across seeds (one run each), whether it reflects scVI itself or its lower dimensionality or training setup (n200 vs n2000 is confounded within the encoder change), whether scVI would compare differently under avgpool, single-profile, or multimodal settings, and how other untested encoders such as scGPT would perform.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best setting so far is RNA-only, multiprofile, transformer aggregation with PCA n2000 (0.573 accuracy, 0.573 F1). Swapping in scVI n200 under the same setting dropped accuracy to 0.435. Multiprofile input and transformer aggregation each gave clear one-factor gains. Adding ResNet50 with concat fusion gave no accuracy gain under avgpool. scGPT is the only RNA encoder not yet tested, so the encoder question is still open. 2. Test: config_009 changes only the RNA encoder to scGPT in the best setting. This makes it a direct one-factor comparison with config_003 (PCA) and config_006 (scVI). It shows whether a pretrained foundation-model representation beats or matches PCA, and completes the encoder comparison under one fixed setup. 3. Why now: The RNA encoder sits upstream of every multimodal configuration, so it should be settled before spending budget on fusion and image variants. If scGPT wins, later multimodal tests should use scGPT rather than PCA. If it loses, PCA is confirmed as the RNA backbone and the multimodal transformer tests (e.g., config_020) can proceed with more confidence. Each configuration has only one run, so a modest difference should not be overinterpreted.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best setup so far fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile input, transformer aggregation, no image branch or fusion) and changed only the RNA encoder to scGPT, making it a direct one-factor comparison with llm_summary_004 (PCA n2000: 0.5729 accuracy / 0.5730 F1) and llm_summary_005 (scVI n200: 0.4348 / 0.4234). scGPT reached validation accuracy 0.5399 (primary) and F1 0.5245 (supporting). This places it between the other two encoders: about 0.03 accuracy below PCA, with a slightly larger F1 gap that hints at less even performance across classes. Under this setup the encoder comparison is now complete, and PCA n2000 remains the preferred RNA backbone for upcoming multimodal tests, but the modest scGPT–PCA gap rests on one run per configuration and may not hold across seeds. It is also uncertain whether the ranking depends on embedding dimensionality, scGPT's embedding or fine-tuning setup, or the aggregator, and whether scGPT would compare differently under avgpool or multimodal fusion settings.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The best result so far is config_003 (RNA-only, multiprofile, PCA n2000, transformer aggregation), at 0.573 accuracy and 0.573 F1. PCA beat scVI and scGPT under the same setup. The only multimodal test, config_018 with avgpool and concat, matched its RNA-only counterpart (0.520) and had slightly lower F1. So it is still unclear whether images add value once a stronger aggregator is used. 2. What this tests: config_020 adds a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the best setup. It is a one-factor comparison against config_003, isolating the effect of adding the image modality. It is also a one-factor comparison against config_018, isolating the effect of the aggregator in the multimodal setting. Together these show whether the transformer's gain carries over to multimodal inputs and whether it lets the image features contribute. 3. Why it is the best use of the budget: It exploits the strongest evidence so far (PCA plus transformer) while directly addressing the main open question, whether the multimodal region is worth exploring further. A gain would justify follow-ups on fusion type and image encoder. A null result would further support RNA-only models and save budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 added a ResNet50 image branch with concat fusion to the best setup so far (PCA n2000 RNA encoder, multiprofile input, transformer aggregation), making it a one-factor comparison with llm_summary_004 (same setup, RNA-only: 0.5729 accuracy / 0.5730 F1) for the effect of adding images, and with llm_summary_003 (same multimodal setup with avgpool: 0.5200 / 0.4791) for the effect of the aggregator. It reached validation accuracy 0.5070 (primary) and F1 0.4548 (supporting), about 0.066 accuracy below the RNA-only transformer and about 0.013 below the multimodal avgpool run, with a widened F1 gap that tentatively suggests less even performance across classes. Taken together with llm_summary_003, this suggests that ResNet50 features with concat fusion do not help, and may hurt, in this setting, and that the transformer's gain in the RNA-only case did not carry over to this multimodal configuration; this weakens the case for further multimodal exploration with concat and supports RNA-only PCA plus transformer as the current best. It remains uncertain whether these gaps hold across seeds (one run each), why the combination underperforms (for example, imbalance between the PCA and ResNet50 feature scales or dimensions, or optimization or overfitting effects, none of which are isolated here), and whether other fusion methods or image encoders could make the image modality useful.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: RNA-only with PCA n2000, multiprofile input and transformer aggregation is the clear best so far (0.573 accuracy / 0.573 F1). Both multimodal runs used ResNet50 with concat fusion. They matched or underperformed RNA-only (0.520 with avgpool, 0.507 with transformer), and their F1 scores were lower. A leading explanation is that naive concatenation lets the ResNet50 features dilute or unbalance the strong PCA signal. Fusion method is a major design axis that has not been tested at all. 2. What this tests: config_021 changes only concat to weighted fusion, keeping config_020's setup (PCA n2000, ResNet50, multiprofile, transformer). This isolates the fusion effect. If weighted fusion recovers or exceeds the RNA-only 0.573, the image modality can add value when weighted properly. If it still falls short, the case for dropping ResNet50-based multimodal models gets much stronger. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: it is a clean one-factor comparison on the strongest backbone. It addresses the main open question about multimodality and offers some chance of a new best. It is more decision-relevant than further RNA encoder or avgpool variants, which current evidence already ranks lower.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the multimodal setup of llm_summary_007 fixed (PCA n2000 RNA encoder, ResNet50 image encoder, multiprofile input, transformer aggregation) and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted, making it a direct one-factor test of fusion. Weighted fusion reached validation accuracy 0.5251 (primary) and F1 0.4979 (supporting), up from concat's 0.5070 / 0.4548. That is a modest accuracy gain (about 0.018) and a larger F1 gain (about 0.043), which tentatively suggests more even class performance, but it remains clearly below the RNA-only PCA plus transformer best (0.5729 / 0.5730) and only roughly matches the multimodal avgpool concat run (0.5200). So weighted fusion did not recover the RNA-only level, and the current evidence still gives no sign that ResNet50 image features add value. Uncertainty remains about whether the small concat-to-weighted gap holds across seeds (one run each), why the image branch still underperforms (e.g., feature quality, scale or dimension imbalance, optimization or overfitting, none isolated here), and whether other image encoders or fusion methods, such as attention-based fusion, would change this conclusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA n2000 with multiprofile transformer aggregation (0.5729 acc / 0.5730 F1). Every multimodal run used ResNet50, and all of them underperformed. Weighted fusion (config_021: 0.5251 / 0.4979) beat concat (config_020: 0.5070 / 0.4548), but it still fell short of RNA-only. The main untested question is whether the image encoder is the bottleneck, because ImageNet ViT-L has not been tried in any setting. 2) Test: config_027 keeps config_021 fixed (PCA n2000, multiprofile, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps only ResNet50 for ViT-L. This is a clean one-factor test of whether a stronger image representation lets the image modality add value. 3) Why now: It answers the largest remaining uncertainty in the multimodal region while staying in the best-performing setting for every other factor. It also has a realistic chance of matching or exceeding the RNA-only best. If it still trails RNA-only, that strengthens the case for dropping image-encoder and fusion exploration. An image-only run could be used later to diagnose image signal directly, but this experiment is more decision-relevant.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the llm_summary_008 setup fixed (multimodal, PCA n2000 RNA encoder, multiprofile input, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and changed only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L, making it a clean one-factor test of the image representation. It reached validation accuracy 0.7250 (primary) and F1 0.6847 (supporting), up from 0.5251 / 0.4979 with ResNet50. It also clearly exceeds the previous best, RNA-only PCA plus transformer (0.5729 / 0.5730), so it is the new best configuration and the first evidence that the image modality can add substantial value. This suggests the ResNet50 image encoder was a key bottleneck in earlier multimodal runs. The F1 now trails accuracy by about 0.04, which tentatively hints at less even performance across classes than the RNA-only best. It remains uncertain whether the roughly 0.20 gain holds across seeds (one run each), how much signal ViT-L carries on its own (no image-only run yet), whether concat fusion, avgpool aggregation, or other RNA encoders (e.g., scGPT) would also benefit with ViT-L, and whether other fusion methods could improve results further.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L in the multimodal setup (config_027: PCA n2000 + ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, weighted fusion) raised validation accuracy from 0.525 to 0.725, well above the RNA-only best of 0.573. We do not know how much of this comes from ViT-L features alone versus a real complementary gain from fusing them with RNA. No image-only run with ViT-L exists. 2) What this tests: config_015 is image-only ViT-L with multiprofile input and transformer aggregation. It matches config_027 except that the RNA branch and fusion are removed, so it is a clean one-factor ablation. If it approaches 0.725, the image representation drives performance and RNA adds little. If it falls clearly below, fusion is adding complementary signal and further work on fusion and RNA encoders with ViT-L is justified. 3) Why now: Tweaking fusion or aggregation around config_027 first would refine a configuration whose source of gain is unexplained. This ablation answers that question, which decides how the remaining budget should be split between image-only, fusion and RNA-encoder experiments.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 was an image-only ablation of the current best configuration (llm_summary_009: PCA n2000 + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion). It kept ViT-L, multiprofile input and transformer aggregation fixed and removed the RNA branch and fusion, to test whether ViT-L features alone explain that run's 0.7250 accuracy. It reached validation accuracy 0.5353 (primary) and F1 0.5187 (supporting), about 0.19 below the multimodal ViT-L run and also somewhat below the RNA-only PCA plus transformer run (0.5729 / 0.5730). Because neither modality alone approaches 0.725, this suggests the llm_summary_009 gain reflects complementary RNA–image signal combined through fusion rather than ViT-L features alone, which supports spending further budget on fusion and RNA-encoder variants paired with ViT-L. Several points remain uncertain: each configuration has one run, so seed variance is uncharacterized; the ablation removes the RNA branch and fusion together, so it cannot separate their contributions; no image-only ResNet50 run exists to show how much ViT-L improves image-only performance; and image-only results under other aggregators such as avgpool are untested.

selection_reason: 1. No experiments have been run yet, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest, lowest-variance configuration. It sets a reference point for validation accuracy and F1. Later runs can then each change one factor against it: scVI/scGPT encoders, image-only models, multiprofile aggregation, or multimodal fusion. 3. With a limited budget, a clean baseline is the most efficient first step because it makes every later comparison easier to interpret. It also avoids assuming that more complex multimodal or multiprofile models are better, and it reveals how much signal the standard RNA representation carries on its own.
experiment_summary: The first experiment (llm_summary_001) set a simple RNA-only, single-profile baseline using a PCA encoder with 2000 components and no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached validation accuracy 0.599 and validation F1 0.578, so a standard PCA RNA representation alone carries moderate predictive signal. The F1 being close to accuracy suggests performance is not driven by one dominant class, but no per-class breakdown is available to confirm this. No other configurations have been run, so it is still unknown whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), image-based models, multiprofile aggregation, or multimodal fusion would improve on this reference point; run-to-run variance is also uncharacterized.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (config_001), with accuracy 0.599 and F1 0.578. We have no evidence at all about the image modality, yet more than two-thirds of the remaining search space (image-only and multimodal configurations) depends on whether images carry useful signal. 2. What this tests: config_010 is an image-only, single-profile ResNet50 baseline. It keeps the simplest setting (single profile, no aggregation, no fusion) and swaps only the modality. Its result can be compared directly with config_001, showing whether images are weaker than, similar to, or stronger than RNA. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Knowing the standalone strength of each modality is the basic information needed to judge whether fusion experiments are worthwhile. It also tells us whether to explore further down the image branch (for example, ViT-L) or concentrate on RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. This narrows the largest uncertainty in the design space for the cost of a single run.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile baseline using a ResNet50 image encoder, with no RNA encoder, aggregation, or fusion, as a counterpart to the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached validation accuracy 0.227 and F1 0.191, far below the RNA PCA baseline (0.599 / 0.578). This is an initial observation that, in this single-profile setting, ResNet50 image features carry much weaker standalone signal than PCA RNA features, and the larger gap between F1 and accuracy hints that performance may be less even across classes, though no per-class breakdown is available. The comparison changes both modality and encoder at once, so it cannot separate weak image signal from a weak ResNet50 representation (ViT-L is untested); it is also unknown whether this is above chance (class count not given), whether images add complementary value in multiprofile aggregation or fusion, and how large run-to-run variance is.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The RNA-only PCA single-profile baseline (config_001) reached 0.599 accuracy and 0.578 F1. That is far above the ResNet50 image-only baseline (config_010) at 0.227 / 0.191, so RNA is currently the strongest single source of signal. It is still unknown whether multiprofile aggregation helps at all, which affects about two-thirds of the remaining search space. 2) Test: config_002 keeps the same RNA-only PCA setup and changes only the profile setting, to multiprofile with the simplest aggregator (avgpool). This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles improves on single-profile prediction, without changing the encoder or modality. 3) Why now: Profile setting is a high-leverage design choice, and testing it on the strongest pathway gives the cleanest read on its effect. If avgpool helps, transformer aggregation and multiprofile multimodal runs become natural next steps. If it does not, the budget can shift toward RNA encoder comparisons (scVI, scGPT) and single-profile fusion.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept the RNA-only PCA (2000 components) setup from llm_summary_001 and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.599 to 0.639 and F1 from 0.578 to 0.620. Because only one variable changed, this is a reasonably clean initial observation that simple multiprofile pooling helps the RNA pathway, and F1 stayed close to accuracy. However, the gain is about 4 points from a single run each, with run-to-run variance uncharacterized, so the gap may not be robust. It is also untested whether stronger aggregators (e.g., transformer), other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), or multiprofile image and multimodal settings would show the same benefit.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA with multiprofile avgpool (config_002: acc 0.639, F1 0.620). Multiprofile pooling beat single-profile RNA (0.599), though this rests on one run each. ResNet50 image-only features were much weaker (acc 0.227), so it is unclear whether images add any complementary signal or just add noise. 2) Test: config_018 keeps config_002 unchanged (PCA, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only ResNet50 image features with concat fusion. Comparing it with config_002 therefore isolates the marginal value of adding the image modality. 3) Why now: most of the remaining search space (36 of 48 configurations) is multimodal, so this result tells us whether that region is worth exploring or whether the budget should go to RNA encoders and aggregators instead. It is a one-variable change from the current best, so either outcome is informative. Concat is the simpler fusion baseline to test first.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: RNA PCA with 2000 components, multiprofile, avgpool; acc 0.639, F1 0.620) unchanged and added only ResNet50 image features via concat fusion. Validation accuracy fell to 0.535 and F1 to 0.519, below both llm_summary_003 and the single-profile RNA-only baseline (0.599). Because this was a one-variable change, it is a fairly clean initial observation that, in this setup, adding ResNet50 image features by simple concatenation hurt rather than helped, consistent with the weak image-only result (acc 0.227). Each configuration was run once with uncharacterized run-to-run variance, and the result covers only concat fusion with ResNet50, so it remains untested whether other fusion methods, a different image encoder (e.g., ViT-L), stronger aggregators, or feature scaling/balancing between modalities could recover complementary image signal; whether the large multimodal region of the search space deserves more budget therefore remains uncertain.

selection_reason: Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool (config_002, acc 0.639, F1 0.620). Multiprofile pooling gave a modest gain over single-profile. Image features look weak, both alone (0.227) and when added by concat fusion (0.535). The RNA encoder choice is still completely untested, yet it underlies the strongest pathway and most of the remaining search space. This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only PCA-2000 for scVI-200. That cleanly isolates the effect of the RNA representation. It is the best use of budget because the result directly sets which encoder to carry into later aggregation (transformer) and fusion (weighted) tests. It also has a realistic chance of beating the current best, so it balances exploitation with resolving a key design choice.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool; acc 0.639, F1 0.620) and swapped only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. Validation accuracy fell to 0.494 and F1 to 0.453, below llm_summary_003 and also below the single-profile PCA baseline (0.599). Because only the encoder changed, this is a fairly clean initial observation that, in this setup, scVI-200 embeddings underperformed PCA-2000, and the slightly wider F1-accuracy gap hints at less even per-class performance, though no per-class breakdown is available. Each configuration was run once with run-to-run variance uncharacterized. The result covers only one scVI variant (200 latent dimensions, no reported tuning or training details), so the comparison cannot separate the encoder family from its dimensionality or training quality. It also remains untested whether scVI behaves differently with other aggregators (e.g., transformer) or in fusion, and how other encoders such as scGPT would compare, so PCA-2000 remains the provisional default RNA encoder.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool (acc 0.639, F1 0.620). Moving from single-profile to multiprofile pooling gave about +4 points. Swapping in scVI-200 and adding ResNet50 concat fusion both hurt. Aggregation is the main untested design axis, since only avgpool has been tried. 2) Test: config_003 keeps the best configuration fixed and changes only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. This isolates whether learned attention-based aggregation pulls more signal from multiple profiles than simple averaging. 3) Why now: it is both an exploitation step and a clean one-variable comparison. The answer will guide aggregator choice across many remaining multiprofile configurations, including unimodal and multimodal ones. It is more informative per experiment than trying scGPT or new fusion variants, which build on less certain parts of the search space. The result is from a single run, so a small gap should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile) fixed and changed only the aggregator, from avgpool to transformer. Validation accuracy fell from 0.639 to 0.537 and F1 from 0.620 to 0.518. That is below the single-profile PCA baseline (0.599) and about equal to the ResNet50 concat-fusion result (0.535). Because only the aggregator changed, this is a fairly clean initial observation that, in this setup, transformer aggregation underperformed simple averaging, and F1 stayed close to accuracy. However, each configuration was run once with run-to-run variance uncharacterized. No transformer hyperparameters or training details (depth, heads, regularization, learning rate, profile count) are reported, so the result cannot separate an inherent weakness of attention-based aggregation from undertraining, overfitting, or poor tuning. Whether transformer aggregation would behave differently with other encoders, image inputs, or fusion is also untested, so avgpool remains the provisional default aggregator.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA is clearly the strongest modality. The best result so far is RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile with avgpool (acc 0.639, F1 0.620). Changing the encoder to scVI-200 (0.494) or the aggregator to transformer (0.537) each hurt, and adding ResNet50 features by concatenation also hurt (0.535). scGPT is the one RNA encoder not yet tested, and it is untested in every setting, so the representation question is still open. 2) Test: config_008 keeps the best configuration fixed and swaps only PCA-2000 for scGPT. This is a clean one-variable comparison that shows whether a foundation-model embedding beats or matches PCA. 3) Why now: RNA carries most of the signal, so the choice of RNA encoder affects every downstream multimodal configuration. Settling it first, at the cost of one run, tells us which encoder to use when we later test weighted fusion or ViT-L image features. It could also directly improve the best result.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best configuration so far (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool; acc 0.639, F1 0.620) fixed and swapped only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scGPT. Validation accuracy fell to 0.435 and F1 to 0.423. That is the lowest RNA result so far, below scVI-200 (0.494), the transformer aggregator (0.537), and the single-profile PCA baseline (0.599). Because only the encoder changed, this is a fairly clean initial observation that, in this setup, scGPT embeddings underperformed PCA-2000, and F1 stayed close to accuracy. Together with the scVI result, PCA-2000 remains the provisional default RNA encoder. However, each configuration was run once with run-to-run variance uncharacterized. No details are reported on how scGPT embeddings were extracted (frozen vs. fine-tuned, gene vocabulary overlap, preprocessing, embedding dimension), so the result cannot separate a limitation of foundation-model representations from a suboptimal integration. It is also untested whether scGPT would behave differently with other aggregators or in multimodal fusion.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: The best result so far is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool (config_002, acc 0.639, F1 0.620). Adding ResNet50 features by concat fusion under the same setup (config_018) dropped accuracy to 0.535. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.227). The alternatives tried for the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT) and the aggregator (transformer) all underperformed, so PCA-2000 with avgpool is a reasonable fixed backbone. The main open question is whether the multimodal region, which makes up most of the remaining space, is inherently unhelpful or was hurt by naive concatenation. Concat can let weak, high-dimensional image features swamp the RNA signal. 2) Test: config_019 keeps config_018 identical and changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. This cleanly isolates the effect of fusion. If weighted fusion recovers to near or above 0.639, the earlier drop was caused by concat, and multimodal ViT-L variants with weighted fusion are worth pursuing. If it stays well below config_002, that strengthens the case that ResNet50 image features add little. Budget would then shift to testing the image encoder (ViT-L) or to refining RNA-only models. 3) Why now: It is a one-variable comparison against an existing run, addresses the most consequential uncertainty about the large multimodal subspace, and has a plausible chance of beating the current best.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 kept the multimodal concat configuration (llm_summary_004: RNA PCA-2000 + ResNet50, multiprofile, avgpool; acc 0.535, F1 0.519) fixed and changed only the fusion method, from concat to weighted. Validation accuracy fell slightly to 0.512 and F1 to 0.477, well below the RNA-only best (llm_summary_003; acc 0.639, F1 0.620) and the single-profile RNA baseline (0.599). This is a fairly clean one-variable observation that weighted fusion did not recover the loss seen when ResNet50 features were added. Together with llm_summary_004 and the weak image-only result (0.227), it provisionally supports the view that ResNet50 image features add little or hurt in this setup, rather than the drop being specific to concatenation. The roughly 2-point concat-vs-weighted gap comes from single runs with uncharacterized variance and may not be meaningful. No weighting-scheme details are reported (learned vs. fixed weights, normalization), so the result cannot rule out poorly tuned fusion. It is also untested whether a stronger image encoder (e.g., ViT-L), other fusion methods, or modality balancing would make the multimodal region competitive, so RNA-only PCA-2000 with avgpool remains the provisional best.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: The best result is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool (acc 0.639). Adding ResNet50 images lowered accuracy with both concat (0.535) and weighted fusion (0.512), and image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.227). The other RNA encoders and the transformer aggregator also underperformed. The main open question is whether images are uninformative here, or whether ResNet50 is simply a poor image representation. ImageNet ViT-L, the only other image encoder, has not been tested, and roughly half the remaining search space depends on it. 2. Test: config_024 is config_018 with one change, swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L. It keeps the strongest RNA pathway (PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool) and the better-performing fusion (concat). This isolates the image-encoder effect within the fusion setting. The direct reference is config_018 (0.535), and the target to beat is the RNA-only best (0.639). 3. Why now: It is a clean one-variable comparison that also has a realistic chance of beating the current best. If ViT-L still falls clearly below 0.639, that is fairly strong evidence to deprioritize the large multimodal region and spend the remaining budget on the RNA side. If it closes the gap or beats 0.639, it justifies further ViT-L fusion experiments, such as weighted fusion or image-only ViT-L diagnostics.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 kept the multimodal concat configuration from llm_summary_004 (RNA PCA-2000, multiprofile, avgpool, concat fusion; acc 0.535, F1 0.519) fixed and changed only the image encoder, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy rose to 0.688 and F1 to 0.659. That is a new best, above the RNA-only best (llm_summary_003; acc 0.639, F1 0.620). Because only the image encoder changed relative to llm_summary_004, this is a fairly clean initial observation that the earlier multimodal losses were tied to the ResNet50 representation rather than to images being uninformative, and that ViT-L features add complementary signal to PCA RNA features under concat fusion. However, each configuration was run once with run-to-run variance uncharacterized, so the roughly 5-point gain over RNA-only may not be robust. Image-only ViT-L performance is unknown, as are ViT-L with weighted fusion, other aggregators, and other RNA encoders, so how much of the gain comes from ViT-L's standalone signal versus its complementarity with RNA is not yet established. This result justifies further exploration of the ViT-L multimodal region.

selection_reason: Evidence: switching the image encoder from ResNet50 to ViT-L, with concat fusion (config_024), produced a new best of 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1. This beats the RNA-only best of 0.639, so the ViT-L multimodal region is promising. Fusion was compared only with weak ResNet50 features. There, weighted fusion was slightly worse than concat (0.512 vs 0.535), a small single-run gap, and neither could help because the image signal was weak. Whether the fusion method matters once both modalities are informative is still untested. Test: config_025 keeps the best configuration fixed (PCA-2000, ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only concat to weighted. This cleanly isolates the fusion choice in the region that matters. Why now: it exploits the strongest direction with a one-variable change that could raise performance further. It also tells us whether fusion is a meaningful design lever or whether simple concat is enough. That shapes how remaining budget is spent, for example on transformer aggregation or image-only ViT-L controls.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 kept the best configuration (llm_summary_009: RNA PCA-2000 + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool; acc 0.688, F1 0.659) fixed and changed only the fusion method from concat to weighted. Validation accuracy was 0.678 and F1 0.646, slightly below concat but still above the RNA-only best (llm_summary_003; acc 0.639, F1 0.620). This is a fairly clean one-variable observation that weighted fusion gave no improvement over concat with informative ViT-L features, matching the small concat advantage seen with ResNet50 (0.535 vs 0.512). It also suggests the ViT-L multimodal gain held up under a second fusion method. The roughly 1-point gap comes from single runs with uncharacterized variance, so fusion choice may simply not matter much here. No weighting-scheme details are reported (learned vs. fixed weights, normalization), so poorly tuned fusion cannot be ruled out. Image-only ViT-L performance, other aggregators with ViT-L, and other fusion methods remain untested, so concat stays the provisional default.
